plain: When the accused person chooses his own punishment, the choice is not arbitrary; it must fit the crime. By choosing a penalty, the accused implies that he accepts the court’s decision and admits his guilt. Socrates refused to choose either a fine or exile, even though he had the option to pick one of these instead of the death penalty proposed by his accusers. He avoided choosing a lesser penalty because, according to Xenophon, the formal process of proposing a counter-penalty would have been an admission of guilt. However, guilt was no longer in question at that stage; only the type of punishment remained to be decided. While this refusal can be seen as a display of moral strength, it somewhat contradicts what Socrates later said in prison. There, he explained that he did not try to escape but stayed because it seemed better for both the Athenians and for him to obey the laws. If he had initially submitted to the process, it would have shown that he respected the Athenians’ verdict of guilt and acknowledged it himself. To be consistent, he should have chosen his own punishment, as this would have demonstrated that he submitted to both the laws and the specific judgment against him.
original: But when it was left to the accused to determine what his punishment should be, it might not be arbitrary, but must be in conformity with the crime, a money implied in the guilty persons constituting himself his own judge, that he submitted himself to the decision of the court and acknowledged himself to be guilty. Now Socrates declined to assign a punishment for himself consisting either of fine or banishment, and he had the choice between these and death, which his accusers proposed. He declined to choose the former punishment because he, according to Xenophon’s account, in the formality of the exchange-penalty (τὸ ὐποτιμᾶσθαι), as he said, would acknowledge guilt; but there was no longer any question as to the guilt, but only as to the kind of punishment. This silence may indeed be considered as moral greatness, but, on the other hand, it contradicts in some measure what Socrates says later on in prison, that he did not wish to flee, but remained there, because it seemed better to the Athenians and better to him to submit to the laws (Vol. I., p. 342). But the first submission would have meant that as the Athenians had found him guilty, he respected this decision, and acknowledged himself as guilty. Consistently he would thus have held it better to impose his punishment, since thereby he would not only have submitted himself to the laws, but also to the judgment.

plain: As a specific individual, the self is just the shape of the subject or of real, concrete action, and it recognizes this shape as such. Similarly, objective reality, or "being," is pure form without any self for this individual; because if that objective reality were truly known, it would cease to be unknown, yet this knowledge recognizes that knowledge itself is the fundamental fact. Absolute freedom has thereby balanced and resolved the conflict between the universal will and the particular will with its own nature. The mindset of self-alienation, pushed to the limit of its conflict where pure will and the agent of that will remain separate, turns that conflict into a clear, transparent form and discovers itself within it. The ethical structure of the community reached its completion and truth in the form of spirit that exists in isolation and separation within it: the individual self. However, this legal person finds its substance and fulfillment outside that ethical order. The development of culture and belief eliminates this abstraction of a mere person. By completing the process of separation and reaching the extreme of abstraction, the self of spirit finds that substance first becoming the universal will, and ultimately becoming its own possession. Here, knowledge finally appears to be completely aligned with the truth it seeks, because its truth is this knowledge itself.
original: Furthermore, qua particular self it is merely the form of the subject or concrete real action, a form which by it is known as form. In the same way objective reality, " being," is for it absolutely self-less form; for that objective' reahty would be what is not known: this knowledge, however, knows knowledge to be the essential fact. Absolute freedom has thus squared and balanced the opposition of universal and particular will with its own nature. The self-ahenated type of mind, driven to the acme of its opposition, where pure vohtion and the purely volitional agent are still kept distinct, reduces that opposition to a transparent form, and therein finds itself. Morality The ethical order of the community found its consummation and its truth in the type of spirit existing in mere solitude and separation within it — the individual self. This legal person, however, has its substance and its fulfilment outside that ethical order. The process of the world of culture and belief does away with this abstraction of a mere person; and by the completion of the process of estrangement, by reaching the extremity of abstraction, the self of spirit finds the substance become first the universal will, and finally its own possession. Here, then, knowledge seems at last to have become entirely at one with the truth at which it aims; for its truth is this knowledge itself.

plain: However, the interdependence of these two concepts, which gives them their true and concrete meaning, must be extracted from the obscurity and confusion that persisted even in Kant’s *Metaphysical Foundations of Natural Science*. In modern times, the significance of atomic theory is more apparent in political science than in physics. According to this view, the will of individuals stands as the creative force behind the State. The attractive force consists of the specific desires and inclinations of individuals, while the Universal, or the State itself, is merely the external connection formed by a contract. First, atomic philosophy represents a crucial stage in the historical development of the Idea. The principle of this system can be described as self-being in the form of multiplicity. Currently, natural scientists who wish to avoid metaphysics listen favorably to atomism. Yet, one cannot escape metaphysics and stop analyzing nature through conceptual terms by simply embracing atomism. In reality, the atom is itself a concept. Therefore, the theory that matter consists of atoms is a metaphysical theory. It is true that Newton explicitly warned physicists to beware of metaphysics. However, to his credit, he did not strictly follow his own warning.
original: But the mutual implication of the two, which makes what is true and concrete in them, would have to be wrested from the obscurity and confusion in which they were left even in Kant's Metaphysical Rudiments of Natural Science.--In modern times the importance of the atomic theory is even more evident in political than in physical science. According to it, the will of individuals as such is the creative principle of the State: the attracting force is the special wants and inclinations of individuals; and the Universal, or the State itself, is the external nexus of a compact. (1) The Atomic philosophy forms a vital stage in the historical evolution of the Idea. The principle of that system may be described as Being-for-self in the shape of the Many. At present, students of nature who are anxious to avoid metaphysics turn a favourable ear to Atomism. But it is not possible to escape metaphysics and cease to trace nature back to terms of thought, by throwing ourselves into the arms of Atomism. The atom, in fact, is itself a thought; and hence the theory which holds matter to consist of atoms is a metaphysical theory. Newton gave physics an express warning to beware of metaphysics, it is true; but, to his honour be it said, he did not by any means obey his own warning.

plain: Stated in general terms, this is how Philosophy relates to Scepticism. The Idea, when viewed as a pure abstraction, is still and inactive. It only truly exists when it recognizes itself as alive. This happens because the Idea is inherently dialectical; it must overcome its own stillness and transform itself. However, if the philosophical Idea is inherently dialectical, this is not accidental. Scepticism, by contrast, applies dialectics accidentally. As material presents itself, Scepticism reveals that the material is inherently negative. We must also distinguish between older and modern Scepticism. We are only concerned with the older form, because it alone has a true, deep nature. Modern Scepticism is more similar to Epicureanism. Recently, Schulze of Göttingen has boasted about his Scepticism. He wrote a book titled “Ænesidemus” to compare himself with that ancient sceptic. In other works, he also used Scepticism to oppose Leibniz and Kant. Nevertheless, Schulze completely ignores the true nature of Scepticism as described above. Instead of showing the real difference between his Scepticism and the ancient kind, Schulze recognizes only Dogmatism and Scepticism, and fails to see the third option of Philosophy at all.
original: This, put quite abstractly, is the relation of Philosophy to Scepticism. The Idea, as abstract Idea, is the quiescent and inert; it only is in truth in as far as it grasps itself as living. This occurs because it is implicitly dialectic, in order to abrogate that inert quiescence, and to change itself. But if the philosophic Idea is thus implicitly dialectic, it is not so in a contingent manner. Scepticism, on the contrary, exercises its dialectic contingently, for just as the material comes up before it, it shows in the same that implicitly it is negative. The older Scepticism must further be distinguished from the modern, and it is only with the former that we have to do, for it alone is of a true, profound nature; the modern more resembles Epicureanism. Thus Schulze of Göttingen has in recent times boasted of his Scepticism; he wrote an “Ænesidemus” in order thus to compare himself with that sceptic; and in other works, too, he put forward Scepticism in opposition to Leibnitz and to Kant. Nevertheless, he ignores entirely the true position of Scepticism as it has just been described, and instead of representing the true distinction which exists between his Scepticism and the ancient, Schulze recognizes nothing but Dogmatism and Scepticism, and not the third philosophy at all.

plain: Just as an action’s external reality involves accidental outcomes, its inner reality includes an uncertain element that depends on the strength of one’s self-awareness and wisdom. However, we only need to account for this uncertainty in cases of severe mental deficiency, insanity, or childhood. These are the only mental states that override thinking and free will, allowing us to view an agent in a way that does not respect their dignity as a free and rational being. Generally, the universal quality of an action is the reduction of its diverse content to the simple form of universality. Yet, the subject who turns inward is particular, standing in contrast to the particulars of the objective world. The subject possesses their own particular content within their goal, which forms the essential core of their act. (Carrying out this specific content of the act embodies the subject’s freedom in its concrete form.) This represents the subject’s right to find satisfaction in the act.
original: Just as actions on the side of their external reality include accidental results, so also the subjective reality contains an indeterminate element, which depends upon the strength of self-consciousness and prudence. But this uncertain element needs to be reckoned with only in the case of imbecility, lunacy, or childhood. These are the only conditions of mind which supersede thought and free will, and permit us to take an agent otherwise than in accordance with his dignity as free and rational. The universal quality of action is in general the manifold content reduced to the simple form of universality. But the subject turned back into himself is particular, in opposition to the particulars of the objective world. He has in his end his own particular content, which constitutes the essential soul of his act. (In the execution of this particular content of the act consists his subjective freedom in its concrete character.) This is the subject's right to find in the act his satisfaction.

plain: Stoicism, Epicureanism, and Scepticism are three essential principles. The first principle is thought, or the idea of universality, though it is defined within itself. In this view, abstract thought serves as the standard for judging truth. The second principle opposes thought; it is the specific, concrete reality, representing individuality, feeling, and sensory observation. These two principles form the basis of Stoic and Epicurean philosophy. Both are one-sided and function as sciences of the understanding precisely because thought here is abstract rather than concrete. Since thought is not concrete, specific details fall outside of it and must become an independent principle, as they have an absolute claim against abstract thought. The third principle is Scepticism, which negates the first two one-sided philosophies, and this negation must be acknowledged. Scepticism actively rejects all standards of judgment and all specific principles, whether they come from the senses, from reflecting on common ideas, or from thought itself. Consequently, the result is that nothing can be known. However, the shared goal and common ground of all these philosophies is a calm, uniform state of mind that is unaffected by anything, suffering from nothing, and free from the influence of pleasure, pain, or any other constraint.
original: The three principles of Stoicism, Epicureanism and Scepticism are necessary; in the first there is the principle of thought or of universality itself, but yet determined in itself; the abstract thought is here the determining criterion of the truth. There is opposed to thought, in the second place, the determinate as such, the principle of individuality, feeling generally, sensuous perception and observation. These two form the principles of the Stoic and Epicurean philosophies. Both principles are one-sided and, as positive, become sciences of the understanding; just because this thought is not in itself concrete but abstract, the determinateness falls outside of thought and must be made a principle for itself; for it has an absolute right as against abstract thought. Besides Stoicism and Epicureanism, there is, in the third place, Scepticism, the negation of these two one-sided philosophies which must be recognized as such. The principle of Scepticism is thus the active negation of every criterion, of all determinate principles of whatever kind they be, whether knowledge derived from the senses, or from reflection on ordinary conceptions, or from thought. Thus the next result arrived at is that nothing can be known. Yet the imperturbability and uniformity of mind in itself, which suffers through nothing, and which is affected neither by enjoyment, pain, nor any other bond, is the common standpoint and the common end of all these philosophies.

plain: She claims that the power of youth is what truly matters everywhere; she treats this as the most important thing. She praises a son as the ruler of the mother who gave birth to him. She views a brother as the man who allows a sister to see an equal. She sees a young man as the one who, by freeing a daughter from her reliance on the family, gives her the happiness and dignity of being a wife. However, the community can only survive by crushing this individual spirit. Yet, because this individual spirit is a necessary part, the community also creates it. It creates this spirit by adopting the very stance of trying to crush it as a hostile force. Still, because this hostile element has cut itself off from the universal goal, it is simply evil and has no real value on its own. It would be completely powerless if the community did not recognize the power of youth—meaning manhood, which is still immature and remains in a state of individual distinction—as the power of the whole.
original: She asserts that it is everywhere the force of youth that really counts; she upholds this as of primary significance; extols a son as one who is the lord and master of the mother who has borne him; a brother, as one in whom the sister finds man on a level with herself; a youth as one through whom the daughter, deprived of her dependence (on the family unity), acquires the satisfaction and the dignity of wifehood. The community, however, can preserve itself only by suppressing this spirit of individualism; and because the latter is an essential element, the community like- wise creates it as well, and creates it, too, by taking up the attitude of seeking to suppress it as a hostile principle. Nevertheless, since, by cutting itself off from the universal purpose, this hostile element is merely evil, and in itself of no account, it would be quite ineffective if the community did not recognise the force of youth, (manhood, which, while immature, still remains in the condition of particularity), as the force of the whole.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The End of Art
plain: So its goal is to wake up and energize sleeping feelings, urges, and passions. It aims to fill the heart, forcing any person, educated or not, to feel the full range of what a human soul can experience and create in its deepest, hidden parts. It wants to stir everything that can move a person’s inner self in all its many forms. It seeks to make emotion and perception enjoy everything real and high in the mind’s thoughts and ideas— all the glory of what is noble, eternal, and true. It must also make suffering, misery, evil, and crime understandable. It should help people grasp the deepest nature of everything shocking and horrible, as well as all pleasure and joy. Finally, it should let imagination wander through idle fantasies and indulge in the attractive power of sensory visions. It is argued that art must include this endlessly varied content. It does this partly to complete the natural experience that makes up our outer life, and partly to trigger our passions. This is so that life’s experiences do not leave us cold, and because we want to be open to welcoming all kinds of phenomena.
original: Its aim is therefore placed in arousing and animating the slumbering emotions, inclinations, and passions; in filling the heart, in forcing the human being, whether cultured or uncultured, to feel the whole range of what man's soul in its inmost and secret corners has power to experience and to create, and all that is able to move and to stir the human breast in its depths and in its manifold aspects and possibilities; to present as a delight to emotion and to perception all that the mind possesses of real and lofty in its thought and in the Idea--all the splendour of the noble, the eternal, and the true; and no less to make intelligible misfortune and misery, wickedness and crime; to make men realize the inmost nature of all that is shocking and horrible, as also of all pleasure and delight; and, finally, to set imagination roving in idle toyings of fancy, and luxuriating in the seductive spells of sense-stimulating visions. This endlessly varied content, it is held, art is bound to embrace, partly in order to complete the natural experience in which our external existence consists, and partly with the general aim of provoking the passions of our nature, both in order that the experiences of life may not leave us unmoved, and because we desire to attain to a receptivity that welcomes all phenomena.

plain: The soul is not a separate, non-physical thing. Wherever nature exists, the soul is its universal non-physical nature, its simple “ideal” life. The soul is the underlying substance or “absolute” foundation for all the specific and individual forms of mind. It is within the soul that mind finds the raw material for developing its character, and the soul remains the consistent, underlying ideal aspect of all of it. However, because it is still viewed in this abstract way, the soul is merely the sleeping state of mind—Aristotle’s passive intellect, which has the potential to be everything. The question of whether the soul is non-physical is only interesting if, on one side, we view matter as truly real and conceive of mind as a distinct object, and on the other side, we do the opposite. But in modern times, even physicists have found that matter becomes less substantial in their hands. They have discovered weightless forms of matter, such as heat and light, to which they might also add space and time. These “weightless” forms, which have lost the property of gravity that is unique to matter and, in a way, even the ability to resist, still have a perceptible existence and a distinct separation of parts. In contrast, “vital” matter, which is also often listed among these weightless forms, not only lacks gravity but also lacks every other characteristic of existence that would lead us to treat it as material.
original: The soul is no separate immaterial entity. Wherever there is Nature, the soul is its universal immaterialism, its simple “ideal” life. Soul is the substance or “absolute” basis of all the particularising and individualising of mind: it is in the soul that mind finds the material on which its character is wrought, and the soul remains the pervading, identical ideality of it all. But as it is still conceived thus abstractly, the soul is only the sleep of mind—the passive νοῦς of Aristotle, which is potentially all things. The question of the immateriality of the soul has no interest, except where, on the one hand, matter is regarded as something true, and mind conceived as a thing, on the other. But in modern times even the physicists have found matters grow thinner in their hands: they have come upon imponderable matters, like heat, light, &c., to which they might perhaps add space and time. These “imponderables,” which have lost the property (peculiar to matter) of gravity and, in a sense, even the capacity of offering resistance, have still, however, a sensible existence and outness of part to part; whereas the “vital” matter, which may also be found enumerated among them, not merely lacks gravity, but even every other aspect of existence which might lead us to treat it as material.

plain: Sometimes the answer differs significantly from what the questioner intended, whereas in written dialogue, the author has complete control over the answers. However, claiming that people in real life actually respond the way they are depicted here is a different matter. Socrates might call his interlocutors flexible young men because they answer the questions directly. These questions are crafted to make answering easy and to prevent any originality in the response. In the Socratic method shown by Plato and Xenophon, the responder respects the specific relationship established by the questioner. Critics object that in real life, we do not answer within that same relationship. Instead, we often introduce a different perspective. This approach certainly captures the spirit of a lively conversation, but such competitive spirit is excluded from the Socratic method, which focuses primarily on staying on topic. The attitude of dogmatism, self-assertion, stopping when difficulties arise, and escaping those difficulties through jokes or dismissal are all excluded here. These behaviors are not considered good manners and have no place in Socrates’ dialogues.
original: For the answer seems occasionally to be quite different from what was intended by the question, while in printed dialogue, answers are altogether under the author’s control; but to say that in actual life people are found to answer as they are here made to do, is quite another thing. To Socrates those who reply may be called pliable youths, because they reply directly to the questions, which are so formed that they make the answer very easy, and exclude any originality in reply. To this plastic manner, which we see in the method of Socrates, as represented by Plato and Xenophon, it is objected that we do not answer in the same relation in which the questioner asks; while, with Socrates, the relation which the questioner adopts is respected in the reply. The other way, which is to bring forward another point of view, is undoubtedly the spirit of an animated conversation, but such emulation is excluded from this Socratic method, in which the principal matter is to keep to the point. The spirit of dogmatism, self-assertion, stopping short when we seem to get into difficulties, and escaping from them by a jest, or by setting them aside—all these attitudes and methods are here excluded; they do not constitute good manners, nor do they have a place in Socrates’ dialogues.

plain: This liberty, which defines the substance and goal of freedom, remains merely a concept. It is a principle of the mind and spirit, meant to evolve into an objective reality, encompassing legal, ethical, religious, and equally scientific facts. The Objective Mind represents the absolute Idea, yet it exists only in potential. Because it resides within the realm of limitation, its actual rationality keeps the appearance of external show. The free will immediately faces distinctions arising from the fact that freedom is its internal function and purpose, while it relates to an external, pre-existing objectivity. This objectivity divides into three categories: anthropological data (meaning private and personal needs), external natural things that exist for consciousness, and the relational bonds between individual wills that recognize their own diversity and specific character. These aspects form the external material for the will’s embodiment.
original: But this freedom, which the content and aim of freedom has, is itself only a notion—a principle of the mind and heart, intended to develope into an objective phase, into legal, moral, religious, and not less into scientific actuality. The objective Mind is the absolute Idea, but only existing in posse: and as it is thus on the territory of finitude, its actual rationality retains the aspect of external apparency. The free will finds itself immediately confronted by differences which arise from the circumstance that freedom is its inward function and aim, and is in relation to an external and already subsisting objectivity, which splits up into different heads: viz. anthropological data (i.e. private and personal needs), external things of nature which exist for consciousness, and the ties of relation between individual wills which are conscious of their own diversity and particularity. These aspects constitute the external material for the embodiment of the will.

plain: Gregory planned two major steps to free the Church from reliance on and vulnerability to worldly force. Yet he pressed the secular rulers for more. A bishop’s new appointment would become valid simply through his consecration by his church superior, and the Pope would hold sole authority over the extensive assets of the religious community. Claiming status as a power established by God, the Church asserted dominance over worldly rule, basing this claim on the general idea that the Divine ranks above the Secular. The Emperor, during his crowning—a rite only the Pope could conduct—had to swear an oath to remain always obedient to the Pope and the Church. Entire nations and realms, including Naples, Portugal, England, and Ireland, entered into a formal relationship of vassalage with the Papal seat. In this manner, the Church secured an independent standing: Bishops called together synods in different lands, and within these gatherings the clergy discovered a lasting hub for unity and backing. Through this process, the Church gained the most powerful role in worldly matters. It claimed the right to grant royal crowns and took on the role of mediator between ruling powers during times of conflict and peace. The specific circumstances that especially aided such Church interventions were the marriages of princes.
original: These were the two grand measures by which Gregory purposed to emancipate the Church from its condition of dependence and exposure to secular violence. But Gregory made still further demands on the secular power. The transference of benefices to a new incumbent was to receive validity simply in virtue of his ordination by his ecclesiastical superior, and the Pope was to have exclusive control over the vast property of the ecclesiastical community. The Church as a divinely constituted power, laid claim to supremacy over secular authority, — founding that claim on the abstract principle that the Divine is superior to the Secular. The Emperor at his coronation — a ceremony which only the Pope could perform — was obliged to promise upon oath that he would always be obedient to the Pope and the Church. "Whole countries and states, such as Naples, Portugal, England and Ireland came into a formal relation of vassalage to the Papal chair. Thus the Church attained an independent position: the Bishops convoked synods in the various countries, and in these convocations the clergy found a permanent centre of unity and support. In this way the Church attained the most influential position in secular affairs. It arrogated to itself the award of princely crowns, and assumed the part of mediator between sovereign powers in war and peace. The contingencies which particularly favoured such interventions on the part of the Church were the marriages of princes.

plain: The connection between the external and the internal combines the two previous relationships while simultaneously suspending simple relativity and general phenomenality. However, as long as the understanding holds the internal and external as strictly separate, they remain empty forms, with each being just as void as the other. In examining both the natural world and the spiritual realm, it is crucial to correctly assess this internal-external dynamic, specifically by rejecting the error that views the internal as the sole essential core while dismissing the external as insignificant. This error appears when people frequently reduce the distinction between nature and mind to the abstract gap between the inner and the outer. Regarding nature, it certainly exists in the crude external, not just relative to the mind, but intrinsically. Yet, describing it as external "in the gross" does not suggest an abstract externality, since no such thing exists. Instead, it indicates that the Idea, which serves as the shared content of nature and mind, appears in nature solely as external, and consequently, solely as internal. The abstract understanding, relying on its "either-or" logic, might resist this view of nature. Nevertheless, this view is clearly evident in our other forms of awareness, especially within religion.
original: The relation of Outward and Inward unites the two relations that precede, and at the same time sets in abeyance mere relativity and phenomenality in general. Yet so long as understanding keeps the Inward and Outward fixed in their separation, they are empty forms, the one as null as the other. Not only in the study of nature, but also of the spiritual world, much depends on a just appreciation of the relation of inward and outward, and especially on avoiding the misconception that the former only is the essential point on which everything turns, while the latter is unessential and trivial. We find this mistake made when, as is often done, the difference between nature and mind is traced back to the abstract difference between inner and outer. As for nature, it certainly is in the gross external, not merely to the mind, but even on its own part. But to call it external 'in the gross' is not to imply an abstract externality--for there is no such thing. It means rather that the Idea which forms the common content of nature and mind, is found in nature as outward only, and for that very reason only inward. The abstract understanding, with its 'Either--or,' may struggle against this conception of nature. It is none the less obviously found in our other modes of consciousness, particularly in religion.

plain: Political science, which begins here, must uncover the rules that guide how large groups of people move within the complex web of their qualitative and quantitative connections. This field emerged from the conditions of the modern era. Its growth shows an intriguing process where thought (see Smith, Say, Ricardo) scrutinizes the endless variety of specific details before it and reveals their simple, active, and regulating principles. These principles reside in the understanding. Just as the principle of reconciliation requires acknowledging the external presence or appearance in the realm of need, where reason is active within the object; so, in the exact opposite way, this is also the domain where the understanding, with its subjective goals and moral views, unleashes its dissatisfaction and moral irritation. It is entirely a matter of chance how such universal needs, like those for food, drink, and clothing, get met. The land is more fertile in some locations than others; harvests vary from year to year; one person is hardworking, while another is idle. Yet this swarm of arbitrary factors generates universal characteristics, and what seems like pure abstraction and a lack of thought becomes tied to a necessity that arises on its own. Finding this element of necessity is the goal of political science, a discipline that honors thought because it identifies laws within a heap of accidents.
original: It is the task of political science, which originates at this point, to detect the laws governing the movement of the masses in the intricacy of their qualitative and quantitative relations. This science has sprung from the soil of modern times. Its development reveals the interesting process by which thought (see Smith, Say, Eicardo) examines the infinite multitude of particulars lying before it, and exposes their simple, active, regulating principles. These principles belong to the understanding. As on the one side the principle of reconciliation involves a recognition of the external presence or appearance in the sphere of want of the reason which is active in the object; so, on the exact contrary, is this also the sphere in which the understanding with its subjective aims and moral opinions lets loose its discontent and moral vexation. It depends altogether on accident how such universal wants, as those of food, drink, and clothing, are to be satisfied. The soil is more fertile in one place than another; years differ in their yield; one man is diligent, while another is lazy. But this swann of arbitrary things begets universal features, and what appears to be pure abstraction and absence of thought becomes bound by a necessity, which enters of itself. To discover the element of necessity is the object of political science, a science which does honour to thought, because it finds laws in a mass of accidents.

plain: These metaphysical arguments for God’s existence fail because they do not clearly state the negative aspects involved when the mind rises from the world to God. If the world is merely a collection of events, it is also temporary and merely an appearance, possessing no actual existence or potential. The mind’s ascent indicates that the world’s existence is only a semblance, lacking real being or absolute truth. It shows that truth resides in God, beyond and above that appearance, making true being synonymous with God. While this ascent might look like a transition using a medium, it remains equally true that all signs of transition and medium are erased. The world, which could seem like the tool for reaching God, is defined as nothing. If the world’s existence is not negated, the foundation for the mind’s ascent disappears. Consequently, the apparent tool disappears, and the process of deriving God is undone by the very action that carries it out.
original: And it is because they do not, with sufficient prominence, express the negative features implied in the exaltation of the mind from the world to God, that the metaphysical proofs of the being of a God are defective interpretations and descriptions of the process. If the world is only a sum of incidents, it follows that it is also deciduous and phenomenal, in esse and posse null. That upward spring of the mind signifies, that the being which the world has is only a semblance, no real being, no absolute truth; it signifies that, beyond and above that appearance, truth abides in God, so that true being is another name for God. The process of exaltation might thus appear to be transition and to involve a means, but it is not a whit less true, that every trace of transition and means is absorbed; since the world, which might have seemed to be the means of reaching God, is explained to be a nullity. Unless the being of the world is nullified, the point d'appui for the exaltation is lost. In this way the apparent means vanishes, and the process of derivation is cancelled in the very act by which it proceeds.

plain: Our understanding would face a serious problem if concepts like freedom, law, ethics, or even the divine were considered inaccessible to precise knowledge simply because they cannot be weighed, counted, or reduced to mathematical equations. In that scenario, we would be forced to accept only a blurry, generalized picture of these concepts, leaving their specific details up to individual whim and personal interpretation. The harmful practical effects of adopting such a theory are immediately obvious. This purely mathematical perspective, which equates the core concept with just one of its specific aspects, namely quantity, is essentially the foundation of materialism. The history of scientific thinking, particularly in France since the mid-eighteenth century, serves as proof of this. Abstract matter is defined as something that, while possessing form, treats that form as merely an irrelevant and external feature. This explanation should not be misunderstood as an attempt to belittle mathematics. By describing quantitative traits as external and irrelevant, we are not offering a justification for laziness or shallow thinking. We are also not claiming that quantitative features can be ignored or that they do not demand meticulous attention. Quantity is, of course, a phase of the core concept. As such, it must be given proper respect, both as a logical category and within the realm of objects, whether natural or spiritual.
original: Our knowledge would be in a very awkward predicament if such objects as freedom, law, morality, or even God Himself, because they cannot be measured and calculated, or expressed in a mathematical formula, were to be reckoned beyond the reach of exact knowledge, and we had to put up with a vague generalised image of them, leaving their details or particulars to the pleasure of each individual, to make out of them what he will. The pernicious consequences, to which such a theory gives rise in practice, are at once evident. And this mere mathematical view, which identifies with the Idea one of its special stages, viz. quantity, is no other than the principle of Materialism. Witness the history of the scientific modes of thought, especially in France since the middle of last century. Matter, in the abstract, is just what, though of course there is form in it, has that form only as an indifferent and external attribute. The present explanation would be utterly misconceived if it were supposed to disparage mathematics. By calling the quantitative characteristic merely external and indifferent, we provide no excuse for indolence and superficiality, nor do we assert that quantitative characteristics may be left to mind themselves, or at least require no very careful handling. Quantity, of course, is a stage of the Idea: and as such it must have its due, first as a logical category, and then in the world of objects, natural as well as spiritual.

plain: My existence is directly tied to the act of thinking. Descartes claims this forms the ultimate foundation for all philosophy. The nature of existence is defined within my self; this link is the primary issue. Thinking is existence, and existence is thinking—this is my certainty, my self. In the famous statement "I think, therefore I am," thinking and existence are joined in an unbreakable bond. Some view this statement as a logical argument where existence is derived from thinking. Kant specifically argues against this, noting that existence is not included in the concept of thinking and is distinct from it. This distinction is valid, yet the two remain inseparable, forming a single identity. Their difference does not harm their unity. However, this rule of pure, abstract certainty—the complete whole where everything is implicitly present—is not proven. Therefore, we should not attempt to turn this statement into a logical argument. Descartes himself notes: "No logical argument is actually present."
original: The ‘I think’ directly involves my Being; this, says Descartes, is the absolute basis of all Philosophy. The determination of Being is in my ‘I’; this connection is itself the first matter. Thought as Being and Being as thought—that is my certainty, ‘I’; in the celebrated Cogito, ergo sum we thus have Thought and Being inseparably bound together. On the one hand this proposition is regarded as a syllogism: from thought Being is deduced. Kant more especially has objected to this that Being is not contained in thinking, that it is different from thinking. This is true, but they are still inseparable, or constitute an identity; their difference is not to the prejudice of their unity. Yet this maxim of pure abstract certainty, the universal totality in which everything implicitly exists, is not proved; we must therefore not try to convert this proposition into a syllogism. Descartes himself says: “There is no syllogism present at all.

plain: As long as the individual lacks legal protection and relies solely on personal effort, vitality, action, and passion appear everywhere. Because people believe the Church guarantees their eternal salvation, and they are required to follow it only in spiritual matters, their drive for worldly pleasure grows stronger. This increase happens in reverse proportion to their fear of harming their spiritual well-being. The reason is that the Church grants indulgences for any kind of harsh, violent, or immoral behavior when asked. Between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries, a new impulse emerged, taking many different shapes. People in various regions started constructing massive churches, specifically cathedrals designed to hold the entire community. Architecture is consistently the first art, representing the inorganic stage and the physical housing of the divine. Only after this structure is complete does art try to show the worshippers the divine itself, the Objective. Coastal cities in Italy, Spain, and Flanders conducted maritime trade with great energy, which boosted the local productive industry of their citizens. The sciences began to recover somewhat, and Scholastic Philosophy reached its peak.
original: While the Individual still remains destitute of the defence of laws and is protected only by his own exertion, life, activity and excitement everywhere manifest themselves. As men are certain of eternal salvation through the instrumentality of the Church, and to this end are bound to obey it only in its spiritual requirements, their ardour in the pursuit of worldly enjoyment increases, on the other hand, in inverse proportion to their fear of its producing any detriment to their spiritual weal; for the Church bestows indulgences, when required, for oppressive, violent and vicious actions of all kinds. The period from the eleventh to the thirteenth century witnessed the rise of an impulse which developed itself in various forms. The inhabitants of various districts began to build enormous churches — Cathedrals, erected to contain the whole community. Architecture is always the first art, forming the inorganic phase, the domiciliation of the divinity; not till this is accomplished does Art attempt to exhibit to the worshippers the divinity himself — the Objective. Maritime commerce was carried on with vigour by the cities on the Italian, Spanish, and Flemish coasts, and this stimulated the productive industry of their citizens at home. The Sciences began in some degree to revive: the Scholastic Philosophy was in its glory.

plain: Following a brief era of splendor, the realm faced internal strife and split apart. Since there existed just a single Levite tribe and a single sanctuary—located in Jerusalem—false worship quickly took hold. It was impossible to honor the single deity across multiple shrines, nor could two separate states share one faith. Even if the idea of God as an external reality is deeply spiritual, the human side—specifically the acts of reverence directed toward Him—remains quite restricted and lacking in spiritual depth. Both realms, equally unsuccessful in their external and internal conflicts, eventually fell under the control of the Assyrians and Babylonians. Later, through Cyrus, the Israelites received authorization to go back and govern themselves according to their own statutes. The Persian Empire is now gone, leaving behind only sad remnants of its former greatness. Its most beautiful and wealthy cities—like Babylon, Susa, and Persepolis—have been completely destroyed, with only a handful of ruins indicating where they once stood. Even in newer major Persian cities, such as Ispahan and Shiraz, half the structures are in ruins. Unlike ancient Rome, these places did not generate fresh vitality; instead, they have nearly vanished from the memory of neighboring peoples. In addition to the other territories previously
original: After a short period of glory the kingdom suffered internal disruption and was divided. As there was only one tribe of Levites and one Temple, — i.e. in Jerusalem,— idolatry was immediately introduced. The One Grod could not be honoured in different Temples, and there could not be two kingdoms attached to one religion. However spiritual may be the conception of Grod as objective, the subjective side — the honour rendered to him— is still very limited and unspiritual in character. The two kingdoms, equally infelicitous in foreign and domestic warfare, were at last subjected to the Assyrians and Babylonians; through Cyrus the Israelites obtained permission to return home and live according: to their own laws. The Persian Empire is one that has passed away, and we have nothing but melancholy relics of its glory. Its fairest and richest towns — such as Babylon, Susa, Persepolis — are razed to the ground; and only a few ruins mark their ancient site. Even in the more modern great cities of Persia, — • Ispahan and Shiraz, — half of them has become a ruin; and they have not — as is the case with ancient Borne — developed a new life, but have lost their place almost entirely in the remembrance of the surrounding nations. plain: Cabalistic philosophy and Gnostic theology engaged with the same concepts that Philo held. For them as well, the First remains abstract, unknown, and without a name. The Second acts as the revelation, the concrete reality that moves outward through emanation. Yet a return to unity also appears to some extent, particularly within Christian philosophical thought. This return, recognized as the Third, is attributed to the λόγος. In Philo’s view, Wisdom, the instructor, and the high priest served as the force that, through the contemplation of God, guides the Third back to the First. Cabala denotes the hidden Jewish wisdom, though it is mixed with much that is obscure and enigmatic. Numerous myths surround its origins. It is said to reside in two texts: one titled Creation and the other Brightness. The former, which carries greater weight, is credited to Rabbi Akibha. Herr von Mayer in Frankfort is preparing to release a more complete edition. The work contains certain intriguing general principles. Its superior section comprises ideas that, in several ways, mirror Philo’s, albeit presented with greater fancy and frequently descending into the fantastical.
original: The Cabalistic philosophy and the Gnostic theology both occupied themselves with these same conceptions which Philo also had. To them also the First is the abstract, the unknown, the nameless; the Second is the unveiling, the concrete, which goes forth into emanation. But there is also to be found in some degree the return to unity, especially among Christian philosophers: and this return, which is accepted as the Third, belongs to the λόγος; so with Philo Wisdom, the teacher, the high priest, was that which in the contemplation of God leads back the Third to the First. Cabala is the name given to the secret wisdom of the Jews, with which, however, much that is dark and mysterious is mingled; regarding its origin also many fables are related. We are told of it that it is contained in two books, Jezirah (Creation) and Sohar (Brightness). Jezirah, the more important of these two books, is ascribed to a certain Rabbi Akibha; it is about to be published in a more complete form by Herr von Mayer, in Frankfort. The book has certain very interesting general principles, and this better portion of it consists of ideas, which in some respects resemble those of Philo, though they are more fancifully presented, and often sink into the fantastic.

plain: This other entity has not yet recognized spirit as its own possession. Alternatively phrased, spirit, when appearing as a distinct individual, does not yet exist as the universal self, which is the entirety of selfhood. Or, the configuration it adopts has not yet attained the structure of the concept. This concept represents the universal self, where the self's immediate actual reality is simultaneously surpassed. It is thought, it is universality, yet it retains its reality within that universality. Consequently, this specific human being, revealed to be Absolute Being, undergoes in its own individual instance the process observed in sensory existence. He is God, present immediately; therefore, His being transitions into His having been. The consciousness for which God is thus present in a sensory manner ceases to perceive Him visually and auditorily. It has perceived Him, and it has heard Him. It is precisely because it has perceived and heard Him that it first becomes spiritual consciousness itself. In other words, He has now emerged in the life of Spirit, just as He previously appeared before consciousness as an object within the realm of sense. A consciousness that perceives and hears Him through the senses is one that is

Or again, the shape it assxunes has not as yet the form of the notion, i.e. of the universal self, of the self which ia its immediate actual reaility is at once transcended, is thought, universahty, without losing its reahty ia this universahty. And it is by the mere fact that it has seen and heard Him, that it first becomes itself spiritual consciousness; or, in other words. He has now arisen in the life of Spirit, as He formerly rose before consciousness as an object existing in the sphere of sense.
