If we look closely at the standpoint of morality as we have to understand it in the best sense at the present day, we soon find that its conception does not immediately coincide with what apart from it we are in the habit of calling in a general way virtue, respectability, uprightness, etc. To be respectable and virtuous is not enough to make a man moral. Morality involves reflection and the definite consciousness of that which duty prescribes, and acting out of such a prior consciousness. Duty itself is the law of the will, which man nevertheless lays down freely out of his own self, and then is supposed to determine himself to this duty for duty's and its fulfilment's sake, by doing good solely from the conviction which he has attained that it is the good.

plain: New Platonists hold the exact contrary perspective, interpreting everything as a sign of spiritual significance, which turns this faith into strict Idealism. Every one of these accounts is partial. They see natural and spiritual forces as deeply joined, though the free spiritual aspect has not yet emerged in this phase of thinking. Yet the opposing ends are merged in the sharpest opposition. We have discussed the Nile, the Sun, and the plant life that relies on them. This narrow view of nature provides the core principle of the religion, and its main content is essentially a historical narrative. The Nile and the Sun form the gods, imagined with human shapes, and the progression of nature matches the mythological story. At the winter solstice, solar strength hits its lowest point and must be reborn. Similarly, Osiris is shown being born, but Typhon, his hostile brother, kills him. Typhon represents the scorching desert wind.
original: The New Platonists take a directly opposite view, regarding all as symbols of a spiritual meaning, and thus making this religion a pure Idealism. Each of these representations is one-sided. Natural and spiritual powers are regarded as most intimately united, — (the free spiritual import, however, has not been developed at this stage of thought), — but in such a way, that the extremes of the antithesis were united in the harshest contrast. "VVe have spoken of the Nile, of the Sun, and of the vegetation depending upon them. This limited view of Nature gives the principle of the religion, and its subject-matter ia primarily a history. The Nile and the Sun constitute the divinities, conceived under human forms; and the course of nature and the mythological history is the same. In the winter solstice the power of the sun has reached its minimum, and must be born anew. Thus also Osiris appears as born; but he is killed by Typhon, — his brother and enemy, — the burning wind of the desert.

plain: The first stance supports the idea of transmutation, while the second holds that the contrary can be proven. It no longer treats water, fire, and similar substances as basic realities, since it breaks them down into hydrogen, oxygen, and other components, yet it claims these components remain unchanged. It correctly argues that whatever is claimed or suggested by the speculative view must also hold true in reality. If being speculative means embodying the true nature and principle of its parts, then this quality must also exist in the actual world. We err when we depict the speculative as something that exists only in thought or internally, located in some unknown place. It is genuinely present, but educated people ignore it due to their narrow perspective. If we hear their reports, they claim to merely observe and state what they see. However, their observation is inaccurate because they unconsciously distort what they perceive through their restricted and fixed concepts. The conflict does not stem from a clash between observation and the absolute Notion, but rather between one Notion and another. They demonstrate that changes, such as water turning into earth, do not occur. Even in recent times, this transformation was still defended, as distilling water yielded a residue of earth. Lavoisier, however, conducted several highly decisive investigations on this matter. He weighed all the containers, proving that the residue came from the vessels themselves.
original: If the former point of view upholds transmutation, the latter believes in the possibility of demonstrating the opposite; it no longer, indeed, maintains water, fire, &c., to be simple realities, for it resolves them into hydrogen, oxygen, &c., but it asserts their immutability. It justly asserts that what is asserted and implied in the speculative point of view, must also have the truth of actuality; for if to be the speculative means to be the very nature and principle of its elements, this must likewise be present. We are wrong in representing the speculative to be something existent only in thought or inwardly, which is no one knows where. It is really present, but men of learning shut their eyes to it because of their limited point of view. If we listen to their account, they only observe and say what they see; but their observation is not true, for unconsciously they transform what is seen through their limited and stereotyped conception; the strife is not due to the opposition between observation and the absolute Notion, but between the one Notion and the other. They show that changes—such as that of water into earth—are non-existent. Even in modern times this transformation was indeed maintained, for when water was distilled, a residuum of earth was found. On this subject, however, Lavoisier carried on a number of very conclusive researches; he weighed all the receptacles, and it was shown that the residuum proceeded from the vessels.

ref: The Elements of the Greek Spirit
plain: A democratic society is not a family-based system. It does not rely on a blind, immature trust. Instead, it requires written rules. People must understand that these rules rest on fair and ethical grounds. They must also accept these rules as binding. During the era of kings, no true political life had yet emerged in Greece. Consequently, there is very little evidence of formal legislation. However, between the Trojan War and the period just before Cyrus, the need for laws became clear. The earliest known lawgivers are called the Seven Sages. This title did not mean what it later came to mean, such as the Sophists. The Sophists were teachers of wisdom who deliberately and systematically announced the Eight and True. The Sages were simply thoughtful individuals. Their thinking did not reach the level of true Science. They were practical politicians. The wise advice given by Thales of Miletus and Bias of Priene to the Ionian cities has already been noted. Solon was asked by the Athenians to create new laws because the existing ones were no longer adequate. Solon provided the Athenians with a constitution that granted equal rights to everyone. However, he did not make the democracy completely abstract. The central feature of democracy is moral character. Montesquieu notes that virtue is the foundation of democracy. This idea is as significant as it is accurate regarding the common understanding of democracy.
original: The Democratical State is not Patriarchal, — does not rest on a still unreflecting, undeveloped confidence, — but implies laws, with the consciousness of their being founded on an equitable and moral basis, and the recognition of these laws as positive. At the time of the Kings, no political life had as yet made its appearance in Hellas; there are, therefore, only slight traces of Legislation. But in the interval from the Trojan War till near the time of Cyrus, its necessitywas felt. The first Lawgivers are known under the name of The Seven Sages, — a title which at that time did not imply any such character as that of the Sophists — teachers of wisdom, designedly [and systematically] proclaiming the Eight and True — but merely thinking men, whose thinking stopped short of Science, properly so called. They were practical politicians; the good counsels which two of them — Thales of Miletus and Bias of Priene— gave to the Ionian cities, have been already mentioned. Thus Solon was commissioned by the Athenians to give them laws, as those then in operation no longer sufficed. Solon gave the Athenians a constitution by which all obtained equal rights, yet not so as to render the Democracy a quite abstract one. The main point in Democracy is moral disposition. Virtue is the basis of Democracy, remarks Montesquieu; and this sentiment is as important as it is true in reference to the idea of Democracy commonly entertained.

plain: In the study of bodily functions, internal organs are viewed simply as components serving the living body. However, these same parts also constitute a physical mechanism for expressing mental conditions, which gives them a completely different meaning. Because sensations are direct and present, they appear as isolated and fleeting moments of mental existence. They represent changes in the substance of the mind, occurring within its self-focused life, of which that substance is a part. Yet this self-focused existence is not just a structural element of sensation. The mind is essentially a complete reflection of all sensations. It experiences within itself the full substance that it essentially is. It is a mind that feels. In common speech, sensation and feeling are not clearly separated. We do not talk about the sensation of right or self, but rather the feeling of them. Sensitivity is linked to sensation. Therefore, sensation highlights the passive aspect—the reality that we discover ourselves feeling, or the directness of the mode of feeling. Meanwhile, feeling emphasizes the fact that it is we who are doing the feeling. (b) The Feeling Soul.—(The Soul as Sentiency.)(122)
original: In physiology the viscera and the organs are treated merely as parts subservient to the animal organism; but they form at the same time a physical system for the expression of mental states, and in this way they get quite another interpretation. Sensations, just because they are immediate and are found existing, are single and transient aspects of psychic life,—alterations in the substantiality of the soul, set in its self-centred life, with which that substance is one. But this self-centred being is not merely a formal factor of sensation: the soul is virtually a reflected totality of sensations—it feels in itself the total substantiality which it virtually is—it is a soul which feels. In the usage of ordinary language, sensation and feeling are not clearly distinguished: still we do not speak of the sensation,—but of the feeling (sense) of right, of self; sentimentality (sensibility) is connected with sensation: we may therefore say sensation emphasises rather the side of passivity—the fact that we find ourselves feeling, i.e. the immediacy of mode in feeling—whereas feeling at the same time rather notes the fact that it is we ourselves who feel. (b) The Feeling Soul.—(Soul as Sentiency.)(122)

plain: In any profession, the primary goal is to practice it with clear comprehension. A judge, for instance, must adhere strictly to legal statutes and deliver rulings based on them. He must remain unmoved by various influences, reject all justifications, and avoid looking in any direction other than the facts. Comprehension is also a constant component in rigorous education. A well-trained mind does not accept vague or ambiguous perceptions; instead, it captures subjects in their stable nature. In contrast, an untrained person remains unsettled and wavering. It frequently requires significant effort to reach a consensus with such an individual on the topic at hand and to direct their attention to the specific issue. It has already been established that the logical principle, in its general form, is not merely a subjective mental activity. Rather, it is the universal itself, which is therefore also objective. This view is demonstrated in the case of understanding, the initial form of logical truths. Understanding, in this broader context, aligns with what we term the benevolence of the divine, specifically in the sense that finite entities exist and persist. In the natural world, for example, we perceive this divine benevolence in the fact that different categories or types of animals and plants are equipped with everything necessary for their survival and well-being.
original: In every calling, too, the great thing is to pursue it with understanding. Thus the judge must stick to the law, and give his verdict in accordance with, it, undeterred by one motive or another, allowing no excuses; and looking neither left nor right. Understanding, too, is always an element in thorough training. The trained-intellect is not satisfied with cloudy and indefinite impressions, but grasps the objects in their fixed character: whereas the uncultivated man wavers unsettled, and it often costs a deal of trouble to come to an understanding with him on the matter under discussion, and to bring him to fix his eye on the definite point in question. It has been already explained that the Logical principle in general, far from being merely a subjective action in our minds, is rather the very universal, which as such is also objective. This doctrine is illustrated in the case of understanding, the first form of logical truths. Understanding in this larger sense corresponds to what we call the goodness of God, so far as that means that finite things are and subsist. In nature, for example, we recognise the goodness of God in the fact that the various classes or species of animals and plants are provided with whatever they need for their preservation and welfare.

plain: Arcesilaus was once told that people flocked to Epicurus, noting that many switched from other schools to his, yet almost no one left the Epicurean system for elsewhere. He replied with a sharp joke, comparing the situation to castration: a man can be made a eunuch, but a eunuch cannot revert to being a man. During his life, Epicurus wrote a vast quantity of material, outproducing even Chrysippus, who was known for his own prolific output. This comparison holds if we exclude Chrysippus’s compilations drawn from other authors or his own earlier texts. Reports suggest Epicurus produced three hundred works. It is not a loss that these texts have vanished. In fact, we should be grateful they are gone, as scholars would have faced significant difficulties analyzing them. Our primary source for understanding Epicurus is the entire tenth book of Diogenes Laërtius. Despite its length, this text provides only limited insight into the subject.
original: When some one called the attention of Arcesilaus to this attachment to Epicurus, by the remark that while so many had gone over from other philosophers to Epicurus, scarcely a single example was known of any one passing over from the Epicurean system to another, Arcesilaus made the witty rejoinder: “Men may become eunuchs, but eunuchs can never again become men.” Epicurus himself produced in his lifetime an immense number of works, being a much more prolific author than Chrysippus, who vied with him in the number of his writings, if we deduct from the latter his compilations from the works of others or from his own. The number of his writings is said to have amounted to three hundred; it is scarcely to be regretted that they are lost to us. We may rather thank Heaven that they no longer exist; philologists at any rate would have had great trouble with them. The main source of our knowledge of Epicurus is the whole of the tenth book of Diogenes Laërtius, which after all gives us but scanty information, though it deals with the subject at great length.

plain: The third phase involves the union itself, which is the sole focus of interest, becoming conscious and turning into an object. As a principle, this union takes the shape of the connection between knowledge and its content. Consequently, the question arises: how is thought identical with the objective, and how can it be so? This step elevates the inner foundation of this metaphysics into clear view and makes it an object. This development encompasses the entire scope of modern philosophy. Regarding the external history and personal lives of philosophers, we notice a sharp contrast with the ancient thinkers, whom we previously saw as self-sufficient individuals. A philosopher is expected to live in accordance with his teachings, to scorn the world, and to avoid engaging with it. The ancients achieved this standard. They were such well-rounded individuals precisely because the internal spiritual goal of philosophy often shaped their external relationships and circumstances as well.
original: c. The third stage is that this union itself which is to be brought about, and which is the only subject of interest, comes to consciousness and becomes an object. As principle the union has the form of the relationship of knowledge to the content, and thus this question has been put: ‘How is, and how can thought be identical with the objective?’ With this the inward element which lies at the basis of this metaphysic is raised into explicitude and made an object; and this includes all modern philosophy in its range. 4. In respect to the external history and the lives of the philosophers, it will strike us that from this time on, these appear to be very different from those of the philosophers of ancient times, whom we regarded as self-sufficing individualities. It is required that a philosopher should live as he teaches, that he should despise the world and not enter into connection with it; this the ancients have accomplished, and they are such plastic individualities just because the inward spiritual aim of philosophy has likewise frequently determined their external relations and conditions.

plain: For actual, concrete spirit, these features belong to its substance. In religion, however, they serve only as descriptions of the subject. Similarly, all general forms exist within spirit, or within every individual spirit, whether intrinsically or for our understanding. Yet, when examining its reality, the crucial factor is solely the specific nature it holds within its awareness. This includes the particular way it has expressed itself or the form in which it recognizes its fundamental nature. The gap between actual spirit and that same spirit aware of itself as spirit, or between it as mere awareness and as self-awareness, vanishes when spirit grasps its true reality. Its awareness and self-awareness reach agreement. However, since religion starts out immediately with this separation, the distinction has not yet returned to spirit. Initially, only the concept and principle of religion are set up. Here, the core component is self-awareness, which recognizes itself as possessing all truth and holding all reality within that truth. Because this self-awareness is a form of awareness, it necessarily has an object, and that object is itself.
original: In the case of actual concrete spirit they are attributes of its substance; in rehgion, on the other hand, they are only predicates of the subject. In the same way, indeed, all forms in general are, in themselves or for us, contained in spirit and contained in every spirit. But the main point of importance, in dealing with its reahty, is solely what determinate character it has in its consciousness, in which specific character it has expressed its self, or in what shape it knows its essential nature. The distinction made between actual spirit and that same spirit which knows itself as spirit, or between itself qua consciousness and qua self-consciousness, is transcended and done away with in the case where spirit knows itself in its real truth. Its consciousness and its self-consciousness have come to terms. But, as religion is here to begin with and immediately, this distinction has not yet reverted to spirit. It is merely the conception, the principle, of rehgion that is established at first. In this the essential element is self-consciousness, which is conscious of being all truth, and which contains all reahty within that truth. This self-consciousness, being consciousness [and so aware of an object], has itself for its object.

plain: Marriage creates a fresh household that stands on its own, distinct from the ancestral lines it originated from. While blood ties link this new unit to those older branches, ethical love serves as its core foundation. Consequently, a person’s assets are fundamentally tied to their marriage rather than to their birth lineage. When couples agree to limit shared ownership or preserve the wife’s separate rights, they do so to protect against the marriage ending through death or separation. Such provisions ensure that family members receive their designated portions of the shared property if the union dissolves. Many legal systems still emphasize the broader kinship network. They view this wider circle as the true unifying force, treating the immediate household as relatively minor. For instance, under ancient Roman law, a woman in a loose marriage remained closer to her own kin than to her spouse and offspring. Similarly, during the feudal era, the drive to maintain family prestige meant only male descendants were counted within the lineage. In these cases, the entire kinship network took priority, overshadowing the new household. Despite this, each new household remains more fundamental than the wider group defined by blood relations.
original: Marriage establishes a new family, which has its own independent footing as against the stems or houses from, which it has proceeded. The connection of the new family with these stems is consanguinity, but the principle of the new family is ethical love. Thus, the individual's property is essentially allied to his marriage, and less intimately to his original stock or house. A marriage-settlement, which imposes a limit to the common possession of goods by the wedded couple, or any other arrangement by which the right of the wife is retained, is intended to be security against the dissolution of the marriage-tie by death or divorce. In such an event the different members of the family are by this arrangement apportioned their shares of the common possession. In many law codes the more extended range of the family circle is retained. It is looked upon as the real bond of union, while the tie of the single family is regarded as comparatively unimportant. Thus in the older Eoman law the wife of the lax marriage is more closely allied to her relatives than to her husband and children. In feudal times, also, the necessity of preserving the splendor famdliae led to reckoning under the family only its male members. Thus the whole family connection was the chief object of concern, and the newly-formed family was placed in the background. Notwithstanding this, every new family is more essential than the vidder circle bounded by the tie of consanguinity.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The Work of Art
plain: One might even look down on deep philosophical insights, valuing them less than concrete facts, technical details, and historical records. However, true art scholarship still seeks solid evidence and facts, along with reasoned judgment. This judgment involves carefully separating the various aspects of an artwork, even those that seem merely external, and assessing how important each one is. (d) Having discussed the study methods that stem from viewing art as a physical object connected to human sensory experience, we now turn to this aspect’s deeper connection to art itself. We will examine (a) the artwork as an object, and (b) the artist’s inner subjectivity, including their genius and talent. We will avoid topics that require understanding the universal concept of art.
original: It may even form a disparaging estimate of the value of more profound considerations in comparison with purely positive, technical, and historical information. Still, even so, art-scholarship, if only it is of a genuine kind, at least strives after definite grounds and information, and an intelligent judgment, with which is closely conjoined the more precise distinction of the different, even if partly external, aspects in a work of art, and the estimation of their importance. (d) After these remarks upon the modes of study which have arisen out of that aspect of a work of art in which, being a sensuous object, it is invested with a relation to man as a sensuous being, we will now consider this aspect in its more essential relation to art as such, and so (a) partly as regards the work of art as object, (b) partly with respect to the subjectivity of the artist, his genius, talent, and so on; but without entering into matter relative to these points that can only proceed from the knowledge of art in its universal idea.

plain: Observing this range of emotions and the damage caused by their intensity, we notice that irrationality is linked not just to these feelings, but particularly to noble intentions and just goals. We witness the harm, wickedness, and collapse that have struck the most successful states ever built by human thought. It is hard to avoid feeling deep sorrow over this widespread corruption. Since this decline stems from human choice rather than nature, it represents a moral souring or a rebellion of the good spirit within us. Without using dramatic language, a straightforward account of the suffering that has destroyed the greatest nations and systems of government, as well as the best examples of personal virtue, creates a terrifying image. This image provokes a deep, hopeless sadness that no comforting outcome can balance. We suffer mentally while looking at it, finding no defense or escape except in the thought that these events were inevitable and could not have been changed by any intervention. Finally, we retreat from the unbearable revulsion caused by these sad thoughts, returning to the more pleasant setting of our personal lives, which are shaped by our own private goals and interests.
original: When we look at this display of passions, and the consequences of their violence; the Unreason which is associated not only with them, but even (rather we might say especially) with good designs and righteous aims; when we see the evil, the vice, the ruin that has befallen the most flourishing kingdoms which the mind of man ever created; we can scarce avoid being filled with sorrow at this universal taint of corruption: and, since this decay is not the work of mere Nature, but of the Human Will — a moral embitterment — a revolt of the Good Spirit (if it have a place within us) may well be the result of our reflections. Without rhetorical exaggeration, a simply truthful combination of the miseries that have overwhelmed the noblest of nations and polities, and the finest exemplars of private virtue,— forms a picture of most fearful aspect, and excites emotions of the profoundest and most hopeless sadness, counterbalanced by no consolatory result. We endure in beholding it a mental torture, allowing no defence or escape but the consideration that what has happened could not be otherwise; that it is a fatality which no intervention could alter. And at last we draw back from the intolerable disgust with which these sorrowful reflections threaten us, into the more agreeable environment of our individual life— the Present formed by our private aims and interests.

plain: We now focus our attention solely on the individual, or rather, observation shifts its target to the individual. The person exists for their own sake and within themselves. They are free activity, yet they also possess an inherent, specific nature that belongs to them. This trait is fundamentally identical to what psychology tried to locate outside the person. Conflict emerges within the self; it has a dual character, acting as a movement of consciousness while simultaneously being the stable existence of a reality with a phenomenal aspect, a reality that is directly its own. This existence, the "body" of the specific individual, serves as its final and primary source or condition, something the individual did not create. However, because the individual is only what they have accomplished, their body also functions as an "expression" of themselves that they have produced. It acts as a sign and indicator that is not just a simple, immediate fact, but rather points to and reveals what is meant by activating their innate nature.
original: Individuahty alone is now the object for observation, or the object to which observation now passes. The individual exists in himself and for himself. He is for himself, or is a free activity; he is, however, also in hunself, or has himself an original determinate being of his own — a characteristic which is in principle the same as what psychology sought to find outside him. Opposition thus breaks out in his own self; it has this twofold nature, it is a process or movement of consciousness, and it is the fixed being of a reality with a phenomenal character, a reality which in it is directly its own. This being, the " body " of the determinate individuahty, is its ultimate and original source or condition, that in the making of which it has had nothing to do. But since the individual at the same time merely is what he has done, his body is also an " expression " of himself which he has brought about; a sign and indication as well, which has not remained a bare immediate fact, but only points to and lets us see what is meant by his setting his original nature to work.

plain: Were the logical structures of the concept truly empty, passive containers for ideas, indifferent to their contents, understanding them would be a pointless pursuit that truth could easily ignore. In reality, as structural aspects of the concept, they constitute the living essence of the real world. Only what is true because of, through, and within these structures is genuinely true in the actual world. However, the validity of these structures has never been analyzed for its own sake, nor has their essential connection been investigated. (a) The Concept as Concept. The Concept as Concept comprises three functional components or moments. (1) The first is Universality, which signifies that it maintains free equality with itself regarding its specific nature. (2) The second is Particularity, defined as that specific nature, where the universal remains calmly identical to itself. (3) The third is Individuality, representing the self-reflection of the specific natures of universality and particularity; this negative self-unity possesses full and primary determinateness, without diminishing its self-identity or universality.
original: If the logical forms of the notion were really dead and inert receptacles of conceptions and thoughts, careless of what they contained, knowledge about them would be an idle curiosity which the truth might dispense with. On the contrary they really are, as forms of the notion, the vital spirit of the actual world. That only is true of the actual which is true in virtue of these forms, through them and in them. As yet, however, the truth of these forms has never been considered or examined on their own account any more than their necessary interconnexion. (a) The Notion as Notion. The Notion as Notion contains the three following 'moments' or functional parts. (1) The first is Universality--meaning that it is in free equality with itself in its specific character. (2) The second is Particularity--that is, the specific character, in which the universal continues serenely equal to itself. (3) The third is Individuality--meaning the reflection-into-self of the specific characters of universality and particularity;--which negative self-unity has complete and original determinateness, without any loss to its self-identity or universality.

plain: Diogenes Laertius explicitly states in his second book, chapter twelve, that Anaxagoras viewed the sun and stars as hot rocks. Plutarch, in his biography of Pericles, chapter six, criticizes him for providing a naturalistic explanation for a phenomenon that prophets had declared a miraculous sign. This aligns with the claim that he predicted a rock would drop from the sky on the day of the Battle of Aegospotami, where the Athenians lost their final fleet to Lysander. A general observation applies to Thales, Anaximander, and others: they regarded the sun, moon, earth, and stars as simple objects, meaning entities outside the mind. They no longer treated these bodies as living deities but instead conceptualized them in various ways. These specific ideas do not merit further analysis here, as they fall under the domain of standard academic study. Thought can generate things. Thought actually produces the outcome where specific objects, which might be termed divine, and specific concepts of them, which might be termed poetic, along with the entire spectrum of superstitious beliefs, are dismantled. They are reduced to what are known as natural objects. Within thought, which is the unity of itself and Being, the mind recognizes itself as the genuinely real. Consequently, for the mind engaged in thought, the non-spiritual and material are reduced to mere objects, serving as the negation of the mind.
original: It is distinctly said by Diogenes Laertius (II. 12) that Anaxagoras believed the sun and stars to be burning stones; and he is, according to Plutarch, (in Pericle, 6) blamed for having explained something that the prophets stated to be a marvellous omen, in a natural way; it quite tallies with this that he is said to have foretold that on the day of Ægos-Potamos, where the Athenians lost their last fleet against Lysander, a stone should fall from heaven. The general remark might be made of Thales, Anaximander, &c., that the sun, moon, earth and stars were counted as mere things, i.e. as objects external to mind, and that they no longer held them to be living gods, but represented them in different ways—which ideas, for the rest, deserve no further consideration, since these matters belong properly to ordinary learning. Things may be derived from thought; thought really brings about the result that certain objects which may be called divine, and certain conceptions of these which may be called poetic, together with the whole range of superstitious beliefs, are demolished—they are brought down to being what are called natural things. For in thought, as the identity of itself and of Being, mind knows itself as the truly actual, so that for mind in thought, the unspiritual and material is brought down to being mere things, to the negative of mind.

plain: Freedom and Fairness often serve as the basic labels for what should actually be the core rule, ultimate goal, and outcome of a political system. While this view holds some truth, the main flaw in these concepts is their complete abstraction. If one clings to them in this purely abstract shape, they act as rules that either stop the state from becoming concrete—meaning its breakdown into a specific constitution and general government—or they dismantle those structures entirely. Inequality emerges alongside the state, creating distinctions between those who rule and those who are ruled, as well as various offices, powers, and leadership roles. If the idea of fairness is applied logically to its end, it denies all distinctions, thereby preventing any political situation from existing. Freedom and fairness do form the basis of the state, but because they are the most abstract, they are also the most shallow, and for that exact reason, they feel the most familiar to people. It is therefore crucial to examine them more closely. Regarding fairness first, the common claim that all people are naturally equal makes a mistake by mixing up the "natural" with the "concept." It should instead state that people are only unequal by nature. However, the concept of freedom, when it exists in itself without any further detail or development, represents abstract subjectivity, specifically as an individual who can own things. This single abstract aspect of personal identity creates the actual equality among human beings.
original: Liberty and Equality are the simple rubrics into which is frequently concentrated what should form the fundamental principle, the final aim and result of the constitution. However true this is, the defect of these terms is their utter abstractness: if stuck to in this abstract form, they are principles which either prevent the rise of the concreteness of the state, i.e. its articulation into a constitution and a government in general, or destroy them. With the state there arises inequality, the difference of governing powers and of governed, magistracies, authorities, directories, &c. The principle of equality, logically carried out, rejects all differences, and thus allows no sort of political condition to exist. Liberty and equality are indeed the foundation of the state, but as the most abstract also the most superficial, and for that very reason naturally the most familiar. It is important therefore to study them closer. As regards, first, Equality, the familiar proposition, All men are by nature equal, blunders by confusing the “natural” with the “notion.” It ought rather to read: By nature men are only unequal. But the notion of liberty, as it exists as such, without further specification and development, is abstract subjectivity, as a person capable of property. This single abstract feature of personality constitutes the actual equality of human beings.

plain: Because these turbulent events failed to fulfill him, he resigned from the army in 1621. He traveled extensively through the remaining parts of Germany, then moved on to Poland, Prussia, Switzerland, Italy, and France. Seeking greater liberty, he settled in the Netherlands to advance his plans. He resided there quietly between 1629 and 1644. During those years, he wrote and published the bulk of his output. He also defended these publications against numerous criticisms, most of which originated with the clergy. Ultimately, Queen Christina of Sweden invited him to her court in Stockholm. This location served as a gathering place for the era’s most renowned scholars. He passed away there in 1650. Regarding his philosophical writings, the ones containing his foundational principles feature a notably accessible presentation style. This approach makes them highly suitable for beginners in philosophy. Descartes begins in a straightforward, almost naive way, recounting his thoughts as they occurred to him. Professor Cousin of Paris published a new edition of Descartes’ works in eleven octavo volumes. The majority of this collection consists of letters discussing natural phenomena. Descartes also revitalized mathematics alongside philosophy. He discovered several key methods. Later, the most impressive achievements in advanced mathematics were constructed upon these discoveries.
original: Yet since the sight of these wild scenes could not satisfy him, he gave up military service in 1621. He made several other journeys through the rest of Germany, and then proceeded to Poland, Prussia, Switzerland, Italy and France. On account of its greater freedom he withdrew to Holland, in order there to pursue his projects; here he lived in peace from 1629 to 1644—a period in which he composed and issued most of his works, and also defended them against the manifold attacks from which they suffered, and which more especially proceeded from the clergy. Queen Christina of Sweden finally called him to her court at Stockholm, which was the rendezvous for all the most celebrated men of learning of the time, and there he died in 1650. As regards his philosophic works, those which contain his first principles have in particular something very popular about their method of presentation, which makes them highly to be recommended to those commencing the study of philosophy. Descartes sets to work in a quite simple and childlike manner, with a narration of his reflections as they came to him. Professor Cousin of Paris has brought out a new edition of Descartes in eleven octavo volumes; the greater part consists of letters on natural phenomena. Descartes gave a new impetus to mathematics as well as to philosophy. Several important methods were discovered by him, upon which the most brilliant results in higher mathematics were afterwards built.

plain: Law and morality are possible only in this manner. The religious injunction to render to the state its due and to the divine its due is inadequate. The critical task is to define what truly belongs to secular power. It is widely recognized that both secular and church authorities have asserted ownership over nearly everything. The divine spirit must permeate all aspects of secular existence. Through this process, wisdom becomes tangible within that existence, and that existence provides the grounds for its own validation. However, this tangible presence is nothing more than the ethical structures mentioned earlier. This means the moral character of marriage stands in contrast to the holiness associated with celibate communities. The moral character of economic and industrial activity opposes the holiness of poverty and the lethargy that accompanies it. The moral character of obedience directed toward state law opposes the holiness of an obedience that lacks law and duty, where conscience is held captive. As the need for law and morality increases, along with the awareness of the spirit’s fundamental freedom, a conflict arises between the spirit and a religion based on unfreedom. It is futile to organize political laws and systems based on fairness and reason if the principle of unfreedom remains in religion. A free state and a religion that enslaves cannot coexist.
original: Thus, and thus only, can law and morality exist. The precept of religion, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s” is not enough: the question is to settle what is Caesar’s, what belongs to the secular authority: and it is sufficiently notorious that the secular no less than the ecclesiastical authority have claimed almost everything as their own. The divine spirit must interpenetrate the entire secular life: whereby wisdom is concrete within it, and it carries the terms of its own justification. But that concrete indwelling is only the aforesaid ethical organisations. It is the morality of marriage as against the sanctity of a celibate order;—the morality of economic and industrial action against the sanctity of poverty and its indolence;—the morality of an obedience dedicated to the law of the state as against the sanctity of an obedience from which law and duty are absent and where conscience is enslaved. With the growing need for law and morality and the sense of the spirit’s essential liberty, there sets in a conflict of spirit with the religion of unfreedom. It is no use to organise political laws and arrangements on principles of equity and reason, so long as in religion the principle of unfreedom is not abandoned. A free state and a slavish religion are incompatible.

plain: Romantic art abandons the effort to depict the divine through external shapes or beauty. Instead, it portrays the divine as merely tolerating the visible world, acting as the core of all hearts within an exterior realm from which it constantly withdraws. Consequently, the external aspect can seem accidental relative to its true meaning. The Philosophy of Religion must uncover the logical necessity driving the process where the Absolute Being takes on more distinct and solid characteristics. It must identify which specific characteristic matches a particular type of worship. Furthermore, it must examine how secular self-awareness, which recognizes humanity’s highest calling, aligns with the core principle of any religion. This includes analyzing how a nation’s moral character, legal foundations, actual freedom, constitutional structure, and its artistic and scientific pursuits all correspond to that religious substance.
original: Romantic art gives up the task of showing him as such in external form and by means of beauty: it presents him as only condescending to appearance, and the divine as the heart of hearts in an externality from which it always disengages itself. Thus the external can here appear as contingent towards its significance. The Philosophy of Religion has to discover the logical necessity in the progress by which the Being, known as the Absolute, assumes fuller and firmer features; it has to note to what particular feature the kind of cultus corresponds,—and then to see how the secular self-consciousness, the consciousness of what is the supreme vocation of man,—in short how the nature of a nation’s moral life, the principle of its law, of its actual liberty, and of its constitution, as well as of its art and science, corresponds to the principle which constitutes the substance of a religion.

plain: In everyday affairs, a single account often suffices for minor issues, while more significant matters demand multiple accounts, and in the most critical cases, we must scrutinize individual accounts by comparing them against one another. Similarly, for trivial concerns, a broadly persuasive idea is enough; for matters of moderate weight, we need a confirmed idea; but for issues concerning a good and happy existence, we require an idea that has been thoroughly examined in its components. This observation highlights a key difference from those who locate truth in immediate experience, particularly recent thinkers who rely on sensory perception or direct knowledge, whether viewed as internal revelation or external observation. Carneades correctly assigns this type of certainty the lowest rank. For him, the truly essential element is the concept that has been fully developed and elaborated, although this appears only in a formal way. Ultimately, truth resides solely in intellectual understanding. Even if Carneades fails to cover every aspect of this understanding’s nature, he rightly stresses a crucial element: the process of unfolding and the act of judging the various components.
original: Just as in common life in some unimportant matter one witness satisfies us, in one more important several are required, and in a case which is more material still the individual witnesses are themselves examined through a comparison of their testimonies, so in less important matters a general convincing conception satisfies us, in things of a certain importance one which is established, but in those which pertain to a good and happy life one which is investigated in its parts is required.” We thus see—in contradistinction to those who place truth in what is immediate, and, especially in recent times, in sensuous perception, in an immediate knowledge, whether as inward revelation or outward perception—that this kind of certainty with Carneades rightly takes the lowest place; the conception worked out and developed really is to him the essential one, and yet it appears in a formal manner only. In fact, the truth is only in thinking knowledge, and if Carneades does not exhaust all that can be said of the nature of this knowledge, he still has rightly emphasized an essential moment in it, the opening out and the judging movements of the moments.

plain: Scholars latch onto this reference to a concept that is fundamentally Egyptian and purely sensory, claiming that Plato asserted specific facts. Yet Plato never made such a claim; his remarks here have no bearing on philosophy, and especially not on his own system, just as his later comments on the divine do not. In other conversations, this story is expanded and presented more vividly. It certainly uses the common meaning of memory, which holds that the human mind previously perceived what now appears to us as genuine and fully real. However, Plato’s main goal is to demonstrate, through this claim of remembering, that the mind, the soul, and thinking are inherently independent. For the ancients, and specifically within the Platonic framework, this independence is tightly linked to what we term the soul’s immortality.
original: Historians seize upon this allusion to what is really an Egyptian idea, and a sensuous conception merely, and say that Plato has laid down that such and such was the case. But Plato made no such statement whatever; what he here says has nothing to do with Philosophy, and more particularly nothing to do with his philosophy, any more than what afterwards is said regarding God. β. In other Dialogues this myth is further and more strikingly developed; it certainly employs remembrance in its ordinary sense, which is that the mind of man has in past time seen that which comes to his consciousness as the true and absolutely existent. Plato’s principal effort is, however, to show through this assertion of recollection, that the mind, the soul, thought, is on its own account free, and this has to the ancients, and particularly to the Platonic idea, a close connection with what we call immortality of the soul.

ref: The Moral View of the World
plain: The initial phase, which serves as the starting point, is the real moral self-consciousness, or simply the fact that such awareness exists. The concept constructs moral self-consciousness in a way that, for it, all reality holds essential being only insofar as it aligns with duty. This concept establishes that essential element as knowledge, meaning in direct unity with the actual self. Consequently, this unity is itself real, forming a moral actual consciousness. Now, as a consciousness, this entity shows its content to itself as an object, namely as the world’s final purpose and the harmony between morality and all reality. Therefore, the first claim states that morally complete actual self-consciousness does not exist. Since the moral is only truly so when it is complete, because duty is the pure, unadulterated ultimate element, and morality consists solely in conforming to this pure principle, the second claim asserts that morally actual existence does not exist at all. However, since it is a self, it inherently unites duty and actual reality. This unity becomes its object, representing completed morality. Yet, this object lies beyond its current reality, serving as a "beyond" that still ought to be real.
original: The first stage, which forms the starting point, is the actual moral self-consciousness, or is the fact that there is such a self-consciousness at all. For the notion establishes moral self -consciousness m. the form that, for it, all reality in general has essential being only so far as such reality is in conformity with duty; and that notion establishes this essential element as knowledge, i.e. in immediate unity with the actual self. This unity is thus itself actual, is a moral actual consciousness. The latter, now, qua consciousness, presents its content to itself as an object, viz. as the final purpose of the world, as the harmony of morality with all reahty. The proposition consequently now runs thus: "there is no morally complete actual self-consciousness"; and, since what is moral only is in the long run so far as it is complete, — for duty is the pure unadulterated ultimate element (Ansich), and morahty consists merely in conformity to this pure principle — the second proposition runs: " there is no morally actual existence at all." Since, however, in the third place, it is a self, it is inherently the unity of duty and actual reahty. This unity thus becomes its object, as completed morality — but as something beyond its actual reality, and yet a " beyond" which still ought to be real.

plain: These specific definitions are actually inadequate and trivial, because life is not a physical object, and neither the soul, the spirit, nor the self can be labeled as an object. Existence is the most basic attribute one can attribute to spirit, representing its simple, direct self-identity. While existence certainly applies to spirit, it is a definition so minimal that it hardly deserves to be used in this context. Second, we encounter the antinomy, which is the contradiction within Reason’s concept of the Unconditioned. This concept is applied to the world to depict it as a finished collection of all conditions. In other words, when looking at existing phenomena, Reason insists on the absolute completeness of the conditions that make them possible, provided these conditions form a sequence, such that the unconditioned is included within the world, meaning the entire sequence. When this completeness is described as actually existing, only an antinomy appears, and Reason shows itself merely as dialectic. This means that within this subject, a total contradiction is found from every angle.
original: But really such determinations are too poor and too mean, for what possesses life is not a thing, nor can the soul, the spirit, the ego, be called a thing. Being is the least or lowest quality that one can assign to spirit, its abstract, immediate identity with itself; Being thus no doubt pertains to spirit, but it must be considered as a determination scarcely worth applying to it. β. In the second place we have the antinomy, i.e. the contradiction in Reason’s Idea of the Unconditioned, an Idea applied to the world in order to represent it as a complete summing-up of conditions. That is to say, in the given phenomena Reason demands the absolute completeness of the conditions of their possibility, so far as these constitute a series, so that the unconditioned is contained in the world, i.e. the totality of the series. If now this completeness is expressed as existing, an antinomy is alone presented, and Reason is presented only as dialectic: i.e. in this object there is on every side a perfect contradiction found.

plain: Kant holds most tightly to this fact (Kritik der reinen Vernunft, p. 467): Being cannot be pulled from the Notion. Consequently, thinking the Infinite is certainly Reason, yet the Idea of Reason lacks any general determination, particularly the one called Being. Experience cannot prove or verify the Ideas of Reason. Defining them via categories generates contradictions. Defining the Idea solely as existent reduces it to the Notion, leaving the Being of that existent distinct. This outcome is vital for understanding the understanding’s knowledge, but Kant does not extend it to Reason. He merely states Reason provides formal unity for systematizing the understanding’s knowledge methodically. He clings to abstract thought, claiming the understanding only imposes order on things. However, order is not self-subsistent; it is merely subjective. Thus, Reason retains only its pure self-identity form. This extends only to arranging the understanding’s diverse laws and relations, along with the classes, kinds, and species the understanding discovers.
original: The fact to which Kant clings most strongly (Kritik der reinen Vernunft, p. 467) is this, that Being cannot be extracted from the Notion. The result of this is the proposition that to have the thought of the Infinite is certainly Reason; but that from the Idea of Reason is separated determination in general, and especially the determination which is known as Being. The Ideas of Reason cannot be proved from experience, or obtain from it their verification: if they are defined by means of categories, contradictions arise. If the Idea in general is to be defined as existent only, it is nothing more or less than the Notion; and the Being of the existent is still distinguished from it. This result, however, so highly important with reference to knowledge of the understanding, Kant does not, with reference to Reason, carry further than to say that Reason has on its own account nothing but formal unity for the methodical systematization of the knowledge of the understanding. Abstract thinking is adhered to; it is said that the understanding can only bring about order in things; but order is nothing in and for itself, it is only subjective. There therefore remains nothing for Reason except the form of its pure identity with itself, and this extends no further than to the arranging of the manifold laws and relations of the understanding, the classes, kinds and species which the understanding discovers.

plain: What appeared as an outside entity, triggering power to act and then retreat into itself, is actually power itself. This other reveals itself as both a universal medium and a singular unit, demonstrating this by making each form it takes seem like a fleeting stage. Therefore, because power has an other and exists for that other, its full significance remains undeveloped. Two powers exist simultaneously. While they share the same concept, that concept has moved from unity into duality. Rather than the opposition remaining a simple, essential phase, it seems to have broken free from the control of unity. Due to this separation, it has become two completely independent powers. We must now examine precisely what kind of situation this independence creates. First, the second power relates to the triggered power as the triggering agent. Furthermore, regarding its content, it functions as the universal medium.
original: What took the character of an external other, and incited force at once to expression and to return into self, turns out directly to be itself force: for the other shows itself to be luiiversal medium as well as one and single, and shows this in such a way that each of the forms assumed appears at the same time to be merely a vanishing moment. Consequently force, in that there is an other for it, and it is for an other, has as a whole not yet developed its complete meaning. There are two forces present at the same time; the notion of both is no doubt the same notion, but it has passed out of its unity into duality. Instead of the opposition continuing to be entirely and essentially a mere moment, it appears to have escaped from the control of the unity and to have become, owing to this diremption, two quite independent forces. We have now to see more precisely what sort of situation this independence introduces. To begin with, the second force stands towards the force incited in the character of inciting force, and, moreover, with respect to its content, plays the part of universal medium.

plain: Now that the opening comments are complete, we must turn to the subject itself. We remain in the introductory phase, which can only outline the general path for the later scientific analysis. Since we described art as emerging from the absolute Idea and defined its goal as the sensory depiction of the absolute, this overview must demonstrate how the specific parts of the topic derive from the concept of artistic beauty as the manifestation of the absolute. Consequently, we need to form a broad understanding of this concept. We previously noted that art’s content is the Idea, while its form consists in the shaping of images perceivable by the senses. Art must harmonize these two aspects into a complete and unified whole. The initial implication of this unity is the demand that the content intended for artistic depiction must inherently possess the quality of being suitable for such representation.
original: 1. After the above introductory remarks, it is now time to pass to the study of our object-matter. But we are still in the introduction, and an introduction cannot do more than lay down, for the sake of explanation, the general sketch of the entire course which will be followed by our subsequent scientific considerations. As, however, we have spoken of art as proceeding from the absolute Idea, and have even assigned as its end the sensuous representation of the absolute itself, we shall have to conduct this review in a way to show, at least in general, how the particular divisions of the subject spring from the conception of artistic beauty as the representation of the absolute. Therefore we must attempt to awaken a very general idea of this conception itself. It has already been said that the content of art is the Idea, and that its form lies in the plastic use of images accessible to sense. These two sides art has to reconcile into a full and united totality. The first attribution which this involves is the requirement that the content, which is to be offered to artistic representation, shall show itself to be in its nature worthy of such representation.

plain: Moreover, the individuals of the god, just like the traits of its essence, merge into the simplicity of a state lacking awareness. This necessity, unlike self-awareness, acts as the negative force behind all emerging forms. It is a power where these forms fail to identify themselves and instead vanish. The self shows up only as distributed among the various traits, rather than acting as the connecting element of the process. However, self-awareness, which is the simple certainty of the self, is actually the negative force. It is the unity of Zeus, combining the substantial essence with abstract necessity. It is the spiritual unity to which all things return. Since real self-awareness remains separate from substance and destiny, it functions partly as the chorus, or more accurately, as the spectators. These onlookers feel fear toward this divine movement because they see it as foreign and odd. Alternatively, because this movement affects them deeply, it only stirs a passive feeling of pity in them. On the other hand, to the extent that awareness participates and aligns with the different characters, this partnership is external. It is a pretense, because the genuine union of self, destiny, and substance has not yet arrived. The hero, who stands before the audience, splits into his mask and the performer. He divides into the character in the drama and his real self.
original: But, further, the persons of the divine Being itself, as well as the characters of its substance, coalesce into the simplicity of what is devoid of consciousness. This necessity has, in contrast to self-consciousness, the characteristic of being the negative power of all the forms that appear, a power in which they do not recognise themselves, but perish therein. The self appears as merely allotted amongst the different characters, and not as the mediating factor of the process. But self-consciousness, the simple certainty of self, is in poiut of fact the negative power, the unity of Zeus, the unity of the substantial essence and abstract necessity; it is the spiritual xmity iato which everything returns. Because actual self-consciousness is still distinguished from the substance and Fate, it is partly the chorus, or rather the crowd looking on, whom this movement of the divine Mfe fills with fear as being something ahen and strange, or in whom this movement, as something closely touching themselves, produces merely the emotion of passive pity. Partly again, so far as consciousness co-operates and belongs to the various characters, this alliance is of an external kind, is a hypocrisy — because the true union, that of self, fate, and substance is not yet present. The hero, who appears before the VOL, II.— z onlookers, breaks up into his mask and the actor, into the person of the play and the actual self.

plain: Cicero’s *Academics Quæstiones* preserves the core tenets of Arcesilaus’s thought, yet Sextus Empiricus serves as a superior source because his account is more exhaustive, precise, philosophical, and organized. a. We understand this system primarily as a dialectic aimed at Stoicism, a school with which Arcesilaus interacted extensively. Its central outcome is summarized by the rule that the wise individual must hold back their approval and agreement. This stance was termed ἐποχή, mirroring the Sceptic position. Conversely, this term links to Stoic doctrine in the following way. For Stoics, truth exists when thought claims a specific aspect of reality as its own, and the grasped concept validates that aspect. Consequently, the material of our concepts, principles, and ideas seems distinct from thought itself. The concrete unity of these two elements emerges only when a specific content is absorbed into the structure of thought, thereby manifesting as truth. Arcesilaus recognized this implication. His insistence on withholding approval effectively asserts that absorbing content in this manner yields no truth, merely appearance. This holds true because, as Arcesilaus argues, conception and thought remain separated.
original: The principal points in the philosophy of Arcesilaus are preserved by Cicero in his Academics Quæstiones, but Sextus Empiricus is more valuable as an authority, for he is more thorough, definite, philosophic and systematic. a. This philosophy is specially known to us as being a dialectic directed against Stoicism, with which Arcesilaus had much to do, and its result, as far as its main principles are concerned, is expressed thus: “The wise man must restrain his approbation and assent.” This principle was called ἐποχή, and it is the same as that of the Sceptics; on the other hand this expression is connected with the principle of the Stoics as follows. Because to Stoic philosophy truth consists in the fact that thought declares some content of existence to be its own, and the conception as comprehended gives its approbation to this content, the content of our conceptions, principles and thoughts undoubtedly appears to be different from thought, and the union of the two, which is the concrete, only arises by means of some determinate content being taken up into the form of thought and thus being expressed as the truth. But Arcesilaus saw this consequence, and his saying that approbation most be withheld is thus as much as saying that by thus taking up the content no truth comes to pass, but only phenomenon; and this is true, because, as Arcesilaus puts it, conception and thought likewise remain apart.

plain: The mind assumes these diverse postures for two distinct purposes. First, it seeks to internalize these modes of its own reality, adapting to the customs, habits, and thought patterns it encounters. It treats these external elements as the true ground of its existence and as objects for its self-awareness. Second, it aims to recognize its own spontaneous activity in contrast to them. It follows the natural direction of its own inclinations, feelings, and emotions, extracting from them only what holds specific, immediate significance for itself. Through this process, it forces the objective world to conform to its own nature. In the first posture, the mind acts negatively against itself as a single, individual entity. In the second posture, it acts negatively against itself as a universal being. In the first case, independence or self-reliance merely gives the encountered reality the shape of conscious individuality in general. Regarding the actual content, it remains within the boundaries of the given general reality. In the second case, however, it imposes at least a specific modification on that reality. This change does not contradict the essential content of the reality, or it may even be a change where the individual, as a particular reality with unique content, sets itself against the general reality. This opposition becomes a type of wrongdoing if the individual negates that reality in a merely particular way. It also becomes a type of wrongdoing if the individual negates the reality in a general way, meaning for everyone. This occurs when the individual substitutes the existing world, right, law, and custom with a different world, right, law, and custom.
original: The mind adopts these various attitudes partly with a view to receiving these modes of its reahty into itself, and conforming to the habits, customs, and ways of thinking it thus comes across, as being that wherein mind is reahty and as such object to itself; partly with a view to knowing its own spontaneous activity in opposition to them, to follow the bent of its own inclinations, affections, and emotions, and carry off thence what is merely of particular and special moment for itself, and thus make what is objective conform to itself. In the former it behaves negatively towards itself as single and individual mind, in the latter negatively towards itself as the universal being. In the former a,spect independence [or self-dependence] gives what is met with merely the form of conscious tadividuahty in general, and as regards the content remains within the general reality given; in the second aspect, however, it gives the reahty at least a certain special modification, which does not contradict its essential content, or even a modification by which the individual qua particular reahty and pecuhar content sets itself against the general reahty. This opposition becomes a form of wrongdoing when the individual cancels that reality in a merely particular manner, or when it does so in a manner that is general and thus for all, when it puts another world, another right, law, and custom in place of those aheady there.

plain: This is merely a potential for damage. Yet the absence of real injury is no longer accidental, because the element of wrongdoing in private actions serves as the final basis for police authority. External realities exist within the infinite domain generated by the understanding, and therefore possess no natural limits. Consequently, no clear line can be drawn regarding what constitutes danger versus safety, suspicion versus innocence, prohibition versus monitoring, pardon with a warning versus retention under police watch, or dismissal on suspended sentence. Decisions rely on custom, the overall constitutional spirit, current conditions, immediate threats, and similar factors. No precise definition or absolute limit can be established here. Everything remains personal and shaped by subjective views. Any sharper distinctions stem from the constitutional spirit or the dangers of the era. For instance, during wartime, many morally neutral acts are treated as harmful. Due to this element of chance and arbitrary personal judgment, police face widespread disdain. They can use remote reasoning to bring any matter under their jurisdiction, since any situation may contain a potential for harm.
original: This is, indeed, only a possibility of harm. But that no actual injury is done is now no longer a matter of accident, since the aspect of wrong in private acts is the ultimate ground for the right of police control. The relations of external reality occur within the realm of the infinity created by the understanding, and have accordingly no inherent limit. Hence, as to what is dangerous and what not, what suspicious and what free from suspicion, what is to be forbidden, or kept under inspection, or pardoned with a reprimand, what is to be retained after pardon under police supervision, and what is to b'e dismissed on suspended sentence, no boundary can be laid down. Custom, the spirit of the constitution as a whole, the condition of the time, the danger of the moment, etc., furnish means for a decision. No fixed definition can here be given, or absolute boundary drawn. Here everything is personal and influenced by subjective opinion. To the spirit of the constitution or the danger of the times are due any more decisive characteristics. In time of war, e.g., many things morally harmless are looked on as harmful. Because of the presence of this aspect of contingency and arbitrary personality the police are viewed with odium. They can by far-fetched conclusions draw every kind of thing within their sphere; for in anything may be found a possibility of harm.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The Work of Art
plain: This drive spans a vast array of phenomena, reaching the way we create ourselves through external materials, as seen in artistic production. Humans do not just treat outside objects this way; they also treat themselves, specifically their natural bodies, which they intentionally modify rather than leaving unchanged. This impulse drives all forms of ornament and decoration, regardless of how crude, bad-tasted, disfiguring, or even harmful they are, such as the binding of Chinese women’s feet or the cutting of ears and lips. Only among educated people does the alteration of body, behavior, and all forms of self-expression stem from spiritual cultivation. Consequently, the widespread desire for artistic expression rests on the human rational drive to elevate the inner and outer worlds into spiritual awareness for oneself, creating an object where one recognizes one’s own identity. One fulfills this need for spiritual freedom by making all existing things clear within oneself and, in a matching manner, manifesting this clarified self externally. This process of self-duplication brings what lies within into sight and understanding for both one’s own mind and the minds of others. This constitutes the free rationality of humanity, which serves as the foundation and necessary source for all action, knowledge, and art.
original: This need traverses the most manifold phenomena, up to the mode of self-production in the medium of external things as it is known to us in the work of art. And it is not only external things that man treats in this way, but himself no less, i.e. his own natural form, which he does not leave as he finds it, but alters of set purpose. This is the cause of all ornament and decoration, though it may be as barbarous, as tasteless, as utterly disfiguring or even destructive as crushing Chinese ladies' feet, or as slitting the ears and lips. It is only among cultivated men that change of the figure, of behaviour, and of every kind and mode of self-utterance emanates from spiritual education. The universal need for expression in art lies, therefore, in man's rational impulse to exalt the inner and outer world into a spiritual consciousness for himself, as an object in which he recognizes his own self. He satisfies the need of this spiritual freedom when he makes all that exists explicit for himself within, and in a corresponding way realizes this his explicit self without, evoking thereby, in this reduplication of himself, what is in him into vision and into knowledge for his own mind and for that of others. This is the free rationality of man, in which, as all action and knowledge, so also art has its ground and necessary origin.

plain: The approach was therefore more restrained and practical. It reintroduced traditional logic and metaphysics, but with a key change: these elements were treated as facts of consciousness. In this way, Fries returned to Jacobi’s belief, specifically regarding immediate judgments that come from reason and obscure ideas that cannot be expressed in words. Fries aimed to refine the critique of pure reason by viewing the categories as facts of consciousness. Under this framework, one could insert whatever one wished. Bouterweck discussed the virtue and living nature of power. He noted that subject and object are seen as a single entity, which constitutes absolute virtue. Through this absolute virtue, we possess all existence and activity. This includes the eternal, absolute, and pure unity. In short, we hold the world within ourselves and ourselves within the world. This happens not through concepts or logical conclusions, but directly through the power that forms our existence and rational nature. However, it is impossible for any human being to know the All, or to know God in any manner. Krug authored a work titled "Groundwork of Philosophy." In it, he presented a "Transcendental Synthesis." He defined this as a transcendental realism and a transcendental idealism that are inseparably linked. He described it as a primordial blend of the real and ideal aspects, uniting the thinking subject with the corresponding external world. This transcendental synthesis must be acknowledged and affirmed. No attempt should be made to explain it.
original: Then it was both more sober and more prosaic, and thus brought the old logic and metaphysic once more into evidence, though with this modification that they are made facts of consciousness. Thus Fries turns back to the faith of Jacobi in the form of immediate judgments derived from reason, and dark conceptions incapable of utterance. He wished to improve the critique of pure reason by apprehending the categories as facts of consciousness; anything one chooses can in such a case be introduced. Bouterweck speaks of “The virtue, the living nature of power; the fact that subject and object are regarded as one, that is as absolute virtue. With this absolute virtue we have all Being and action, namely the eternal, absolute and pure unity; in one word we have grasped the world within us and we have grasped ourselves in the world, and that indeed not through conceptions and conclusions, but directly through the power which itself constitutes our existence and our rational nature. To know the All, or indeed to know God in any way, is, however, impossible for any mortal.” Krug wrote a “Groundwork of Philosophy,” setting forth a “Transcendental Synthesis—that is a transcendental realism and a transcendental idealism inseparably bound together,” It is an “original, transcendental synthesis of the real and the ideal, the thinking subject and the corresponding outer world;” this transcendental synthesis must “be recognized and asserted without any attempt being made at explaining

plain: Through this process, a conflict inevitably arises between the individual and both other individuals and the universal. We must examine this relationship and how it unfolds. Alternatively, this universality and duty carry a completely opposite meaning; they represent a specific individuality that separates itself from the universal. This individuality views pure duty as a universality that exists only on the surface and has been flipped inside out. It claims that duty is just a matter of words and treats it as something that exists only for the sake of something else. Conscience, which initially adopts a negative stance toward duty as a specific, given obligation, feels separated from it. However, because conscience fills this empty duty with specific content taken from its own self, it becomes positively aware that it, as this particular self, creates its own content. Its pure self, being empty knowledge, lacks any content or definiteness. The content it provides to that knowledge comes from its own self, specifically as this determinate self, and is derived from itself as a natural individuality.
original: By this means there necessarily comes about the opposition of individuality to other individuals and to the universal. And this relation and its procedure we have to consider. Or, agaia, this universality and duty have the absolutely opposite significance; they signify determinate individuahty, exempting itself from what is universal, individuality which looks on pure duty as universality that has appeared merely on the surface and is turned on its outside: " duty is merely a matter of words," and passes for that whose being is for something else. Conscience, which in the first instance takes up merely a negative attitude towards duty, qva a given determinate duty, feels itself detached from it. But since conscience fills empty duty with a determinate content drawn from its own self, it is positively aware of the fact that it, qua this particular self, makes its own content. Its pure self, as it is empty knowledge, is without content and without definiteness. The content which it supphes to that knowledge is drawn from its own self, qna this determinate self, is drawn from itself as a natural individuahty.
