plain: Within this connection, the simple act of the subject turning inward, along with the narrow focus of the wise person, is also eliminated. The same freedom, happiness, and constancy that Epicureanism, Stoicism, and Scepticism sought are certainly still goals for the subject. However, achieving them now requires turning toward God and paying attention to absolute truth, rather than escaping from the objective. Consequently, through the objective itself, the subject gains liberty and happiness. This is the position of honoring and fearing God. By directing himself toward this object, which stands before him as free and stable, the subject achieves the goal of his own freedom. Furthermore, this view contains contradictions that inevitably draw the mind's attention, and resolving them is necessary. If we take this partial stance, God occupies one side while human freedom occupies the other. A freedom that opposes the objective, where the thinking self-consciousness views the relationship of its pure interiority to itself as absolute, is only absolute in form, not in concrete reality. Therefore, when the human will defines itself negatively against the objective, we find the source of sin, which is evil in contrast to the absolute Affirmative.
original: In this relation the mere turning of the subject on himself, this talk of the wise man. in his one-sidedness, is likewise done away with. The same liberty, happiness, steadfastness, which were the aim of Epicureanism, Stoicism and Scepticism are doubtless still to be reached by the subject, but now this can only be brought about by turning to God, by giving heed to absolute truth, not by fleeing from the objective; so that by means of the objective itself, liberty and happiness are attained for the subject. This is the standpoint of reverencing and fearing God, so that by man’s turning to this his object, which stands before him free and firm, the object of the subject’s own freedom is attained. In the second place, there are contradictions herein contained which necessarily attract the attention of mind, and whose reconciliation is essential. If we adopt this one-sided position, God is on the one side, and man in his freedom is on the other. A freedom such as this, standing in contrast to the objective, a freedom in which man, as thinking self-consciousness, conceives as the absolute the relation of his pure inwardness to himself, is, however, only formally, and not concretely absolute. In so far then as the human will determines itself negatively towards the objective, we have the origin of sin, evil in contrast to the absolute Affirmative.

plain: Art starts closer to the mind and its thinking processes than does raw, unthinking external nature. In artistic creations, the mind deals only with its own substance. Even though art is not abstract thought or concept, but rather a development of the concept out of itself, a separation from itself toward the sensory world, the power of the thinking spirit remains present. This power allows the spirit to recognize itself not only in its specific form as self-consciousness, but also in its separated state, appearing as feeling and sensory experience. By transforming this changed thought back into clear ideas, the spirit restores itself. In this focus on its own opposite, the thinking spirit does not betray itself, nor does it forget or give itself up. It is not so weak that it cannot understand what is different from itself. Instead, it understands both itself and its opposite. The concept is universal, maintaining itself within its specific forms. It controls both itself and its "other." It becomes the power and activity that ends the separation it created. Therefore, the artwork where thought separates itself belongs, like thought itself, to the domain of understanding thought. When the mind examines this scientifically, it simply fulfills a need of its deepest nature.
original: In this respect art is, to begin with, nearer to mind and its thinking activity than is mere external unintelligent nature; in works of art, mind has to do but with its own. And even if artistic works are not abstract thought and notion, but are an evolution of the notion out of itself, an alienation from itself towards the sensuous, still the power of the thinking spirit (mind) lies herein, not merely to grasp itself only in its peculiar form of the self-conscious spirit (mind), but just as much to recognize itself in its alienation in the shape of feeling and the sensuous, in its other form, by transmuting the metamorphosed thought back into definite thoughts, and so restoring it to itself. And in this preoccupation with the other of itself the thinking spirit is not to be held untrue to itself as if forgetting or surrendering itself therein, nor is it so weak as to lack strength to comprehend what is different from itself, but it comprehends both itself and its opposite. For the notion is the universal, which preserves itself in its particularizations, dominates alike itself and its "other," and so becomes the power and activity that consists in undoing the alienation which it had evolved. And thus the work of art in which thought alienates itself belongs, like thought itself, to the realm of comprehending thought, and the mind, in subjecting it to scientific consideration, is thereby but satisfying the want of its own inmost nature.

plain: Solger died too young to fully work out the concrete form of the philosophical Idea. Consequently, he remained stuck on this side of negativity, which resembles the way Irony breaks down definite things and things that have real value in themselves. He viewed this specific type of negativity as the driving force behind artistic creation. However, looking at his real life and the solid, serious, and strong nature of his character, he was not actually an ironical artist in the way described earlier. Furthermore, his deep appreciation for true art, which grew through long periods of study, did not have an ironical quality. This point defends Solger, as his life, philosophy, and art should be kept separate from the earlier mentioned champions of irony. Regarding Ludwig Tieck, his intellectual development also comes from the era when Jena served as the literary hub. Tieck and other prominent figures of that time show great ease with the terms in question, yet they fail to clarify what they mean by them. For instance, Tieck frequently insists that Irony is necessary. But when he turns to critiquing major works of art, his identification and description of their greatness are excellent. Yet, if we expect this to be the moment when he explains where the Irony lies, perhaps in a piece like "Romeo and Juliet," we are disappointed, because he says nothing more about the Irony.
original: Unhappily Solger's life was too soon interrupted for him to have achieved the concrete development of the philosophical Idea. And so he never got beyond this aspect of negativity, which has affinity with the dissolution that Irony effects of what is determinate and of what has substantive value in itself, a negativity in which he saw the principle of artistic activity. Yet in his actual life, considering the solidity, seriousness, and strength of his character, he neither was himself, in the sense above depicted, an ironical artist, nor was his profound feeling for genuine works of art, developed in protracted art studies, in this respect of an ironical nature. So much in vindication of Solger, whose life, philosophy, and art merit to be distinguished from the previously mentioned apostles of irony. As regards Ludwig Tieck, his culture, too, dates from that period in which for some time Jena was the literary centre. Tieck and others of these distinguished people display great familiarity with the phrases in question, but without telling us what they mean by them. Thus, Tieck no doubt always says there ought to be Irony; but when he himself approaches the criticism of great works of art, though his recognition and portrayal of their greatness is excellent, yet, if we fancy that now is the best opportunity to explain where the Irony is, e.g. in such a work as "Romeo and Juliet," we are taken in--for we hear no more about the Irony.

plain: It is reasonable to expect any historical account, regardless of its topic, to present facts impartially and without pursuing a specific agenda. However, this simple requirement offers little guidance. The history of any field is deeply tied to how we define that field. This definition dictates what matters, and the connection between events and the field’s purpose guides which facts are chosen, how they are understood, and the perspective from which they are viewed. A reader’s understanding of what a state truly is might lead them to find nothing of value in a country’s political history. This disconnect is even more likely in the history of philosophy. Some accounts of philosophical history contain everything except what is actually considered philosophy. In other historical works, the subject is clearly defined, at least in its main aspects. We know if the focus is on a specific region, group, or race, or if it covers a science like mathematics or physics, or an art form like painting.
original: The demand that a history, whatever the subject may be, should state the facts without prejudice and without any particular object or end to be gained by its means, must be regarded as a fair one. But with a commonplace demand like this, we do not get far; for the history of a subject is necessarily intimately connected with the conception which is formed of it. In accordance with this what is important in it is determined, and the relation of the events to the end regulates the selection of facts to be recorded, the mode of comprehending them, and the point of view under which they are regarded. It may happen from the ideas formed of what a State really is, that a reader of the political history of a country may find therein nothing of what he looks for. Still more may this be the case in the history of Philosophy, and representations of this history may be instanced in which everything, excepting what was supposed to be Philosophy, appears to be found. In other histories we have a clear conception of their subjects, at least so far as their principal points are concerned; we know whether they concern a particular land, people or race, or whether their subject is the science of mathematics, physics, &c., or an art, such as painting.

plain: In section three, line eight, chapter nine, regarding the mind, his second principle, the single absolute Good acts as a fountain that possesses no higher cause. It serves as the origin for all outflows, yet it does not get consumed by them. Instead, it stays still within itself while holding these outflows as they are. Consequently, these flows move in various directions without actually leaving, fully aware of their origin and destination. Plotinus frequently returns to this distinction. Moving from the hidden to the revealed, and this act of creation, is a significant point. Next, the first thing produced by this Unity, the Son, is limited understanding, the mind, which is the second divine being and the other principle. Here we face the central difficulty, a task identified and acknowledged for many years: understanding how the One chose to define itself. The attempt to clarify this fact remains the key area of interest. The ancients did not pose this question in the specific form we use today, but they still engaged with it.
original: III. l. 8, c. 9) of the νοῦς, his second principle, “The one absolute Good is a source which has no other principle, but is the principle for all streams, so that it is not swallowed up by these, but as source remains at rest in itself,” and thus contains these streams as such in itself; so that they, “flowing out in one direction and another, have yet not flowed away, but know whence and whither they are flowing.” This distinction is the point to which Plotinus often returns, and this advance from the unrevealed to the revelation, this production, is a point of importance. b. Now what is first begotten by this Unity, the Son, is finite understanding (νοῦς), the second Divine Being, the other principle. Here the main difficulty confronts us—the task known and recognized long years ago—the comprehension of how the One came to the decision to determine itself; and the endeavour to elucidate this fact still constitutes the essential point of interest. The ancients did not frame this question in the definite form in which we have it; but they nevertheless occupied themselves with it.

plain: In a properly structured monarchy, the objective aspect of law is present, and the ruler adds only their personal "I will" to it. The two components—the ultimate, unmotivated self of the will and the similar, unmotivated existence on the natural side—fuse inseparably within the concept of what lies beyond arbitrary whim. Together, they form the monarch's majesty. This unity represents the state’s realized oneness. Only through its unmotivated directness in both external and internal aspects does the unity escape the risk of being degraded by the willfulness, goals, and perspectives of particular interests. It is thereby shielded from the weakening and collapse of state functions, as well as from the conflict between factions vying for power around the throne. Legitimacy rests on the rights of birth and inheritance, not just in terms of positive law, but also within the idea itself. By having a self-determined or natural succession to the empty throne, all factional disputes are prevented. This has rightly been considered one of the benefits of inheritance. Nevertheless, it is merely a consequence, and treating it as a motive pulls majesty down into the realm of mere reasoning. The essence of majesty is unmotivated directness and final, self-contained existence.
original: In a well-ordered monarchy only the objective side of law comes to hand, and to this the monarch subjoins merely the subjective " I will." Both elements, the final motiveless self of the will, and the like motiveless existence on the side of nature, indissolubly unite in the idea of that which is beyond the reach of caprice, and constitute the majesty of the monarch. In this unity lies the actualized unity of the state. Only by means of its uumotived directness on both its external and its internal side is the unity taken beyond the possibility of degradation to the wilfulness, ends, and views of particularity. It is thus removed also from the enfeeblement and overthrow of the functions of state and from the struggle of faction against faction around the throne. Right of birth and right of inheritance constitute the basis of legitimacy, not as regards positive right merely, but likewise in the idea. — Through the self-determined or natural succession to the vacant throne all factious disputes are avoided. This has rightly been reckoned as one of the advantages of inheritance. However, it is only a consequence, and to assign it as a motive is to drag majesty down into the sphere of mere reasonings. The character of majesty is unmotived directness, and final self-involved existence.

plain: Reason is fully justified in holding this ground and rejecting the pull of mental constructs that merely should exist. It refuses to accept truth based on this "should," even if such things never appear in experience. It also rejects hypothetical hints and other intangible fictions created to serve an eternal "should" that never actually is. Reason is precisely the certainty of possessing reality. Therefore, anything this awareness does not recognize as an existing entity, meaning anything that does not show up, is nothing to this awareness at all. The true nature of law, which is essentially reality, will likely appear to awareness as an opposite to the concept and the inherently universal, provided awareness remains at the level of observation. In other words, this awareness does not view its law as a reality of reason; instead, it perceives the object as external and alien. However, it contradicts its own idea by failing to recognize that its universality does not require every individual sensory thing to have demonstrated the law before its truth can be claimed.
original: The instinct of reason is entirely within its rights when it stands firm on this point, and refuses to be led astray by entia intellectus which merely ought to be, and would have truth in the sense of this " ought to be," even though they are to be met with nowhere in experience; and dechnes to be turned aside by the hypothetical suggestions and all the other impalpable unreahties designed in the interest of an everlasting " ought to be " which never is. For reason is just this certainty of having reality, and what this consciousness is not aware of as an existent entity, i.e. what does not appear, is nothing for consciousness here at all. The true nature of law, viz.: that it essentially is reality, will, no doubt, again assume for consciousness, if it stops at the level of observation, the form of an opposite over against the notion and the inherently universal; in other words, this consciousness does not take such an object as its law to be a reality of reason; it ttinks it has got there something external and foreign. But it contradicts its own idea by actually and in fact not taking its universality to mean that all individual things of sense must have given evidence of the law to enable the truth of the law to be asserted.

plain: The Absolute constitutes Essence. This definition aligns with the earlier claim that the Absolute is Being, given that Being also functions as a simple self-relation. However, this new definition stands at a higher level because Essence represents Being that has turned inward. In other words, the simple self-relation found in Being is explicitly framed as the negation of the negative, serving as an internal process of self-mediation. Unfortunately, when people define the Absolute as Essence, they frequently interpret the implied negativity merely as the removal of all specific attributes. This act of withdrawal or abstraction ends up existing outside of Essence itself. Consequently, Essence remains as a bare outcome, separated from its underlying assumptions, becoming the lifeless residue of abstraction. Since this negativity is not external to Being but rather its own dialectical movement, the truth of Being—which is Essence—appears as Being that has withdrawn into itself, or immanent Being. This reflection, or the light cast back upon itself, creates the distinction between Essence and immediate Being. It serves as the unique feature of Essence. Any reference to Essence requires us to separate it from Being. Being is immediate, and when viewed against Essence, we regard it as mere appearance. Yet, this appearance is not complete non-existence or absolute nothingness. Instead, it is Being that has been overtaken and set aside.
original: The Absolute is the Essence. This is the same definition as the previous one that the Absolute is Being, in so far as Being likewise is simple self-relation. But it is at the same time higher, because Essence is Being that has gone into itself: that is to say, the simple self-relation (in Being) is expressly put as negation of the negative, as immanent self-mediation.--Unfortunately when the Absolute is defined to be the Essence, the negativity which this implies is often taken only to mean the withdrawal of all determinate predicates. This negative action of withdrawal or abstraction thus falls outside of the Essence--which is thus left as a mere result apart from its premisses,--the caput mortuum of abstraction. But as this negativity, instead of being external to Being, is its own dialectic, the truth of the latter, viz. Essence, will be Being as retired within itself,--immanent Being. That reflection, or light thrown into itself, constitutes the distinction between Essence and immediate Being, and is the peculiar characteristic of Essence itself. Any mention of Essence implies that we distinguish it from Being: the latter is immediate, and, compared with the Essence, we look upon it as mere seeming. But this seeming is not an utter nonentity and nothing at all, but Being superseded and put by.

plain: The state achieves its concept and inner stability by merging universal and particular interests. Holding an official role does not rest on a contract, even though it requires mutual agreement and reciprocal duties. Unlike a lawyer, who is hired for a specific, one-time task, a public official finds the core of both their spiritual and personal life in their work. Consequently, the duties assigned to them are not just external or specific tasks. The intrinsic worth of these duties differs from their outward appearance, so they are not damaged simply by failure to act, the way a contract is. The tasks a public official must carry out possess inherent, absolute value. Therefore, any positive harm or failure to act contradicts the nature of service and constitutes a wrong against the universal good, making it a fault or crime.
original: Here is found the conjunction of universal and particular interests, a union which constitutes the conception and the internal stability of the state. Official position is not based upon contract, although it involves the consent of the two sides and also a double performance. The public servant is not called to a single chance act of service, as is the attorney, but finds in his work the main interest of both his spiritual and his particular existence. So also it is not a matter merely external and particular, the performance of which is intrusted to him. The value of such a matter on its inner side is different from the externality of it, and thus is not as yet injured, as a stipulation is, merely by non-performance. That which the public servant has to perform is as it stands of absolute value. Hence positive injury or non-performance, either being opposed to the essence of service, is a wrong to the universal content, and therefore a fault or crime.

ref: The First Principles of Fichte’s Philosophy
plain: Since the self is locked in conflict with what is not itself, and exists only through that conflict, it vanishes within that oneness. Reaching this goal is therefore pushed endlessly into a false, sensory infinity. This progression contains the exact same contradiction seen in Kant’s work and lacks any immediate reality on its own; the self possesses all reality only within its opposition. Fichte’s philosophy acknowledges only the finite mind, not the infinite. It fails to see mind as universal thinking, just as Kant’s philosophy fails to see the untrue; alternatively, it remains merely formal. Understanding absolute unity is grasped as a moral belief in the world’s arrangement, an absolute assumption that leads us to trust that every ethical deed we carry out will yield a positive outcome. Similar to Kant’s view, this concept resides within universal thought.
original: For because the ego is fixed in its opposition to the non-ego, and is only as being opposed, it becomes lost in that unity. The attainment of this aim is hence sent further and further back into the false, sensuous infinitude: it is a progression implying just the same contradiction as that found in Kant, and having no present actuality in itself; for the ego has all actuality in its opposition only. The Fichtian philosophy recognizes the finite spirit alone, and not the infinite; it does not recognize spirit as universal thought, as the Kantian philosophy does not recognize the not-true; or it is formal. The knowledge of absolute unity is apprehended as faith in a moral disposition of the world, an absolute hypothesis in accordance with which we have the belief that every moral action that we perform will have a good result. As in Kant’s case, this Idea belongs to universal thought.

plain: Design, similar to a mechanical object, exists as a complete whole. Yet, it is enhanced by the principle of differentiation, which emerged in chemism. Consequently, it relates to the object that opposes it. Ultimately, the actualization of design marks the shift toward the Idea. (a) Mechanism. (1) In its immediate state, the object holds the notion only in potential. The subjective aspect of the notion lies primarily outside it. All specific traits are forced upon it from the outside. Therefore, as a unity of differing parts, it is a composite or an aggregate. Its ability to affect other things remains an external connection. This constitutes Formal Mechanism. Despite this connection and lack of independence, the objects stay independent and resist one another externally. Pressure and impact serve as examples of mechanical relations. We call our knowledge mechanical or rote when words lack meaning for us. They remain external to sense, conception, and thought. Since they are similarly external to one another, they create a meaningless sequence. Conduct and piety are mechanical in the same way. This happens when a person’s behavior is dictated by ceremonial laws or a spiritual advisor. In short, it occurs when his own mind and will are absent from his actions, making those actions foreign to himself.
original: Design, like the mechanical object, is a self-contained totality, enriched however by the principle of differentiation which came to the fore in chemism, and thus referring itself to the object that stands over against it. Finally, it is the realisation of design which forms the transition to the Idea. (a) Mechanism. The object (1) in its immediacy is the notion only potentially; the notion as subjective is primarily outside it; and all its specific character is imposed from without. As a unity of differents, therefore, it is a composite, an aggregate; and its capacity of acting on anything else continues to be an external relation. This is Formal Mechanism.--Notwithstanding, and in this connexion and non-independence, the objects remain independent and offer resistance, external to each other. Pressure and impact are examples of mechanical relations. Our knowledge is said to be mechanical or by rote, when the words have no meaning for us, but continue external to sense, conception, thought; and when, being similarly external to each other, they form a meaningless sequence. Conduct, piety, &c. are in the same way mechanical, when a man's behaviour is settled for him by ceremonial laws, by a spiritual adviser, &c.; in short, when his own mind and will are not in his actions, which in this way are extraneous to himself.

plain: The idea of an acid contains the idea of a base, much like the concept of positive charge suggests negative charge. However, while we observe that dense fur often appears in northern regions, or that fish anatomy aligns with water and bird anatomy with air, the concept of the north does not inherently suggest dense fur. Similarly, the concept of fish anatomy does not contain the concept of the sea, nor does the concept of bird anatomy contain the concept of air. Because these two concepts can be freely separated, we find land animals that possess the key traits of birds, fish, and so on. Since this necessity cannot be imagined as an internal necessity of the object itself, it also loses its basis in sensory experience. It can no longer be seen in actual reality, having moved beyond the realm of reality.
original: In the concept of an acid lies the notion of a base, just as the notion of positive electricity implies that of negative; but even though we do find as a fact a thick coat of hair associated with northerly latitudes, the structure of a fish with water, or that of birds with air, there is nothing in the notion of the north implying the notion of a thick covering of hair, the notion of the structure of fish does not he in the notion of the sea, nor that of birds in that of the air. Because of this free detachment of the two notions from one another, there are as a fact also land animals with the essential characters of a bird, of fish, and so on. The necessity, just because it cannot be conceived to be an inner necessity of the object, ceases also to have a foothold in sense, and can be no longer observed ia actual reahty, but has quitted the sphere of reahty.

plain: Such an entity must consider its requirements in a general manner, examine its whole existence, and secure a durable, enduring benefit. Given this reality, the notion that an item might randomly fall into the hands of the first self-aware person (Lehen) who requires it is self-contradictory. In a communal system, where resources are distributed through a method that is both general and permanent, one of two outcomes occurs. Either every individual receives exactly what they need, which creates a conflict between this disparity and the fundamental character of consciousness, whose core rule is the equality of persons. Or, if one follows that rule of equality, goods are split evenly, meaning the portion each person receives bears no connection to their actual needs, even though this is the only thing that "share," or fair portion, truly signifies.
original: For such a being has to think of his need in a universal way, to look to his existence in its entirety, and procure himself a permanent lasting good. This being so, the idea that a thing is to become by chance the possession of the first self-conscious individual (Lehen) who happens to need it, is inconsistent with itself. In a communistic society, where provision would be made in a way which is universal and permanent, either each comes to have as much as he requires — in which case there is a contradiction between this inequality and the essential nature of consciousness, whose principle is the equality of individuals — or, acting on this last principle, there is an equal division of goods, and in this case the share each gets has no relation to his needs, and yet this is solely what "share," i.e. fair share, really means.

plain: Generated entities drift further away from oneness, sharing in it to a diminishing degree. The next stage in defining the Idea is called the trinity. Proclus, in his *Theology of Plato* (III, p. 140), initially offers an abstract definition, stating that its three forms are three gods. We must now examine specifically how he characterized this trinity. While the Neo-Platonists found this concept engaging, Proclus made it particularly significant because he refused to leave it in its abstract stages. He treated each of these three abstract aspects of the absolute, individually, as a complete triune whole, thereby creating a single, real trinity. Consequently, the entire structure contains three distinct spheres that are separated yet form a total unity. Each sphere must be viewed as complete and concrete within itself. This perspective is rightly considered a correct achievement. Since each difference within the Idea, while maintaining its own unity, actually embodies the whole of these moments, distinct sequences emerge in the process of generation. The whole is the movement of these three totalities establishing themselves in each other as identical. We will soon identify these specific sequences. Proclus devotes considerable attention to them, as he attempts to demonstrate the various powers within them.
original: Thus things that are begotten ever remove themselves more and more from unity, and partake of it less and less. The further determination of the Idea is known as the trinity (τριάς). Of this Proclus (Theol. Plat. III. p. 140) first of all gives the abstract definition that its three forms are three gods, and now we have more especially to find out how he defined the trinity. This trinity is certainly interesting in the Neo-Platonists, but it is specially so in the case of Proclus, because he did not leave it in its abstract moments. For he again considers these three abstract determinations of the absolute, each on its own account, as a totality of triunity, whereby he obtains one real trinity. Thus in the whole there are three spheres, separated from one another, which constitute the totality, but in such a way that each has again to be considered as complete and concrete in itself; and this must be acknowledged as a perfectly correct point of view which has been reached. Because each of these differences in the Idea, as remaining in unity with itself, is really again the whole of these moments, there are different orders in production; and the whole is the process of the three totalities establishing themselves in one another as identical. It will be shown directly which orders these are, and Proclus occupies himself much with these, because he tries to demonstrate the different powers again in them.

ref: Culture and its Sphere of Reality
plain: Spirit preserves this mode of reality here, since the opposing poles, whose oneness constitutes Spirit, directly possess the nature of independent realities. Their oneness fragments into fixed aspects, each serving as a concrete object for the other, while each remains excluded from the other. Consequently, the oneness takes on the role of a mediating element, set apart and distinct from the separated reality of the two sides. It therefore holds the actual character of something objective, separate, and distinct from its aspects, and objective toward them; in other words, the oneness is an existing objective fact. In this manner, Spirit acts as the mediating element, assuming those extremes and arising through their existence. Yet it is also the spiritual whole that erupts between them, splitting its self into them, and generating each solely by virtue of the contact with the whole that belongs to its own principle. The fact that both extremes are inherently and from the outset transcended and fragmented reveals their unity. This is the process that merges both, swaps their distinctive traits, and binds them, doing so within each extreme. Thus, this mediating process actualizes the core essence of every opposing pole, or renders what each inherently is in itself its governing and driving spirit.
original: Spirit maintains this form of reahty here, because the extremes, too, whose unity spirit is, have directly the character of being realities each on its own accoimt. Their unity is disintegrated into rigid aspects, each of which is an actual object for the other, and each is excluded from the other. The unity, therefore, appears in the rdle of a mediating term, which is excluded and distinguished from the separated reahty of the two sides; it has, therefore, itself the actual character of something objective, apart, and distinguished from its aspects, and objective for them, i.e. the unity is an existent objective fact. Spirit in this way is the mediating term, presupposing those extremes and produced through their existence; but it is also the spiritual whole breaking out between them, which sunders its self into them, and creates each solely in virtue of that contact with the whole which belongs to its very principle. The fact that both extremes are from the start and in their very nature transcended and disiategrated brings out their unity; and this is the process which fuses both together, interchanges their characteristic features, and binds them together, and does so in each extreme. This mediating process consequently actuahses the principle of each of the two extremes, or makes what each is inherently in itself its controlling and moving spirit.

plain: Bringing these two parts together forms its education. The initial stage concludes when its powers merge to generate true strength, which then attacks the very foundation that supported it. The next stage brings triumph and success. However, as the nation focuses its energy outward, it betrays its own values internally, and domestic conflict arises once external stimulation stops. This split between the Ideal and the Real also appears in Art and Science. This marks the beginning of decline. The final stage involves destruction, caused by contact with a nation that represents a superior Spirit. We can state once and for all that this same pattern occurs in the history of every major people. Greece represents the Substantial, meaning Moral and Intellectual Principle, in a form that is also individual. The Universal, or the Abstract, is defeated in this context. Immersion in Nature no longer exists, and consequently, the clumsy nature of geographical connections has disappeared. The region in question consists of land spreading in various forms across the sea, including many islands and a mainland that itself shows island-like traits. The Peloponnesus links to the mainland only via a narrow strip of land. The entire area of Greece is cut into by bays in countless shapes.
original: The uniting of these two elements constitutes its training; and the first period ends with the combination of its forces to produce its real and proper vigour, which then turns against the very element that had been its basis. The second period is that of victory and prosperity. But while the nation directs its energies outwards, it becomes unfaithful to its principles at home, and internal dissension follows upon the ceasing of the external excitement. In Art and Science, too, this shews itself in the Separation of the Ideal from the Real. Here is the point of decline. The third period is that of ruin, through contact with the nation that embodies a higher Spirit. The same process, it may be stated once for all, will meet us in the life of every world-historical people. Greece is [that form of] the Substantial [i.e. of Moral and Intellectual Principle,'] which is at the same time individual. The Universal [the Abstract], as such, is overcome; the submersion in Nature no longer exists, and consentaneously the unwieldy character of geographical relations has also vanished. The country now under consideration is a section of territory spreading itself in various forms through the sea, — a multitude of islands, and a continent which itself exhibits insular features. The Peloponnesus is connected with the continent only by a narrow isthmus: the whole of Greece is indented by bays in numberless shapes.

plain: Grasping the natural world remains standard, non-speculative scientific understanding. When it asserts itself as philosophy, its core is just a broad speaking style that manipulates terms like "forces," "relations," and "diverse linkages" without reaching any concrete conclusion. Likewise, in the spiritual domain, it holds some truth that the metaphysics of the spirit acts as a specific arrangement through which capacities named sensation and perception arise. Yet this manner of discourse is tedious and renders nothing clear. It takes appearances and perceptions at face value and reasons about them, while simultaneously reducing their hidden existence to distinct forces whose internal character remains unknown. Defining and knowing the moral sphere likewise aims to revert humans to their so-called natural drives. Its essence takes the form of a natural impulse, which is called self-love, selfishness, or benevolence. Humans are required to live in accord with nature; however, this nature extends no further than general phrases and characterizations, like the state of nature depicted by Rousseau.
original: The knowledge of nature remains the ordinary, scientifically unspeculative knowledge, and as to its essence, in so far as it claims to be philosophy, it is a general way of speaking that plays with the words, “forces, relations, manifold connections,” but arrives at nothing definite. Similarly, in the spiritual sphere, it is so far true that the metaphysic of the spirit is of such a nature that it is nothing more nor less than a particular organization by means of which the powers which are termed sensation, perception, &c., come into existence; but this is a wearisome way of talking, which can make nothing intelligible, which accepts appearances and perceptions and reasons about them, but none the less reduces their implicit existence to certain determinate forces, of the inward nature of which we know nothing further. The determination and knowledge of the moral sphere has similarly for its object to bring man back to his so-called natural promptings; its essence has the form of a natural impulse, and this natural impulse is termed self-love, selfishness, or benevolence. It is required that man should live in conformity with nature; but this nature does not reach further than general expressions and descriptions, such as the state of nature we find depicted by Rousseau.

plain: Old religious beliefs portrayed both humans and deities as bound by fate, a force we should understand as hidden necessity, completely without personality, self-interest, or sight. In contrast, the Christian deity is not just known by others but also aware of itself. This being is not merely a mental image but exists as an absolute reality. A deeper look at these points belongs in the study of religious philosophy. However, it is worth noting how vital it is for individuals to face all events with the attitude suggested by the old saying that each person builds their own luck. This implies that a person ultimately has the right to enjoy only what comes from themselves. The alternative approach involves blaming other people, bad conditions, or similar factors for our experiences. This represents another instance of the language of lack of freedom and serves as the source of dissatisfaction. If people realized that everything occurring to them is merely the result of their own nature, and that they carry only their own responsibility, they would be free. In every situation, they would possess the awareness that they have not been treated unjustly.
original: In the ancient creeds not only men, but even gods, were represented as subject to destiny (πεπρωμένον or εἱμαρμένη), a destiny which we must conceive as necessity not unveiled, and thus as something wholly impersonal, selfless, and blind. On the other hand, the Christian God is God not known merely, but also self-knowing; He is a personality not merely figured in our minds, but rather absolutely actual. We must refer to the Philosophy of Religion for a further discussion of the points here touched. But we may note in passing how important it is for any man to meet everything that befalls him with the spirit of the old proverb which describes each man as the architect of his own fortune. That means that it is only himself after all of which a man has the usufruct. The other way would be to lay the blame of whatever we experience upon other men, upon unfavourable circumstances, and the like. And this is a fresh example of the language of unfreedom, and at the same time the spring of discontent. If man saw, on the contrary, that whatever happens to him is only the outcome of himself, and that he only bears his own guilt, he would stand free, and in everything that came upon him would have the consciousness that he suffered no wrong.

plain: The driving force that sets these processes in motion and grants them specific reality is human necessity, instinct, preference, and passion. I deeply want my mental concepts to become actions and tangible realities. I aim to assert my personal identity through this connection. I seek fulfillment through carrying them out. If I am to work toward any goal, it must somehow be my own goal. While achieving specific plans, I must simultaneously experience personal satisfaction, even though the broader purpose involves a complex mix of outcomes, many of which hold no appeal for me. This is the fundamental right of personal existence: to find oneself fulfilled through one’s own efforts and labor. For people to care about anything, they must, in a sense, have a stake in it. They must feel their unique identity is rewarded by its success. A common error must be avoided here. We rightly assign blame and identify it as a flaw when we describe a person as "interested" in certain dealings. By this, we mean they pursue only their own private gain.
original: The motive power that puts them in operation, and gives them determinate existence, is the need, instinct, inclination, and passion of man. That some conception of mine should be developed into act and existence, is my earnest desire: I wish to assert my personality in connection with it: I wish to be satisfied by its execution. If I am to exert myself for any object, it must in some way or other be my object. In the accomplishment of such or such designs I must at the same time find my satisfaction; although the purpose for which I exert myself includes a complication of results, many of which have no interest for me. This is the absolute right of personal existence — to find itself satisfied in its activity and labour. If men are to interest themselves for anything, they must (so to speak) have part of their existence involved in it; find their individuality gratified by its attainment. Here a mistake must be avoided. We intend blame, and justly impute it as a fault, when we say of an individual, that he is " interested" (in taking part in such or such transactions,) that is, seeks only his private advantage.

plain: So, answering the query about which traits are good and rational, and how to align them, amounts to laying out the rules and structures of everyday life that the mind creates as it becomes an objective mind. In this process, the specific goals of self-directed action stop being accidental or optional. Consequently, analyzing the genuine value of drives, desires, and emotions is fundamentally the study of legal, ethical, and social obligations. The focus here is on the act of fulfilling these drives. This act possesses at least a formal kind of reason. It shifts the drives from their subjective nature, where they exist merely as aims, into an objective realm. In that realm, the subject comes to agree with itself. If we separate the specific matter or task from the act of executing it, and we view the resulting outcome as holding the element of personal individuality and its activity, we call that outcome an interest. Therefore, no result occurs without an interest.
original: The answer to the question, therefore, What are the good and rational propensities, and how they are to be co-ordinated with each other? resolves itself into an exposition of the laws and forms of common life produced by the mind when developing itself as objective mind—a development in which the content of autonomous action loses its contingency and optionality. The discussion of the true intrinsic worth of the impulses, inclinations, and passions is thus essentially the theory of legal, moral, and social duties. The subject is the act of satisfying impulses, an act of (at least) formal rationality, as it translates them from the subjectivity of content (which so far is purpose) into objectivity, where the subject is made to close with itself. If the content of the impulse is distinguished as the thing or business from this act of carrying it out, and we regard the thing which has been brought to pass as containing the element of subjective individuality and its action, this is what is called the interest. Nothing therefore is brought about without interest.

ref: Culture and its Sphere of Reality
plain: The words used to describe the state of falling apart, where spiritual life is torn to pieces, actually represent the ideal way of speaking for this whole phase of spiritual growth and culture. They capture the process of shaping self-awareness (Bildung) and reflect the spirit in its most genuine form. This self-awareness, which suits the rebellion that rejects its own rejection, is by definition absolute self-identity within absolute fragmentation. It is the pure act of connecting pure self-awareness with itself. It is the unity shown in the identical judgment, where the same personality serves as both the subject and the predicate. Yet, this identical judgment is also the infinite judgment. This is because the personality is completely split in two. The subject and predicate are entities that are totally indifferent to one another. They have no connection, no necessary unity, and each holds the power of an independent personality on its own.
original: The language expressing the condition of disintegration, wherein spiritual hfe is rent asunder, is, however, the perfect form of utterance for this entire stage of spiritual culture and development, the formative process of moulding self-consciousness (Bildung), and expresses the spirit in which it most truly exists. This self-consciousness, which finds befitting the rebelhon that repudiates its own repudiation, is eo ipso absolute self-identity in absolute disintegration, the pure activity of mediating pure self-consciousness with itself. It is the oneness expressed in the identical judgment, where one and the same personahty is subject as well as predicate. But this identical judgment is at the same time the infinite judgment; for this personahty is absolutely spht in two, and subject and predicate are entities utterly indifierent one to the other, which have nothing to do with each other, with no necessaryunity, so much so that each has the power of an independent personahty of its own.

plain: In fact, the reasoning turns harmful when it claims that because every completed task brings personal pleasure, that pleasure must be the agent’s true goal, with the external objective serving merely as a tool to secure it. The individual is defined by the sequence of their actions. If those actions produce nothing of value, the will behind them is equally worthless; if the actions are solid and meaningful, the person’s inner will shares that quality. The individual’s right to feel satisfied with their own existence, or the right to subjective freedom, marks the pivot between the ancient and modern worlds. Christianity expresses this right in its boundless form and establishes it as the driving force behind a new global structure. Specific expressions of this principle include love, romantic relationships, the hope for personal eternal salvation, morality, and conscience. It also encompasses other forms, some of which will appear later as the basis for civil society and components of political systems, while others show up throughout history, particularly in art, science, and philosophy. This principle of individuality currently forms one side of a contradiction, and initially, it is just as closely aligned with the universal as it is separate from it.
original: Nay, more, the argument becomes a positive evil when it is held that, because subjective satisfaction is always found in every finished work, it must be the essential intention of the agent, the objective end being only a means to the attainment of this satisfaction. The subject is the series of his acts. If these are a series of worthless productions, the subjectivity of the will is also worthless; if the acts are substantial and sound, so likewise is the inner will of the individual. The right of the subject's particular being to find himself satisfied, the right, in other words, of subjective freedom, constitutes the middle or turning-point between the ancient and the modem world. This right in its infinite nature is expressed in Christianity, and has been made the universal active principle of a new form of the world. The more definite manifestations of this principle are love, romance, the hope of the eternal salvation of the individual, morality also, and conscience. It includes, moreover, various other forms, which will be, in a measure, introduced in the sequel as the principle of the civic society, and as elements of the political constitution, but partly, however, appear in history generally, especially in the history of art, the sciences, and philosophy. This principle of particularity is now, indeed, one side of the contradiction, and, in the first resort, is at least quite as much identical with the universal as distinct from it.

plain: So, the meaning and the sign merge into a single representation. The inner aspect of this representation becomes concrete and gains existence for its meaning, a task accomplished by memory that holds onto names, known as retentive Memory. Within the realm of ideas, the name stands for the thing insofar as it exists and matters. Second, Reproductive memory possesses and identifies the thing through the name, and holds the name alongside the thing, independent of any direct perception or mental picture. By granting existence to content within intelligence, the name serves as intelligence’s external relation to itself. Recalling the name, which is an intuition of intellectual origin, simultaneously acts as a self-externalization where intelligence lowers itself to its own foundation. The linking of specific names resides in the significance of features described as sensitive, representative, or cogitant. Intelligence moves through these series as it experiences, represents, or thinks. When we have the name lion, we do not require the actual sight of the animal, nor even its mental image. The name alone, provided we comprehend it, constitutes a simple representation without an image. We think using names. Recent efforts, which were rightly forgotten, aimed to restore the ancient Mnemonic method. These attempts involved converting names into images, thereby demoting memory back to the level of imagination.
original: Thus the import (connotation) and sign, being identified, form one representation: the representation in its inwardness is rendered concrete and gets existence for its import: all this being the work of memory which retains names (retentive Memory). The name is thus the thing so far as it exists and counts in the ideational realm. (2) In the name, Reproductive memory has and recognises the thing, and with the thing it has the name, apart from intuition and image. The name, as giving an existence to the content in intelligence, is the externality of intelligence to itself; and the inwardising or recollection of the name, i.e. of an intuition of intellectual origin, is at the same time a self-externalisation to which intelligence reduces itself on its own ground. The association of the particular names lies in the meaning of the features sensitive, representative, or cogitant,—series of which the intelligence traverses as it feels, represents, or thinks. Given the name lion, we need neither the actual vision of the animal, nor its image even: the name alone, if we understand it, is the unimaged simple representation. We think in names. The recent attempts—already, as they deserved, forgotten—to rehabilitate the Mnemonic of the ancients, consist in transforming names into images, and thus again deposing memory to the level of imagination.

plain: The growth of the artistic spirit inherently possesses two aspects. First, this progression is spiritual and universal because the structured sequence of specific worldviews, which serve as a definite yet all-encompassing awareness of nature, humanity, and the divine, finds expression through art. Second, this broad artistic evolution must secure an external, sensory presence, and the specific ways this sensory existence manifests form a complete set of essential distinctions within the artistic domain, which constitute the individual arts. While the required forms of artistic expression are spiritually broad and not limited to any single substance, and sensory existence offers many material variations, the latter shares a potential connection with the Idea as its inner core. Consequently, specific sensory materials possess a deep compatibility and hidden harmony with the spiritual categories and types of artistic presentation. In its full scope, our discipline splits into three main sections. The first is a general section. Its subject matter is the universal Idea of artistic beauty, understood as the Ideal, along with the closer connections this Ideal holds with both nature and subjective artistic creation.
original: This evolution within the art-spirit has again in its own nature two sides. In the first place the development itself is a spiritual and universal one, in so far as the graduated series of definite conceptions of the world as the definite but comprehensive consciousness of nature, man and God, gives itself artistic shape; and, in the second place, this universal development of art is obliged to provide itself with external existence and sensuous form, and the definite modes of the sensuous art-existence are themselves a totality of necessary distinctions in the realm of art--which are the several arts. It is true, indeed, that the necessary kinds of artistic representation are on the one hand qua spiritual of a very general nature, and not restricted to any one material; while sensuous existence contains manifold varieties of matter. But as this latter, like the mind, has the Idea potentially for its inner soul, it follows from this that particular sensuous materials have a close affinity and secret accord with the spiritual distinctions and types of art presentation. In its completeness, however, our science divides itself into three principal portions. First, we obtain a general part. It has for its content and object the universal Idea of artistic beauty--this beauty being conceived as the Ideal--together with the nearer relation of the latter both to nature and to subjective artistic production.

plain: Leo X’s Council of Benevento rejected these two views in 1513. Pomponatius claimed the vegetative and sensitive soul perish (see chapter 8, page 36; chapter 9, pages 51, 62-65). He argued that humans share in immortality solely via reasoning and thinking. Inquisitors summoned Pomponatius, but because cardinals shielded him, officials ignored the case. Many other strict Aristotelians existed; they became common among later Protestants. Mislabeling Scholastics as Aristotelians was wrong. Thus, the Reformation seemed anti-Aristotle but actually opposed Scholasticism. People engaged more with Plato when his manuscripts reached Europe from Greece. Greek exiles from Constantinople taught Plato’s ideas. Cardinal Bessarion, formerly Constantinople’s Patriarch, actively promoted Plato in Western lands. Ficinus, a famous Florentine born 1433 and died 1499, translated Plato extensively. He chiefly revived Neo-Platonism, focusing on Proclus and Plotinus. Ficinus also authored a Platonic Theology. Cosmo II. of the Medici family founded a Platonic Academy in fifteenth-century Florence.
original: Both of these opinions were condemned in 1513 at the Council of Benevento, under Leo X. The vegetative and sensitive soul Pomponatius asserted to be mortal (c. VIII. p. 36; c. IX. pp. 51, 62-65): and he maintained that it is only through thought and reason that man partakes of immortality. Pomponatius was summoned before the Inquisition; but as cardinals protected him, no further notice was taken of the matter. There were many other pure Aristotelians; especially among the Protestants at a later time were they general. The Scholastics were erroneously termed Aristotelians; therefore the Reformation was opposed to Aristotle only in appearance, but to the Scholastics it was opposed in fact. Men now began to form acquaintance more especially with Plato, when manuscripts of his works were brought from Greece; Greeks, refugees from Constantinople, gave lectures on Plato’s philosophy. Cardinal Bessarion of Trapezunt, at one time Patriarch of Constantinople, was specially active in making Plato known in the West. Ficinus, who was born in Florence in 1433, and died in 1499, the accomplished translator of Plato, was a man of note; it was mainly due to him that the study of Neo-Platonism, as presented by Proclus and Plotinus, was again revived. Ficinus wrote also a Platonic Theology. One of the Medici in Florence, Cosmo II., went so far as to found a Platonic Academy even in the fifteenth century.

plain: Comparing the two types of evidence, or rather the two components of a legal verdict that reflect the actual situation regarding the defendant, forms the core issue in the debate over jury trials. This comparison hinges on whether the verdict relies solely on circumstantial evidence and testimony from others, or if it also demands a statement from the defendant admitting guilt. It is crucial that the two parts of a legal assessment—the determination of what actually happened and the application of legal rules to those facts—be treated as distinct roles, since they are fundamentally different aspects of the process. Under this system, these roles are assigned to groups with different qualifications, one of which explicitly bars members of the professional judiciary. Extending this division of labor to the courts themselves depends on factors that are not strictly essential; the primary goal remains simply ensuring that these inherently different tasks are performed separately. A more significant issue is whether a defendant’s admission should be required for a criminal sentence. The jury system overlooks this requirement. The argument here is that on this specific point, absolute certainty and actual truth are completely intertwined. An admission is viewed as the peak of certainty, a quality that is inherently personal and subjective. Consequently, the final judgment rests on that admission.
original: The comparison of the two species, or rather two elements in the judicial conviction, bearing on the actual state of the case in relation to the accused,—(1) according as that conviction is based on mere circumstances and other people’s witness alone,—or (2) in addition requires the confession of the accused, constitutes the main point in the question of the so-called jury-courts. It is an essential point that the two ingredients of a judicial cognisance, the judgment as to the state of the fact, and the judgment as application of the law to it, should, as at bottom different sides, be exercised as different functions. By the said institution they are allotted even to bodies differently qualified,—from the one of which individuals belonging to the official judiciary are expressly excluded. To carry this separation of functions up to this separation in the courts rests rather on extra-essential considerations: the main point remains only the separate performance of these essentially different functions.—It is a more important point whether the confession of the accused is or is not to be made a condition of penal judgment. The institution of the jury-court loses sight of this condition. The point is that on this ground certainty is completely inseparable from truth: but the confession is to be regarded as the very acmé of certainty-giving which in its nature is subjective. The final decision therefore lies with the confession.

plain: Pure theoretical thought locks onto this aspect as it stands apart from and conflicts with the universal. It puts forward the idea that ethics must wage a constant war against self-gratification. This same narrow perspective claims that since major deeds, along with the actual outcomes achieved through a sequence of them, have significantly impacted the world and naturally granted the actor power, honor, and fame, the individual is entitled only to these specific, external rewards, not to the greatness itself. The justification offered is that because the specific outcome was clearly a goal, it must be the only goal. This kind of abstract reasoning perceives only the personal dimension of great figures, the very dimension that defines its own character. In its self-created arrogance, it misses their true nature. It adopts the perspective of the "psychological servant who finds no heroes, not because heroes do not exist, but because he is merely a servant."
original: But abstract reflection fastens upon this element in its difference from and opposition to the universal, and propounds the view that morality must carry on a continued warfare against the satisfaction of oneself, demanding of us — This same abstract point of view asserts that because great acts, and the real result brought to pass by a series of them, have produced a great effect upon the world, and have naturally resulted to the agent in power, honour, and renown, therefore there belongs to the individual not the greatness, but merely these particular and external results. The reason assigned is that the particular consequence, since it was admittedly an end, must be the sole end. Such abstract thinking sees only the subjective side of great men, the side which constitutes its own essence. In its self-constituted vanity it overlooks their real nature. It takes the view of the " psychological valet for whom there are no heroes, not because there are no heroes, but because he is only a valet."

plain: Throughout life, each person tries to become who they truly are, and actually succeeds in doing so. When it comes to beauty and art, this means living like an artist and shaping one’s existence with artistic intent. From the perspective where the artist is the =I= that freely binds and releases, where no aspect of consciousness holds absolute or essential reality, but exists only as a constructed and breakable appearance, such sincerity cannot exist. This is because nothing is granted validity except the formalism of the =I=. Others might take my self-presentation seriously, interpreting my actions as if I were genuinely invested in the subject at hand. However, they are merely deceived, limited and unskilled individuals who lack the ability to grasp or reach my viewpoint. This reveals that not everyone possesses the formal freedom to view everything typically valued, dignified, or sacred by humanity as merely a product of their own whim. Such freedom allows one to stamp their own value onto these matters, choosing whether to define themselves and find content through them, or to reject them entirely.
original: For every human being while he lives, seeks to realize himself, and does realize himself. With respect to beauty and art this receives the meaning of living as artist and forming one's life artistically. At the standpoint according to which the artist is the =I= that binds and looses of its own power, for whom no content of consciousness counts as absolute and as essentially real, but only as itself an artificial and dissoluble semblance, such earnest can never come into being, as nothing has validity ascribed to it but the formalism of the =I=. By others, indeed, my self-display in which =I= present myself to them may be taken seriously, inasmuch as they interpret me as though I were really concerned about the matter in hand; but therein they are simply deceived, poor borné creatures, without talent and capacity to apprehend and to attain my standpoint. And this shows me that not every one is so free (formally free, that is) as to see in all that usually has value, dignity, and sanctity for mankind, simply a product of his own power of caprice, whereby he is able to set his seal on the value of such matters, and to determine himself and obtain a content by their means, or not.

plain: Yet the creature never advances far enough within its species to possess an independent existence; instead, it yields to the force of the species. Within the dynamic of the species, the direct living entity reconciles itself with itself, thereby transcending its directness, only to fall back into that directness once more. Consequently, life initially retreats merely into the illusory infinity of an endless progression. Nevertheless, the genuine outcome of the life process, when viewed through the lens of its concept, is to dissolve and surpass that directness which still entangles the idea, appearing in the form of life. In this way, the concept of life has shed not a single, specific, direct "this," but rather this initial directness in its entirety. It thereby returns to itself, to its truth: it begins to exist as a free species that is self-sustaining. The demise of purely direct and individual vitality constitutes the "procession" of spirit.
original: But the animal never gets so far in its Kind as to have a being of its own; it succumbs to the power of Kind. In the process of Kind the immediate living being mediates itself with itself, and thus rises above its immediacy, only however to sink back into it again. Life thus runs away, in the first instance, only into the false infinity of the progress ad infinitum. The real result, however, of the process of life, in the point of its notion, is to merge and overcome that immediacy with which the idea, in the shape of life, is still beset. In this manner however the idea of life has thrown off not some one particular and immediate 'This,' but this first immediacy as a whole. It thus comes to itself, to its truth: it enters upon existence as a free Kind self-subsistent. The death of merely immediate and individual vitality is the 'procession' of spirit.

plain: In the phase of individuality itself, where subjectivity and the concept merge, and the distinction between the universal and the particular dissolves into a shared foundation, the role of the starting assumption shifts. Here, the universal substance serves as that base, having moved from abstractness into an individual self-awareness. This individual, who is equated with the essence and known as the Son in the eternal realm, is placed within the realm of time. Within him, evil is quietly defeated. Next, this direct, sensory existence of the fully concrete is depicted as undergoing judgment and dying in the suffering of negation. In this process, he remains unaltered as infinite subjectivity. Consequently, he becomes the absolute return from that negation and the universal unity of universal and individual essence, thereby realizing his existence as the Idea of the spirit. This spirit is eternal, yet it is alive and present in the world. This complete, objective form of the divine human, which is the Idea of the spirit, acts as the hidden foundation for the finite, immediate experience of the single subject. For this subject, it initially appears as something external, an object of contemplative sight. However, this is the sight of hidden truth. Through the spirit’s witness within him, and due to his immediate nature, he initially defines himself as nothing and as wicked.
original: (γ) Under the “moment” of individuality as such,—of subjectivity and the notion itself, in which the contrast of universal and particular has sunk to its identical ground, the place of presupposition (1) is taken by the universal substance, as actualised out of its abstraction into an individual self-consciousness. This individual, who as such is identified with the essence,—(in the Eternal sphere he is called the Son)—is transplanted into the world of time, and in him wickedness is implicitly overcome. Further, this immediate, and thus sensuous, existence of the absolutely concrete is represented as putting himself in judgment and expiring in the pain of negativity, in which he, as infinite subjectivity, keeps himself unchanged, and thus, as absolute return from that negativity and as universal unity of universal and individual essentiality, has realised his being as the Idea of the spirit, eternal, but alive and present in the world. (2) This objective totality of the divine man who is the Idea of the spirit is the implicit presupposition for the finite immediacy of the single subject. For such subject therefore it is at first an Other, an object of contemplating vision,—but the vision of implicit truth, through which witness of the spirit in him, he, on account of his immediate nature, at first characterised himself as nought and wicked.

plain: Metaphysics seeks substance, which means holding onto a single unity and a single thought against dualism, mirroring how the ancients viewed Being. Yet within metaphysics itself, substantiality and individuality stand in opposition. The initial phase is a spontaneous, though uncritical, metaphysics, embodied by Descartes and Spinoza, who claim that Being and thought are one. The next stage appears in Locke, who examines this opposition by analyzing the metaphysical concept of experience. He looks at where thoughts come from and how they are justified, without yet asking if they are absolutely true. Third, we find Leibniz’s monad, which views the world as a complete whole. Here we meet the innate ideas that Descartes proposed. Spinoza’s philosophy, in the second place, relates to Descartes’ only as its necessary development, with method playing a key role. A third approach, which stands beside Spinozism and also represents a refined evolution of Cartesianism, is the method used by Malebranche to present this philosophy.
original: Metaphysics is what reaches after substance, and this implies that one unity, one thought is maintained in opposition to dualism, just as Being was amongst the ancients. In metaphysics itself we have, however, the opposition between substantiality and individuality. What comes first is the spontaneous, but likewise uncritical, metaphysics, and it is represented by Descartes and Spinoza, who assert the unity of Being and thought. The second stage is found in Locke, who treats of the opposition itself inasmuch as he considers the metaphysical Idea of experience, that is the origin of thoughts and their justification, not yet entering on the question of whether they are absolutely true. In the third place we have Leibnitz’s monad—the world viewed as a totality. We here encounter the innate ideas of Descartes. The philosophy of Spinoza, in the second place, is related to the philosophy of Descartes as its necessary development only; the method is an important part of it. A method which stands alongside of Spinozism and which is also a perfected development of Cartesianism, is, in the third place, that by which Malebranche has represented this philosophy.

plain: God’s primary quality is that He is truthful and the source of all illumination. Therefore, it is completely opposed to His character to mislead us. Consequently, the natural light, or the capacity for gaining understanding that God granted us, cannot interact with any subject that is not genuinely true, specifically in the way it is engaged by that capacity. This refers to how things are perceived clearly and distinctly. We attribute truthfulness to God. Based on this, Descartes deduces the universal link between absolute knowledge and the objective nature of what we know through it. Knowledge possesses objects and a content that is understood; we label this relationship as truth. God’s truthfulness is precisely this union of what the subject thinks or perceives clearly, and external reality or existence. This concludes the possibility of doubt, as though what seems entirely obvious to us might not actually be true. We can therefore no longer suspect mathematical truths. Similarly, if we pay attention to what we distinguish through our senses while awake or asleep, clearly and distinctly, it is straightforward to identify the true aspects of each thing.
original: “Now the first attribute of God is that He is true and the Giver of all light; it is hence quite contrary to His nature to deceive us. Hence the light of nature or the power of acquiring knowledge given us by God can affect no object which is not really true in as far as it is affected by it” (the power of acquiring knowledge) “i.e. as it is perceived clearly and distinctly.” We ascribe truth to God. From this Descartes goes on to infer the universal bond which exists between absolute knowledge and the objectivity of what we thus know. Knowledge has objects, has a content which is known; we call this connection truth. The truth of God is just this unity of what is thought by the subject or clearly perceived, and external reality or existence. “Thereby an end is put to doubt, as if it could be the case that what appears quite evident to us should not be really true. We can thus no longer have any suspicion of mathematical truths. Likewise if we give heed to what we distinguish by our senses in waking or in sleeping, clearly and distinctly, it is easy to recognize in each thing what in it is true.”

plain: The sensory aspect forms one part of the reflective will, while the abstract universality of thinking forms the other. The absolute will targets the will itself, specifically in its pure, universal form. Within this universality, the immediate nature of the natural will is overcome, as is the private individuality created by reflection that contaminates the natural state. Overcoming these elements and elevating them to the universal level defines the activity of thought. Consequently, self-consciousness, which cleanses its object, content, or goal and raises it to a universal level, represents thought moving into will. Here it becomes evident that the will is genuine and free only when it acts as a thinking intelligence. The slave fails to recognize his own nature, his boundlessness, or his freedom; he does not perceive himself in his essential nature, and failing to perceive oneself is equivalent to failing to think oneself. Self-consciousness, which uses thought to grasp that it is the essence and thereby discards the accidental and false, establishes the foundation for law, morality, and every form of ethical practice.
original: Now this sensible side is one of the two elements of the reflecting will, and the other is the abstract universality of thought. But the absolute will has as its object the will itself as such in its pure universality. In this universality the directness of the natural will is superseded, and so also is the private individuahty which is produced by reflection and infects the natural condition. But to supersede these and Uft them into the universal, constitutes the activity of thought. Thus the self- consciousness, which purifies its object, content or end, and exalts it to universality, is thought carrying itself through iato will. It is at this point that it Ibecomes clear that the will is true and free only as thinking intelligence. The slave knows not his essence, his infinitude, his freedom; he does not know himself in his essence, and not to know himself is not to think himself. (The self-consciousness, which by thought apprehends that itself is essence, and thus puts away from itself the accidental and untrue, constitutes the principle of right, morality, and all forms of ethical observance.

plain: Goethe, for example, produced extensive writings on art and specific pieces. The primary goal of this approach is not theoretical speculation, even though it often engages with abstract principles and categories, and might inadvertently drift toward that tendency. However, for a reader who does not allow this to impede them, but instead maintains focus on the concrete descriptions of artworks mentioned earlier, this approach provides the philosophy of art with tangible examples and illustrations. These details fall into specific historical contexts that philosophy itself cannot fully explore. Therefore, this can be considered the first method of studying art, which begins with existing, particular works. There is a fundamental difference between this method and the opposite perspective, which is purely theoretical reflection. That perspective attempted to comprehend beauty in its own right, solely from itself, and to uncover the essence of its concept.
