original: Thus Goethe, for instance, wrote much about art and particular works of art. Theorizing proper is not the purpose of this mode of consideration, although no doubt it frequently busies itself with abstract principles and categories, and may give way to this tendency without being aware of it. But for a reader who does not let this hinder him, but keeps before him the concrete accounts of works of art, which we spoke of just now, it at all events furnishes the philosophy of art with the perceptible illustrations and instances, into the particular historical details of which philosophy cannot enter. This, then, may be taken to be the first mode of the study of art, starting from particular and extant works. 2. There is an essential distinction between this and the opposite aspect, the wholly theoretical reflection, which made an effort to understand beauty as such out of itself alone, and to get to the bottom of its idea.

plain: Suppose we treat this supreme good as the fundamentally real. Then, consciousness is not fully sincere regarding morality. In this supreme good, nature does not operate under a law distinct from morality. Consequently, moral action itself disappears, because action occurs only when there is a negative or opposing element that the act must eliminate. However, if nature already aligns with the moral law, then acting would certainly violate that law by eliminating what is already present. Under this interpretation, the fundamental situation becomes one where moral action is unnecessary and does not occur at all. Therefore, the requirement for harmony between morality and reality — a harmony inherent in the concept of moral action, which involves aligning the two — is expressed on this view as follows: since moral action is the ultimate goal, the ultimate goal is that moral action never happens.
original: If, then, we allow this highest good to stand for the essentially real, consciousness is not altogether in earnest with morahty. For, in this highest good, nature has not a different law from what morahty has. Moral action itself, in consequence, drops, for action takes place only under the assumption of a negative or opposiag element which is to be cancelled by means of the act. But if nature conforms to the moral law, then undoubtedly this moral law would be violated by actiug, by cancelling what already exists. On that mode of interpretation, then, there has arisen as the essential situation one which renders moral action superfluous and in which moral action does not take place at all. Hence the postulate of the harmony between morahty and reahty — a harmony involved in the very notion of moral action, which means bringing the two into agreement — finds on this view, too, an expression which takes the form: — " because moral action is the absolute purpose, the absolute purpose is — that moral action do not take place at all."

plain: Boehme asserts that reality consists entirely of this triad, and this triad embodies all existence. He regards the cosmos as a single divine life, manifesting God within every object. Upon closer inspection of God’s singular reality, which aggregates all powers and qualities, the Son shines forth from these attributes and is eternally generated. The internal oneness of this light with the essence of the powers constitutes the Spirit. The exposition sometimes lacks clarity, while at other times it is distinct. The subsequent section explains this Trinity, where the various forms he employs to highlight the distinction emerging within the identical become particularly prominent. In the *Aurora*, which he calls the foundational source for Philosophy, Astrology, and Theology, he proposes a division placing these disciplines near one another, yet seems to shift from one to the next without precise definition or determination. He states that Philosophy addresses divine power, explaining what God is and how nature, stars, and Elementa are structured within God’s Being. It covers the source of all things, the nature of heaven and earth, as well as angels, humans, demons, heaven, hell, and all created entities. It also addresses the two qualities in nature, which are examined from a correct foundation in spiritual knowledge, driven by the impulse and movement of God.
original: Everything that exists is, according to Boehme, this three-fold alone, and this three-fold is everything. To him the universe is thus one divine life and revelation of God in all things, so that when examined more closely, from the one reality of God, the sum and substance of all powers and qualities, the Son who shines forth from these powers is eternally born; the inward unity of this light with the substance of the powers is Spirit. Sometimes the presentation is vague, and then again it is clearer. What comes next is the explanation of this Trinity, and here the different forms which he uses to indicate the difference becoming evident in the same, more especially appear. In the Aurora, the “Root or Mother of Philosophy, Astrology and Theology,” he gives a method of division in which he places these sciences in proximity, and yet appears merely to pass from one to the other without any clear definition or determination. “(1) In Philosophy divine power is treated of, what God is, and how in the Being of God nature, stars and Elementa are constituted; whence all things have their origin, what is the nature of heaven and earth, as also of angels, men and devils, heaven and hell and all that is creaturely, likewise what the two qualities in nature are, and this is dealt with out of a right ground in the knowledge of spirit, by the impulse and motion of God.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The Work of Art
plain: Music ability typically reveals itself in early childhood, when the mind is still blank and emotions have barely stirred. During this phase, one can reach a high level of skill before the intellect and life experience have fully developed. In practice, we frequently observe high technical proficiency in both writing and performing music coexisting with a striking lack of intellectual depth or character. Poetry works differently. Its core lies in depicting human beings, their deep concerns, and the forces driving them. This depiction requires substance and thought. Consequently, the mind and heart must be deeply shaped by life, experience, and reflection before a gifted person can produce work that is mature, solid, and complete. The early works of Goethe and Schiller show a level of immaturity, roughness, and crudeness that is truly shocking. The fact that most of these early efforts contain a large amount of dull, ordinary, and even cold, common elements strongly challenges the widespread belief that inspiration is tied to youth and its fiery energy. These two geniuses were the first to provide our culture with authentic poetry. However, it was only in their mature adulthood that they offered us creations that were deep, substantial, born of true inspiration, and perfectly formed.
original: It is for this reason that musical talent generally announces itself in very early youth, while the head is still empty and the heart has been but little moved, and is capable of attaining to a very considerable height in early years, before mind and life have experience of themselves. And again, as a matter of fact we often enough see very great expertness in musical composition, as also in execution, subsist along with remarkable barrenness of mind and character. The reverse is the case with poetry. In poetry all depends on the representation,--which must be full of matter and thought--of man, of his profounder interests, and of the powers that move him; and therefore mind and heart themselves must be richly and profoundly educated by life, experience, and reflection, before genius can bring to pass anything mature, substantial, and self-complete. Goethe's and Schiller's first productions are of an immaturity, and even of a rudeness and barbarism, that are absolutely terrifying. This phenomenon, that the greater part of those attempts display a predominant mass of thoroughly prosaic and in part of frigid and commonplace elements, furnishes the chief objection to the common opinion, that inspiration is inseparable from youth and youthful fire. Those two men of genius, it may be said, were the first to give our nation works of true poetry, and yet it was only their mature manhood that presented us with creations profound, substantial, and the outcome of genuine inspiration, while no less thoroughly perfect in form.

plain: This is a hollow concept; there is no value in these arid, muddled notions of circular movement and what later gets named attraction and repulsion, except for the fact that various types of motion are viewed as the principle of matter. In other words, only the void and the indivisible, along with their specific characteristics, are implied here; non-essential, distinct Being, like heat and similar things, belongs elsewhere. However, this immediately paves the way for a mistaken idealism that tries to eliminate the objective by linking it to consciousness, simply claiming that it is my sensation. Through this, sensory individuality is certainly canceled out in the form of Being, yet it persists as the same sensory variety; a sensory, concept-free variety of sensation is created, containing no rationality, and this idealism stops caring about it. He also thwarted multiple efforts by citizens of Agrigentum to take control of their city; and when the respect of his peers grew so great that they proposed he become king, he turned down their proposals and continued living among them as a respected private citizen. Many legendary stories were told about both his life and his death. Because he was renowned while alive, we are told he did not want to seem to die an ordinary death, to prove he was not a mortal, but had simply vanished from view.
original: This is an empty representation; there is no interest in these dry, confused ideas of circle-motion, and of what is later on called attraction and repulsion, beyond the fact that the different kinds of motion are looked at as the principle of matter. That is to say, only the void and indivisible and their determinations are implicit; unessential, different Being, such as warmth, &c., is for another. But by this the way is at once opened up to the false idealism that means to be done with what is objective by bringing it into relation with consciousness, merely saying of it that it is my feeling. Thereby sensuous individuality is, indeed, annulled in the form of Being, but it still remains the same sensuous manifold; a sensuously notionless manifold of feeling is established, in which there is no reason, and with which this idealism has no further concern. He likewise frustrated several attempts which were made by people of Agrigentum to seize upon the rulership of their city; and when the esteem of his fellow-citizens rose so high that they offered him the crown, he rejected their offers, and lived ever after amongst them as a respected private individual. Both of his life and death much which was fabulous was told. Seeing that he was famous in life, we are told that he wished not to appear to die an ordinary death, as a proof that he was not a mortal man, but had merely passed out of sight.

plain: Descriptive psychology begins by reporting what we find in active, conscious activity. It identifies numerous abilities, desires, and emotions. As it lists these items, it must not forget that the self is a unified whole. This creates a puzzling situation: how can such a diverse and chaotic mix of elements coexist in the mind like items in a sack? The confusion deepens because these are not static objects but dynamic, active processes. When describing these various abilities, the focus remains on their general nature. The unity of these many capacities represents the opposite side of this generality; it is the specific, concrete individuality. Returning to these distinct individualities to explain why one person prefers one thing while another prefers something else, or why one person is smarter than another, is far less engaging than cataloging insects or mosses. In the case of insects and mosses, it is appropriate to study them as separate, disconnected items because they naturally belong to the realm of accidental, specific details.
original: Observational psychology, which in the first instance states what observation finds regarding the general forms brought to its notice in the active functioning consciousness, discovers all sorts of faculties, inclinations, and passions; and since, while narrating what this collection contains, the remembrance of the unity of self-consciousness is not to be suppressed, observational psychology is bound to get the length at least of wonderment that such a lot and such a miscellany of things can happen to be somehow alongside one another in the mind as in a kind of bag, more especially when they are seen to be not hfeless inert things, but restless active processes. In telling over these various faculties observation keeps to the universal aspect: the unity of these multifarious capacities is the opposite aspect to this universahty, is the actual concrete individuahty. To take up again the different concrete individuahties, and to describe how one man has more inclination for this, the other for that, how one has more intelhgence than the other— all this is, however, something much more uninteresting than even to reckon up the species of insects, mosses, and so on. For these latter give observation the right to take them thus individually and disconnectedly (begrifflos), because they belong essentially to the sphere of fortuitous detailed particulars.

plain: In both scenarios, the difference lacks intrinsic or essential character. Either the universal, identified as force, remains neutral toward the partition into components observed within the law, or the various distinctions, constituting the law’s components, remain neutral toward one another. Nevertheless, the understanding holds the concept of this inherent distinction, simply because the law partly represents the inner being, the inherent nature, yet is simultaneously differentiated within it. The fact that this distinction is internal is evident because the law is bare and simple force, or represents the concept of that differentiation, and thus constitutes a conceptual differentiation. Yet, this internal differentiation initially resides only within the understanding and has not yet been established in the actual fact itself. Therefore, the understanding merely articulates its own necessity. This implies the distinction is created solely to simultaneously express that it must not be a differentiation inherent to the fact’s nature. This necessity, being purely verbal, functions as a rehearsal of the moments comprising the cycle of necessity. Although these moments are indeed distinct, their distinction is explicitly declared not to be a differentiation of the fact itself, and consequently, it is immediately negated and transcended. This process is designated as Explanation.
original: The distinction is, then, in both cases no distinction of an inherent or essential kind. Either the universal, force, is indifferent to the division into parts, which is found in the law, or else the distinctions, the parts of the law, are indifferent to one another. Understanding, however, does have the notion of this distinction per se, just by the fact that law is in part the inner being, the inherent nature, but is in it at the same time distinguished. That this distinction is in this way mner distinction is shown by the fact that law is bare and simple force, or is the notion of that distinction, and thus is a distinction of the notion. But still this inner distinction falls to begin with only within understanding, and is not yet estabhshed in the fact itself. It is thus only its own necessity to which un.derstanding gives expression — the distinction, that is to say, is one which it makes only so as at the same time to express that the distinction is not to be a distinction in the nature of the fact itself. This necessity, which is merely verbal, is thus a rehearsal of the moments which make up the cycle of necessity. They are no doubt distinct, but their distinction is at the same time explicitly stated to be not a distinction of the fact itself, and consequently is itself again straightway cancelled and transcended. This process is called Explanation.

plain: In this structure, the State’s single entity holds absolute power. This core element remains rigid and unyielding, resembling only itself and containing no other components. When defined more precisely to match its underlying concept, this dynamic corresponds to the Family. The Chinese political system relies entirely on this specific type of moral bond, which is defined by an objective form of familial respect. The Chinese people view themselves as part of their kin groups while simultaneously seeing themselves as offspring of the State. Within the family unit, individuals do not possess distinct personal identities, because the unified whole they inhabit is defined by blood ties and natural duties. They lack independent personal identity in the State as well, since the patriarchal relationship dominates there. Governance rests on the Emperor’s paternal oversight, who maintains order across all state functions. Family obligations are strictly enforced and codified by law. A son cannot address his father upon his entry into a room. He must shrink himself to insignificance near the doorway and cannot exit without his father’s consent. Upon his father’s death, the son must grieve for three years, during which he forbids himself from consuming meat or wine. Any professional activity he was pursuing, including state duties, must be halted, as he is required to abandon them.
original: Here we have the One Being of the State supremely dominant, — the Substance, which, still hard and inflexible, resembles nothing but itself — includes no other element. This relation, then, expressed more definitely and more conformably with its conception, is that of the Family. On this form of moral union alone rests the Chinese State, and it is objective Family Piety that characterizes it. The Chinese regard themselves as belonging to their family, and at the same time as children of the State. In the Family itself they are not personalities, for the consolidated unity in which they exist as members of it is consanguinity and natural obligation. In the State they have as little iiide'- pendent personality; for there the patriarchal relation is predominant, and the government is based on the paternal management of the Emperor, who keeps all departments of the State in order. The duties of the Family are absolutely binding, and established and regulated by law. The son may not accost the father, when he comes into the room; he must seem to contract himself to nothing at the side of the door, and may not leave the room without his father's permission. When the father dies, the son must mourn for three years — abstaining from meat and wine. The business in which he was engaged, even that of the State, must be suspended, for he is obliged to quit it.

plain: Beyond this, because the entire political entity is inherent in the most profound spiritual sentiment, the government can reasonably require each person to join a specific religious group. Naturally, the state cannot meddle with the unique nature of these groups, which relies on internal imaginative thought. When the government is properly structured and powerful, it can afford to be tolerant in this area and ignore minor issues that affect it. It can even allow groups within its borders whose beliefs stop them from acknowledging any direct obligations to the government. However, this allowance must rely on the population size of the relevant sects. The government is willing to leave the members of these religious organizations to the rules of the civil society, accepting that they fulfill their direct duties to the state passively through proxies. It can be said that Quakers, Anabaptists, and similar groups are simply active participants in the civil society, possessing only private connections with others as individuals. Yet, even in this context, they have been allowed to avoid taking oaths. Direct
original: More than that, since to the deepest religious feeling there is present the state as a whole, it may fairly be demanded by the state that every individual should connect himself with some congregation. Of course, with its special character, depending on inner imaginative thinking, the state cannot interfere. When well organized and strong, the state can afford to be liberal in this matter, and may overlook small details affecting itself. It may even give room within itself to congregations, whose creed prevents them from recognizing any direct duties to it. But this concession must depend upon the numerical strength of the sects in question. The members of these religious bodies the state is content to leave to the laws of the civic community, and to accept a passive fulfilment of their direct duties to it by means of substitutes. ' Of Quakers, Anabaptists, etc., it may be said that they are merely active members of the civic community, having as private persons only private relations with others. Even here, however, they have been permitted to forego the use of the oath. Direct

plain: Moving from the general concept of occupying space to specific substances like water or earth is a distinct and harder task. In fact, the Pythagoreans never made this move. For them, the universe retains a simple, theoretical shape, evident in how it is depicted as a network of numerical connections. Consequently, the physical realm remains undefined. Another way to display the core nature of numerical determination appears in musical relationships, where numbers serve as the primary deciding element. Here, variations manifest as different numerical ratios, and this numerical method is the sole way to define musical qualities. The connection between tones rests on measurable differences that create harmonies, as opposed to other differences that produce dissonance. Porphyry notes in his work on Pythagorean life that the Pythagoreans viewed music as a tool for guiding the soul and for education. Pythagoras was the first to recognize that these audible distinctions in music can be defined mathematically, meaning that what we perceive as harmony or clash is actually a mathematical structure. He elevated the subjective, basic feeling inherent in hearing to the level of rational understanding by establishing fixed numerical definitions.
original: On the other hand, the transition from the occupation of space generally to what is determined, to water, earth, &c., is quite another thing and is more difficult; or rather the Pythagoreans have not taken this step, for the universe itself has, with them, the speculative, simple form, which is found in the fact of being represented as a system of number-relations. But with all this, the physical is not yet determined. b. Another application or exhibition of the essential nature of the determination of numbers is to be found in the relations of music, and it is more especially in their case that number constitutes the determining factor. The differences here show themselves as various relations of numbers, and this mode of determining what is musical is the only one. The relation borne by tones to one another is founded on quantitative differences whereby harmonies may be formed, in distinction to others by which discords are constituted. The Pythagoreans, according to Porphyry (De vita Pyth. 30), treated music as something soul-instructing and scholastic [Psychagogisches und Pädagogisches]. Pythagoras was the first to discern that musical relations, these audible differences, are mathematically determinable, that what we hear as consonance and dissonance is a mathematical arrangement. The subjective, and, in the case of hearing, simple feeling which, however, exists inherently in relation, Pythagoras has justified to the understanding, and he attained his object by means of fixed determinations.

plain: Conflict defines this dynamic. As long as I perceive another person as a distinct, immediate being, I cannot recognize myself in them. Therefore, I am driven to eliminate that immediate presence. Conversely, I cannot be acknowledged as an immediate being unless I overcome my own raw immediacy, thereby actualizing my freedom. However, this immediacy also constitutes the physical body of self-consciousness. Just as a sign or tool provides self-consciousness with its sense of self, its existence for others, and the means to engage with them, so does the body. Since life is just as essential as liberty for resolving this tension, the struggle initially results in a lopsided negation marked by inequality. One participant chooses to preserve life, keeping their individual self-consciousness but giving up the demand for recognition. The other clings to self-assertion and is acknowledged by the first as their superior. This dynamic creates the relationship between master and slave. In this struggle for recognition and the resulting subjugation under a master, we observe, from a phenomenal perspective, the rise of human social life and the beginning of political association.
original: The process is a battle. I cannot be aware of me as myself in another individual, so long as I see in that other an other and an immediate existence: and I am consequently bent upon the suppression of this immediacy of his. But in like measure I cannot be recognised as immediate, except so far as I overcome the mere immediacy on my own part, and thus give existence to my freedom. But this immediacy is at the same time the corporeity of self-consciousness, in which as in its sign and tool the latter has its own sense of self, and its being for others, and the means for entering into relation with them. But because life is as requisite as liberty to the solution, the fight ends in the first instance as a one-sided negation with inequality. While the one combatant prefers life, retains his single self-consciousness, but surrenders his claim for recognition, the other holds fast to his self-assertion and is recognised by the former as his superior. Thus arises the status of master and slave. In the battle for recognition and the subjugation under a master, we see, on their phenomenal side, the emergence of man’s social life and the commencement of political union.

plain: Second, a country’s wisdom and power might not be enough for this task, so it could stick to the lower law. Alternatively, another nation might reach its higher form of government, climbing the ladder, causing the first nation to abandon its identity and submit to the other. Consequently, understanding the genuine form of government is crucial. Anything opposing it lacks stability and truth, eventually vanishing. It exists only briefly and cannot maintain its position. While people accept it, they cannot guarantee lasting acceptance. The fact that it must be discarded is inherent in the nature of the constitution. Only Philosophy can provide this understanding. When this realization becomes widespread, revolutions occur within a state without any violence. Institutions somehow collapse and vanish, with everyone agreeing to relinquish their rights. Nevertheless, a government must acknowledge that this moment has arrived. If it instead clings to temporary institutions, unaware of the truth, treating what is recognized but non-essential as a shield against the essential (where the essential is what exists within the Idea), that government will collapse along with its institutions under the power of the mind. The dissolution of its government dissolves the nation itself. A new government emerges, or perhaps the government and the non-essential elements remain dominant.
original: In the second place, a nation’s intelligence and strength may not suffice for this, and it may hold to the lower law; or it may happen that another nation has reached its higher constitution, thereby rising in the scale, and the first gives up its nationality and becomes subject to the other. Therefore it is of essential importance to know what the true constitution is; for what is in opposition to it has no stability, no truth, and passes away. It has a temporary existence, but cannot hold its ground; it has been accepted, but cannot secure permanent acceptance; that it must be cast aside, lies in the very nature of the constitution. This insight can be reached through Philosophy alone. Revolutions take place in a state without the slightest violence when the insight becomes universal; institutions, somehow or other, crumble and disappear, each man agrees to give up his right. A government must, however, recognize that the time for this has come; should it, on the contrary, knowing not the truth, cling to temporary institutions, taking what—though recognized—is unessential, to be a bulwark guarding it from the essential (and the essential is what is contained in the Idea), that government will fall, along with its institutions, before the force of mind. The breaking up of its government breaks up the nation itself; a new government arises,—or it may be that the government and the unessential retain the upper hand.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The Work of Art
plain: The most basic form of perception, which is least fitting for the mind, is purely sensory perception. It naturally involves simple seeing, hearing, and feeling, much like how walking around without thinking and just observing our surroundings can be pleasant during periods of mental exhaustion. However, the mind does not stop at merely perceiving external things through sight and sound. Instead, it turns them into objects for its own inner nature. This inner nature is then driven, in a correspondingly sensory way, to express itself within those things, relating to them as desire. In this appetitive relationship with the outside world, the person stands as a sensory individual opposite the things, which are also individuals. He does not approach them with general concepts as a thinking entity would. Rather, he has connections driven by specific impulses and interests toward the objects, which are themselves specific. He maintains his existence within them by using them, consuming them, and fulfilling his self-satisfaction by giving them up for its sake. Within this negative stance, desire demands not just the surface appearance of external things, but the things themselves in their concrete sensory existence. Simple images of the wood it intends to use, or of the animals it intends to eat, would be useless to desire.
original: (aa) The lowest mode of apprehension, and that least appropriate to the mind, is purely sensuous apprehension. It consists naturally in mere looking, listening, feeling, just as in seasons of mental fatigue it may often be entertaining to go about without thought, and just to hear and look around us. The mind, however, does not rest in the mere apprehension of external things by sight and hearing, it makes them objects for its own inner nature, which then is itself impelled in a correspondingly sensuous form to realize itself in the things, and relates itself to them as desire. In this appetitive relation to the outer world, the man stands as a sensuous particular over against the things as likewise particulars; he does not open his mind to them with general ideas as a thinking being, but has relations dictated by particular impulses and interests to the objects as themselves particulars, and preserves himself in them, inasmuch as he uses them, consumes them, and puts in act his self-satisfaction by sacrificing them to it. In this negative relation desire requires for itself not merely the superficial appearance of external things, but themselves in their concrete sensuous existence. Mere pictures of the wood that it wants to use, or of the animals that it wants to eat, would be of no service to desire.

plain: In their view, both the world and God possess equal material reality. From this, they conclude that the philosophical concept of God includes both God and the world. This is the notion of pantheism they attribute to philosophy. Because their own thinking rarely moves beyond these basic categories, they project them onto philosophy, where such concepts do not exist. In doing so, they introduce the very flaw they later criticize. When they encounter trouble understanding how God relates to the world, they easily dismiss the issue by claiming it holds an unresolvable contradiction. Consequently, they settle for a vague idea of this relationship, often using familiar labels like omnipresence or providence. For them, faith simply means refusing to define the concept or examine the problem closely. It is expected that untrained minds accept such ambiguity. However, when a trained mind with a serious interest in reflection accepts indefinite ideas in matters of supreme importance, it becomes difficult to tell if the thinker is truly serious about the subject.
original: And as in their judgment either of the two,—the world as much as God—has the same solid substantiality as the other, they infer that in the philosophic Idea God is composed of God and the world. Such then is the idea they form of pantheism, and which they ascribe to philosophy. Unaccustomed in their own thinking and apprehending of thoughts to go beyond such categories, they import them into philosophy, where they are utterly unknown; they thus infect it with the disease against which they subsequently raise an outcry. If any difficulty emerge in comprehending God’s relation to the world, they at once and very easily escape it by admitting that this relation contains for them an inexplicable contradiction; and that hence, they must stop at the vague conception of such relation, perhaps under the more familiar names of, e.g. omnipresence, providence, &c. Faith in their use of the term means no more than a refusal to define the conception, or to enter on a closer discussion of the problem. That men and classes of untrained intellect are satisfied with such indefiniteness, is what one expects; but when a trained intellect and an interest for reflective study is satisfied, in matters admitted to be of superior, if not even of supreme interest, with indefinite ideas, it is hard to decide whether the thinker is really in earnest with the subject.

plain: Just as the German emperors tried to make their title a reality in Italy, Italy’s political heart lay in Germany. The interests of these two lands were therefore bound together, and neither could achieve political stability on its own. During the shining era of the Hohenstaufen dynasty, leaders with strong personalities upheld the dignity of the throne. Rulers like Frederick Barbarossa displayed imperial power at its most majestic and used their personal traits to bind the subordinate princes to his cause. However, even if the history of the Hohenstaufen dynasty looks impressive and the struggle against the Church seems dramatic, the former is largely just the tragedy of that specific family, while the latter produced no significant outcome in the realm of Spirit. The cities were forced to accept imperial authority, and their representatives promised to follow the rulings of the Roncalian Diet. Yet they honored these promises only for as long as they were forced to. Their feeling of duty relied entirely on the immediate awareness of a higher power prepared to enforce it.
original: As, on the one hand, the German emperors sought to realize their title in Italy, so, on the other hand, Italy had its political centre in Germany. The interest of the two countries were thus linked together, and neither could gain political consolidation within itself. In the brilliant period of the Holienstaufen dynasty, individuals of commanding character sustained the dignity of the throne; — sovereigns like Frederick Barbarossa, in whom the imperial power manifested itself in its greatest majesty, and who by his personal qualities succeeded in attaching the subject princes to his interests. Yet brilliant as the history of the Hohenstaufen dynasty may appear, and stirring as might have been the contest with the Church, the former presents on the whole nothing more than the tragedy of this house itself, and the latter had no important result in the sphere of Spirit. The cities were indeed compelled to acknowledge the imperial authority, and their deputies swore to observe the decisions of the Eoncalian Diet; but they kept their word no longer than they were compelled to do so. Their sense of obligation depended exclusively on the direct consciousness of a superior power ready to enforce it.

plain: The term "indifference" carries a double meaning, applying to both parties involved. This creates the illusion that the specific content defining indifference—the sole element giving it concrete form—is itself neutral. Schelling’s subsequent condition demands that the subject remain free from the constraints of reflection. To impose reflection would subject it to the understanding’s determinations, a process that, like sensory perception, necessitates the separation of sensory objects. Regarding its mode of existence, Schelling defines absolute indifference as A = A. For him, this equation represents the knowledge of absolute identity, which remains inextricably linked to the existence of that identity. Consequently, opposition does appear within this Absolute, both as form and as reality. However, it is characterized as a merely relative or non-essential opposition. The only possible distinction between subject and object is one of quantity.
original: But the expression “indifference” is ambiguous, for it means indifference in regard to both the one and the other; and thus it appears as if the content of indifference, the only thing which makes it concrete, were indifferent. Schelling’s next requirement is that the subject must not be hampered with reflection; that would be bringing it under the determination of the understanding, which, equally with sensuous perception, implies the separateness of sensuous things. As to the form of its existence, absolute indifference is with Schelling posited as A = A; and this form is for him the knowledge of absolute identity, which, however, is inseparable from the Being or existence of the same. Thus, therefore, opposition, as form and reality or existence, no doubt appears in this Absolute, but it is determined as a merely relative or unessential opposition: “Between subject and object no other than quantitative difference is possible.

plain: If the latter existed, it would quickly locate the appropriate term. The primary conclusion reached here is simply that the skull serves as the dead part, just as the brain acts as the living part. Consequently, within this dead entity, the brain’s mental activities and distinct capabilities must display their external manifestation and expression, a reality that remains inherent to the individual. Regarding the connection between these processes and functions and the dead entity, which lacks any mind residing inside it, the initial explanation provided is the external and mechanical component, specifically the rigid solid structure mentioned earlier. Thus, the actual organs, located within the brain, push the skull outward in some areas, widen it in others, flatten it in still others, or produce whatever other specific effects one wishes to describe.
original: If the latter were there, it would soon find the right word. What has been here determined is, in the first instance, merely that just as the brain is the cafut vivum, the skull is the cafut mortuum. It is in this ens mortuum, then, that the mental processes and specific functions of the brain would have to find their external reality manifested and set forth, a reality which is none the less in the individual himself. For the relation of those processes and functions to what, being an ens mortuum, does not contam mind indwelling within it, there is offered, m the first instance, the external and mechanical factor, the fixed solid element above mentioned, so that the organs proper— and these are in the brain— here press the skull out round, there make it broad, or force it flat, or in whatever way we care to state the effect thus exerted.

ref: The Roman World, Rome to the Second Punic War
plain: Tullus Hostilius succeeded Numa, and the very title of this monarch hints at his non-local background. Ancus Marcius, the fourth ruler, was Numa’s grandson. Tarquinius Priscus came from a Corinthian lineage, a fact we noted earlier. Servius Tullius originated in Corniculum, a Latin settlement that had been subjugated. Tarquinius Superbus was a descendant of the previous Tarquinius. During the reign of this final king, Rome achieved significant wealth. Even at this early stage, reports claim a trade agreement was signed with the Carthaginians. To dismiss this as legend would ignore the ties Rome maintained with the Etruscans and other neighboring groups, whose economic success relied on commerce and sea activities. The Romans likely knew how to write by then. They also already displayed the sharp insight that defined them, a trait that produced the clear historical records for which they are renowned.
original: Numa was followed by Tullus Jfostilius, and the very name of this king points to his foreign origin. A.HCUS JUartius, the fourth king, was the grandson of Numa. Tarquinius Prisons sprang from a Corinthian family, as we had occasion, to observe above. Servius Tullius was from Corniculum, a conquered Latin town; Tarquinius Superbus was descended from the elder Tarquinius. Under this last king Rome reached a high degree of prosperity: even at so early a period as this, a commercial treaty is said to have been concluded with the Carthaginians; and to be disposed to reject this as mythical would imply forgetfulness of the connection which Rome had, even at that time, with the Etrurians and other bordering peoples whose prosperity depended on trade and maritime pursuits. The Romans were probably even then acquainted with the art of writing, and already possessed that clear-sighted comprehension which was their remarkable characteristic, and which led to that perspicuous historical composition for which they are famous.

plain: Today, people attempt to shield education from current trends, yet they cannot escape the State’s supreme authority. Even when they try to detach themselves, they unknowingly remain subject to this overarching power. The theoretical significance of Pythagoras’s practical philosophy lies in the idea that individual awareness gains moral existence within the brotherhood. Since number sits between the sensory and the Concept, the Pythagorean group serves as a middle ground between universal, real morality and the view that individuals are personally accountable for their actions. In this latter view, morality stops being a universal spirit. If we look for the return of practical philosophy, we will find it; however, it does not truly become speculative until very recently. This overview should suffice to convey the essence of the Pythagorean system. I will briefly outline the main points of Aristotle’s critique (Metaphysics I. 8) of the Pythagorean number structure. He correctly notes first that if the limited and unlimited, along with even and odd, are treated as basic concepts, the Pythagoreans fail to explain how motion occurs. They also cannot account for how generation and decay happen without motion and change, nor can they explain the conditions and activities of celestial bodies. This flaw is important because arithmetic numbers are empty forms and sterile principles lacking life and motion.
original: Nowadays men try to keep education free from the spirit of the times, but they cannot withdraw themselves from this supreme power, the State, for even if they try to separate themselves, they unconsciously remain beneath this universal. The speculative meaning of the practical philosophy of Pythagoras thus is, that in this signification, the individual consciousness shall obtain a moral reality in the brotherhood. But as number is a middle thing between the sensuous and Notion, the Pythagorean brotherhood is a middle between universal, actual morality and maintaining that in true morality the individual, as an individual, is responsible for his own behaviour; this morality ceases to be universal spirit. If we wish to see practical philosophy reappear, we shall find it; but, on the whole, we shall not see it become really speculative until very recent times. We may satisfy ourselves with this as giving us an idea of the Pythagorean system. I will, however, shortly give the principal points of the criticism which Aristotle (Met. I. 8) makes upon the Pythagorean number-form. He says justly, in the first place: “If only the limited and the unlimited, the even and odd are made fundamental ideas, the Pythagoreans do not explain how movement arises, and how, without movement and change there can be coming into being and passing away, or the conditions and activities of heavenly objects.” This defect is significant; arithmetical numbers are dry forms and barren principles in which life and movement are deficient.

plain: The following outcome of this approach is that awareness is startled to discover within itself something it had never sought. Consider, for instance, the widely recognized concept of Becoming. We observe that whatever is in the process of becoming is simultaneously not present and yet present. It represents the unity of existence and non-existence. It can be startling to realize that such a profound distinction resides within this straightforward notion. The achievement was partly a purely formal and negative one. It forced those who debated with Socrates to accept that, despite believing they understood the topic well, they now concluded that their prior knowledge had proven itself false. Socrates posed questions with the aim of leading the speaker to concede points that contradicted their initial stance. Socrates interrupts by stating that the specific instance is not the subject of inquiry, but rather virtue as a whole, which encompasses all aspects within itself. Meno responds that it involves governing and ruling over other people. Socrates points out that the virtue displayed by boys and slaves does not involve governing. Meno admits he cannot identify what is shared by all forms of virtue. Socrates answers that it is similar to shape, which is the common element found in roundness, squareness, and so on. A digression then takes place. Meno states that virtue is the ability to obtain the good things one desires.
original: c. The next result of this method of procedure may be that consciousness is surprised that what it never looked for should be found in consciousness. If we reflect, for example, on the universally known idea of Becoming, we find that what becomes is not and yet it is; it is the identity of Being and non-being, and it may surprise us that in this simple conception so great a distinction should exist. The result attained was partly the altogether formal and negative one of bringing home to those who conversed with Socrates, the conviction that, however well acquainted with the subject they had thought themselves, they now came to the conclusion, “that what we knew has refuted itself.” Socrates thus put questions in the intent that the speaker should be drawn on to make admissions, implying a point of view opposed to that from which he started. Socrates interrupts him by saying, that it is not that about which he inquires, but virtue in general, which comprehends every thing in itself. Meno says “It is to govern and rule over others.” Socrates brings forward the fact that the virtue of boys and slaves does not consist in governing. Meno says that he cannot tell what is common in all virtue. Socrates replies that it is the same as figure, which is what is common in roundness, squareness, &c. There a digression occurs. Meno says, “Virtue is the power of securing the good desired.”

plain: Each side must seek to kill the other, even though doing so puts its own survival in danger. This is because the rival holds no more value than the self does. The rival appears as something external and separate. The self must eliminate this separation. The rival exists as a simple, immediate awareness, but it is complicated by many factors. It must see its difference from the self as pure being or as total negation. However, this test, conducted through a fight to the death, destroys the truth that was supposed to come from it. It also destroys the complete certainty of the self. Life is the natural state of consciousness, representing independence without total negation. Death is the natural negation of consciousness, representing negation without independence. Because of this, death lacks the necessary meaning of real recognition. Through dying, it is certainly true that both parties risked their lives. They valued their own lives and the other’s life equally. But this realization does not belong to the people who fought. They destroy the consciousness that existed in this foreign realm of natural existence. In other words, they destroy themselves. They are overcome, like opposing ends that tried to exist independently.
original: In the same way each must aim at the death of the other, as it risks its own life thereby; for that other is to it of no more worth than itself; the other's reality is presented to the former as an external other, as outside itself; it must cancel that externality. The other is a purely' existent consciousness and entangled in manifold ways; it must regard its otherness as pure existence for itself or as absolute negation. This trying and testing, however, by a struggle to the death, cancels both the truth which was to result from it, and therewith the certainty of self altogether. For just as Ufe is the natural " position " of consciousness, independence without absolute negativity, so death is the natural " negation " of consciousness, negation without independence, which thus remains without the requisite significance of actual recognition. Through death, doubtless, there has arisen the certainty that both did stake their hfe, and held it hghtly both in their own case and in the case of the other; but that is not for those who underwent this struggle. They cancel their consciousness which had its place in this ahen element of natural existence; in other words, they cancel themselves and are sublated, as terms or extremes seeking to have existence on their own account.

plain: Since he never presented himself as an instructor in his texts, but instead cast other figures as the philosophers within his conversations, no clear separation has ever been drawn between what historically belonged to those figures and what he contributed through his own advancement of their ideas. For example, the *Parmenides* contains the Eleatic philosophy, yet the specific elaboration of that doctrine is uniquely Plato’s. Second, Aristotle serves as our most extensive source; he deliberately and thoroughly examined the earlier thinkers, and he discussed them in chronological sequence, particularly at the start of his *Metaphysics* and significantly in other works. He combines philosophical depth with scholarly breadth, making him a reliable authority. For Greek philosophy, we cannot do better than examine the first book of his *Metaphysics*. If someone dismisses Aristotle by claiming he failed to grasp Plato correctly, one can respond that, having interacted directly with Plato, his profound and wide-ranging intellect likely understood the Athenian better than anyone else. Third, Cicero’s name also comes to mind here—though he is certainly a confused source—because he provides substantial information. However, due to his lack of philosophical inclination, he treated Philosophy more like a subject of historical record.
original: But because in his writings he never himself appeared as teacher, but always represented other people in his dialogues as the philosophers, a distinction never has been made between what really belonged to them in history and what was added by him through the further development which he effected in their thoughts. In the Parmenides, for instance, we have the Eleatic philosophy, and yet the working out of this doctrine belongs peculiarly to Plato. 2. Aristotle is our most abundant authority; he studied the older philosophers expressly and most thoroughly, and he has, in the beginning of his Metaphysics especially, and also to a large extent elsewhere, dealt with them, in historical order: he is as philosophic as erudite, and we may rely upon him. We can do no better in Greek philosophy than study the first book of his Metaphysics. When the would-be-wise man depreciates Aristotle, and asserts that he has not correctly apprehended Plato, it may be retorted that as he associated with Plato himself, with his deep and comprehensive mind, perhaps no one knew him better. 3. Cicero’s name may also occur to us here—although he certainly is but a troubled spring—since he undoubtedly gives us much information; yet because he was lacking in philosophic spirit, he understood Philosophy rather as if it were a matter of history merely.

plain: He responded well to a tyrant who inquired about the proper material for casting statues. He suggested using the same metal that had been used for the statues of Harmodius and Aristogiton. He attempted to consume uncooked flesh, but it disagreed with his system. He was unable to process it and eventually passed away at an advanced age, just as he had spent his life: living on the streets. Later Cynics. As noted previously, Antisthenes and Diogenes possessed significant cultural refinement. The Cynics who followed them are equally notable for their extreme lack of shame. Generally, however, they were no more than pig-like beggars who derived pleasure from the rude behavior they directed at others. They do not merit further attention within Philosophy, and they fully deserve the label of dogs, a term applied to them early on. This is because the dog is an animal devoid of shame. Crates from Thebes and the Cynic Hipparchia held their wedding ceremony in the public marketplace. The independence that the Cynics claimed is actually a form of subjection. While every other area of active life includes the positive aspect of free intelligence, this approach denies oneself the very sphere where the element of freedom can be experienced.
original: He gave a good answer to a tyrant who asked him from what metal statues should be cast: “From the metal from which the statues of Harmodius and Aristogiton were cast.” He tried to eat raw meat, which did not, however, agree with him; he could not digest it, and died at a very great age, as he lived—in the streets. c. LATER CYNICS. Antisthenes and Diogenes, as already mentioned, were men of great culture. The succeeding Cynics are not any the less conspicuous by their exceeding shamelessness, but they were, generally speaking, nothing more than swinish beggars, who found their satisfaction in the insolence which they showed to others. They are worthy of no further consideration in Philosophy, and they deserve in its full the name of dogs, which was early given to them; for the dog is a shameless animal. Crates, of Thebes, and Hipparchia, a Cynic, celebrated their nuptials in the public market. This independence of which the Cynics boasted, is really subjection, for while every other sphere of active life contains the affirmative element of free intelligence, this means the denying oneself the sphere in which the element of freedom can be enjoyed.

plain: The conflict between the two parties has completely disappeared. This is not just a perspective for us, the observers tracking this development, nor is it merely a hidden implication. It is a reality for self-consciousness itself. In other words, knowledge has gained control over the conflict that consciousness previously had to confront. This shift depends on the tension between the certainty of the self and the object. However, for self-consciousness, the object is now the certainty of the self, which is knowledge. Similarly, the certainty of the self no longer has its own specific goals. It is no longer limited or defined by conditions. Instead, it is pure knowledge. Consequently, self-consciousness now regards its own self-knowledge as the substance itself. For it, this substance is both immediate and thoroughly mediated within a single, inseparable unity. It is immediate in the same way that ethical consciousness understands and performs its duties. It feels bound to the substance as if it were its own nature. Yet, it does not constitute character. This parallels the way ethical consciousness, due to its directness, represents a specific form of spirit. It belongs only to one key aspect of ethical life. It has the distinctive feature of lacking explicit, conscious knowledge.
original: All opposition between the two sides has vanished, and that, too, not for us (who are tracing the process), not merely implicitly, but actually for self-consciousness itself. That is to say, knowledge has itself got the mastery over the opposition which consciousness had to face. This rests on the opposition between certainty of self and the object. Now, however, the object for it is the certainty of self, knowledge: just as the certainty of itself as such has no longer ends of its own, is no longer conditioned and determinate, but is pure knowledge. Self-consciousness thus now takes the knowledge of itself to be the substance itself. This substance is, for it, at once immediate and absolutely mediated in one indivisible unity. It is immediate — just ia the way the " ethical " consciousness knows and itself does its duties, and is bound to the substance as to its own nature: but it is not character, just as that ethical consciousness, which iu virtue of its immediacy is a determinate type of spirit, belongs merely to one of the essential features of ethical hfe, and has the pecuharity of not being conscious exphcit knowledge.

plain: God, the supreme monad, stands as the ultimate substance. Since individual monads originate from His volition, their own substantial nature ceases to exist. This creates an unresolved internal contradiction. The conflict lies between the single substantial monad and the multitude of monads that assert independence, given that their very nature depends on having no connections with each other. However, to demonstrate the harmony within the world, Leibniz broadens the concept of monad-to-monad relations into the unity of opposing existences, specifically soul and body. He characterizes this unity as a relation devoid of distinction and concept, which he terms pre-established harmony. To illustrate this, he employs the analogy of two clocks synchronized to the same hour, maintaining identical time. Similarly, the progression of the intellectual realm, guided by purposes, runs parallel to the advancement of the physical realm, which follows a general causal link. This situation mirrors Spinoza’s view: these two aspects of the universe lack any connection. One does not affect the other, and both remain completely indifferent to each other. What is truly missing is the differentiating relationship of the concept.
original: If now the Monad of monads, God, is the absolute substance, and individual monads are created through His will, their substantiality comes to an end. There is therefore a contradiction present, which remains unsolved in itself—that is between the one substantial monad and the many monads for which independence is claimed, because their essence consists in their standing in no relation to one another. Yet at the same time, in order to show the harmony that exists in the world, Leibnitz understands the relation of monads to monads more generally as the unity of contrasted existences, namely of soul and body. This unity he represents as a relation without difference, and notionless, i.e. as a pre-established harmony. Leibnitz uses here the illustration of two clocks, which are set to the same hour, and keep the same time; in the same way the movement of the kingdom of thought goes on, determined in accordance with ends, and the movement onward of the corporeal kingdom which corresponds with it, proceeds according to a general causal connection. The case is the same as with Spinoza, that these two sides of the universe have no connection with each other, the one does not influence the other, but both are entirely indifferent to one another; it is really the differentiating relation of the Notion that is lacking.

plain: Speeches delivered by one group to another, or speeches aimed at nations and rulers, form an essential part of history. Even if we accept that Thucydides crafted the speeches attributed to Pericles, a truly skilled, sincere, and noble leader, we must still argue that these words fit the speaker’s nature. In these speeches, the speakers state the beliefs held by their fellow citizens, beliefs that shaped their own identities. They describe their views on political relationships, their moral and spiritual nature, and the guiding principles behind their plans and actions. What the historian places in their mouths is not a made-up set of ideas, but a pure record of their intellectual and moral habits. We must fully adopt these historians and spend long time with them if we wish to live alongside their respective nations and deeply understand their spirit. There are fewer such historians than one might think, and we can turn to their pages not just for scholarly knowledge, but for deep and real pleasure. We have already named Herodotus, the founder of history, and Thucydides. Xenophon’s account of the Ten Thousand’s retreat is equally original. Caesar’s Commentaries are a simple masterpiece by a powerful mind. Among the ancients, these recorders had to be great military leaders and statesmen.
original: But addresses of peoples to peoples, or orations directed to nations and to princes, are integrant constituents of history. Granted that such orations as those of Pericles — that most profoundly accomplished, genuine, noble statesman — were elaborated by Thucydides; it must yet be maintained that they were not foreign to the character of the speaker. In the orations in question, these men proclaim the maxims adopted by their countrymen, and which formed their own character; they record their views of their political relations, and of their moral and spiritual nature; and the principles of their designs and conduct. What the historian puts into their mouths is no supposititious system of ideas, but an uucorrupted transcript of their intellectual and moral habitudes. Of these historians, whom we must make thoroughly our own, with whom we must linger long, if we would live with their respective nations, and enter deeply into their spirit: of these historians, to whose pages we may turn not for the purposes of erudition merely, but with a view to deep and genuine enjoyment, there are fewer than might be imagined. Herodotus the Father, i.e. the Founder of History, and Thucydides have been already mentioned. Xenophon's Retreat of the Ten Thousand, is a work equally original. Csesar's Commentaries are the simple masterpiece of a mighty spirit. Among the ancients, these annalists were necessarily great captains and statesmen.

plain: Irony represents the immediate shape of this negative stance. From one perspective, it renders all factual, moral, or inherently substantive matters useless. It treats every objective thing possessing essential or real worth as void. If the self stays fixed on this viewpoint, everything seems worthless and futile to it, except its own subjectivity. That subjectivity, however, becomes hollow, empty, and merely self-conceited. Conversely, the self might find its self-enjoyment unsatisfying. It may feel inadequate to itself, leading to a desire for solid, substantial, and determinate interests. This creates misfortune and contradiction. The subject wants to reach truth and craves objectivity, yet it cannot leave its isolation or retreat into itself. It fails to shed this unsatisfied, abstract inwardness of mind. Consequently, it suffers from a sickly longing, a trait also visible in Fichte’s school. The dissatisfaction with this passive weakness—where one avoids acting or touching anything to preserve inner harmony—remains unreal and empty despite its purity. This state, even while craving the absolute, is the root of morbid saintliness and yearning.
original: The proximate form of this negativity which displays itself as irony is, then, on the one hand the futility of all that is matter of fact, or moral and of substantive import in itself; the nothingness of all that is objective, and that has essential and actual value. If the =I= remains at this point of view, all appears to it as nothing worth and as futile, excepting its own subjectivity, which thereby becomes hollow and empty, and itself mere conceit. But on the other hand, the reverse may happen, and the I may also find itself unsatisfied in its enjoyment of itself, and may prove insufficient to itself, so as in consequence to feel a craving for the solid and substantial, for determinate and essential interests. Out of this there arises misfortune and antinomy, in that the subject desires to penetrate into truth and has a craving for objectivity, but yet is unable to abandon its isolation and retirement into itself, and to strip itself free of this unsatisfied abstract inwardness (of mind), and so has a seizure of sickly yearning which we have also seen emanate from Fichte's school. The discontent of this quiescence and feebleness,--which does not like to act or to touch anything for fear of surrendering its inward harmony, and, for all its craving after the absolute, remains none the less unreal and empty, even though pure in itself,--is the source of morbid saintliness and yearning.

ref: Virtue and the Course of the World
plain: Nevertheless, its genuine aim and essence consist in mastering the actuality of the global process. The good that results from this mastery inherently entails the halt of that activity, meaning the end of individual self-awareness. How this conflict resolves, what virtue uncovers during the course, and whether the global process fails while virtue triumphs through the suffering virtue accepts, all depend on the nature of the living instruments the participants wield. These instruments are nothing but the essential being of the participants themselves, a being that manifests to each only reciprocally. Consequently, the nature of these instruments is already clear from what is essentially contained within this struggle. The universal serves as a valid component for the virtuous mind as a matter of conviction; it is "implicitly" or "inherently" correct, though it remains an abstract universality rather than an actual one. It functions as the goal for this mind and as the internal principle for the global process. Precisely because of this character, the universal also appears in the relationship between virtue and the global process; virtue initially "wills" to execute the good, without first claiming actuality for it.
original: Its purpose and true nature, however, he in conquering the reahty of the world's process; and the existence of the good thereby effec- tuated carries with it the cessation of its action, i.e. of the consciousness of individuality. How this struggle itself will come off, what virtue finds out in the course of it, whether, by the sacrifice which virtue takes upon itself to undergo, the world's process succumbs while virtue triumphs — all this must be decided from the nature of the hving weapons the combatants carry. For the weapons are nothing else than the essential being of the combatants themselves, a being which only makes its appearance for them both reciprocally. What their weapons are is in this way aheady evident from what is inherently implied in this struggle. The universal is an authentic element for the virtuous consciousness as a matter of belief; it is "implicitly" or " inherently " true; not yet an actual, but an abstract universahty. It plays the part of purpose in the case of this consciousness, and of inner principle in that of the world's process. Precisely by having this character the universal also manifests itself in the relation of virtue to the world's process; for virtue first " wills " to carry out the good, and does not in the first instance claim reahty for it.

plain: (a) Consciousness Proper(127). (α) Sensuous consciousness. Initially, consciousness is direct awareness, and its link to the object is therefore a straightforward, unmediated certainty regarding that object. Similarly, because the object is direct, an existing entity that reflects upon itself, it is further defined as being immediately unique. This constitutes sense-consciousness. Consciousness, viewed as a relationship, contains only the concepts associated with the abstract self or formal thought; it interprets these concepts as attributes of the object. Consequently, sense-consciousness perceives the object as an existing entity, a something, a present thing, a unique instance, and so forth. It seems richest in content but poorest in conceptual depth. This richness of content consists of sensations: they form the substance of consciousness, the substantial and qualitative aspects that the soul possesses and discovers within itself in its anthropological domain. The self (the soul’s reflection of itself) detaches this substance from itself and initially classifies it under the concept of being. Spatial and temporal uniqueness, the here and now (the terms I used in the second volume, page 73, of the Phenomenology of the Mind to describe the object of sense-consciousness) strictly pertains to intuition. For now, the object must be considered solely in its relation to consciousness, meaning it is something outside of consciousness, not yet as something external in its own right, or as existing apart from and outside of itself.
original: (a) Consciousness Proper(127). (α) Sensuous consciousness. Consciousness is, first, immediate consciousness, and its reference to the object accordingly the simple and underived certainty of it. The object similarly, being immediate, an existent, reflected in itself, is further characterised as immediately singular. This is sense-consciousness. Consciousness—as a case of correlation—comprises only the categories belonging to the abstract ego or formal thinking; and these it treats as features of the object. Sense-consciousness therefore is aware of the object as an existent, a something, an existing thing, a singular, and so on. It appears as wealthiest in matter, but as poorest in thought. That wealth of matter is made out of sensations: they are the material of consciousness, the substantial and qualitative, what the soul in its anthropological sphere is and finds in itself. This material the ego (the reflection of the soul in itself) separates from itself, and puts it first under the category of being. Spatial and temporal Singularness, here and now (the terms by which in the Phenomenology of the Mind (W. II. p. 73), I described the object of sense-consciousness) strictly belongs to intuition. At present the object is at first to be viewed only in its correlation to consciousness, i.e. a something external to it, and not yet as external on its own part, or as being beside and out of itself.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The Work of Art
plain: External sensory data, observations, and perceptions frequently mislead and err, yet internal concepts are even more prone to this flaw, even when they possess the highest vividness and compel us irresistibly into passion. The uncertainty regarding whether an object of internal concepts and inner perception truly exists, along with the incidental query about whether subjective consciousness generated it internally, and whether the manner in which it presented itself was adequate to the object’s essential and independent nature, precisely triggered the higher scientific need. This requirement demands that, even if we hold the concept that an object exists or that such an object is present, the object must still be shown or proven according to its necessity. If this proof is developed in a genuinely scientific manner, it must also answer the further question of what an object is. However, explaining this relationship would take us too far in this context, so we can only offer the following comments. If we aim to show the necessity of the beautiful within art, we must demonstrate that art or beauty resulted from prior conditions which, when viewed in their true conception, lead us with scientific necessity to the concept of fine art.
original: Our external intuitions, observations, and perceptions are often deceptive and erroneous, but still more is this the case with the inner ideas, even if they have in themselves the greatest vividness, and are forcible enough to transport us irresistibly into passion. This doubt whether an object of inward ideas and inward perception as such is or is not, as also the accidental question whether the subjective consciousness has produced it in itself, and whether the act or mode in which it brought it before itself was in its turn adequate to the object in its essential and independent nature--all this is just what aroused in men the higher scientific need, which demands that, even if we have an idea that an object is, or that there is such an object, the object must yet be displayed or demonstrated in terms of its necessity. This proof, if it is developed in a really scientific way, must also satisfy the further question What an object is. But to expound this relation would carry us too far in this place, and we can only make the following remarks on the point. If we are to display the necessity of our object, the beautiful in art, we should have to prove that art or beauty was a result of antecedents such as, when considered in their true conception, to lead us on with scientific necessity to the idea of fine art.

plain: Ethical sentiment is essential, yet it cannot generate state functions on its own. Because specific duties contain the entire concept in potential, their real existence embodies the full idea. People typically name three state roles: making laws, enforcing them, and judging cases. Lawmaking aligns with universal principles, while enforcement deals with specific instances. However, judging is not the third part of this concept. The individual aspect that unites the other two exists outside these areas. The political state splits into three core parts. First, the authority to define and set universal rules, which is lawmaking. Second, the authority to apply universal rules to specific groups and cases, which is governing. Third, the role of the ruler, who holds the final decision as a subjective authority. In this role, the other two parts merge into a single individual unity. This position serves as both the peak and the start of the entire system. This structure is constitutional monarchy.
original: But, necessary as ethical feeling is, it cannot evolve from itself the functions of state. Whence it comes to pass that since the definite functions are the whole implicitly, they comprise in their actual existence the total conception. We usually speak of the three functions of state, the legislative, executive, and judicial. The legislative corresponds to universality, and the executive to particularity; but the judicial is not the third element of the conception. The individuality uniting the other two lies beyond these spheres. The political state is divided into three substantive branches: (a) The power to fix and establish the universal. This is legislation. (6) The power, which brings particular spheres and individual cases under the universal. This is the function of government. (c) The function of the prince, as the subjectivity with which rests the final decision. In this function the other two are brought into an individual unity. It is at once the culmination and beginning of the whole. This is constitutional m.onarchy.

plain: Officials will not miss the weight of these facts, even if someone argues that the person holding such dangerous ideas deserves trust, or if official status grants them protection. They will not be stopped by the request to safeguard and freely allow a theory that attacks the core foundation of behavior, which is universal principles. They will not ignore rude behavior just because it is claimed to be part of a teacher’s duty. The old joke that God gives understanding to those He gives office to is so worn out that no one today would treat it as true. In the approaches to instructing philosophy, which the state has revived under these conditions, the vital part involving protection and aid cannot be overlooked. The discipline requires this kind of help in many respects. Often, in scientific, religious, and other writings, one can find a disdain for the field. Some individuals, who lack notable schooling and know nothing about the subject, treat it like an old, discarded piece of clothing. They even attack it, viewing its attempts to understand God and both physical and spiritual nature as foolish and sinful arrogance. They mock its effort to discover the truth. They accuse, despise, and condemn the endless repetition of reason, reason, and reason.
original: The significance of these facts for the authorities will not be obscured by the claim that the holder of these perilous doctrines should be trusted, or by the immunity of office. The authorities will not be deterred by the demand that they should protect and give free play to a theory which strikes at the substantial basis of conduct, namely, uni- versal principles, and that they should disregard insolence on the ground of its being the exercise of the teacher's function. To him, to whom Ood gives office, He gives also understanding is a well-worn jest, which no one in our time would like to take seriously. In the methods of teaching philosophy, which have under the circumstances been reanimated by the government, the important element of protection and support cannot be ignored. The study of philosophy is in many ways in need of such assistance. Frequently in scientific, religious, and other works may be read a contempt for philosophy. Some, who have no conspicuous education and are total strangers to philosophy, treat it as a cast-off garment. They even rail against it, and regard as foolishness and sinful presumption its efforts to conceive of God and physical and spiritual nature. They scout its endeavour to know the truth. Eeason, and again reason, and reason in endless iteration is by them accused, despised, condemned.

plain: Kant argues that, from this perspective, beauty does not display its purposefulness as an outside shape stuck onto it. Instead, the purposeful match between the inside and outside is the inherent nature of the beautiful thing.
