Finally, Kant defines beauty, as a fourth point, as something we identify, without using any concept, as the target of a required enjoyment. Necessity is an abstract category that points to a deep, essential link between two sides. If one side exists, and because it exists, then the other side must also exist. The nature of one side includes the other side along with itself, much like a cause has no meaning without an effect. The enjoyment that beauty brings is this kind of required result, completely independent of concepts, meaning independent of the categories of understanding. For example, we certainly feel pleasure from symmetry, which is built according to a concept of understanding. However, Kant insists that, for something to please us, it needs more than just the unity and equality found in such a concept of understanding.
original: The beautiful, Kant maintains, when considered from this point of view, does not wear its teleology as an external form attached to it; but the teleological correspondence of the inner and outer is the immanent nature of the beautiful object. (d) Lastly, Kant's treatment determines the beautiful, in the fourth place, as being recognized, without a conception, as object of a necessary delight. Necessity is an abstract category, and indicates an inner essential relation of two aspects; if the one is, and because the one is, then (and therefore) the other is. The one in its nature involves the other as well as itself, just as cause, e.g., has no meaning without effect. The delight which the beautiful involves is such a necessary consequence, wholly without relation to conceptions, i.e. to categories of the understanding. Thus, for instance, we are pleased no doubt by what is symmetrical, and this is constructed in accordance with a conception of the understanding. But Kant requires, to give us pleasure, even more than the unity and equality that belong to such a conception of the understanding.

ref: The Greek World, The Peloponnesian War
plain: The Greek ideal of liberty inherently contains the liberation of thinking. We saw the first stirrings of thought among the group previously identified by their famous title, the Seven Sages. These individuals were the first to voice universal statements, even though wisdom back then relied more on direct, concrete understanding of things rather than the ability to form abstract concepts. As religious art and political structures evolved, thinking grew stronger, acting as both a rival and a dismantler of those forms. By the era of the Peloponnesian War, scientific knowledge had already advanced significantly. The Sophists initiated the practice of reflecting on current conditions and engaging in logical reasoning. The same energy and diligence we saw in Greek daily life and artistic creation appeared in the complex paths these ideas followed. Just as physical objects are altered, processed, and repurposed for uses different from their original intent, the core nature of Spirit—what is thought and known—gets manipulated in various ways. It becomes a subject for the mind to engage with, and this engagement turns into an interest that exists for its own sake. The internal movement of thought, which operates within its own domain without relying on outside objects, a process that previously held no appeal, now gains value purely on its own merits.
original: In the principle of Greek Freedom, inasmuch as it is Freedom, is involved the self-emancipation of Thought. "We observed the dawn of Thought in the circle of men mentioned above under their well-known appellation of the Seven Sages. It was they who first uttered general propositions; though at that time wisdom consisted rather in a concrete insight [into things, than in the power of abstract conception]. Parallel with the advance in the development of Religious Art and with political growth, we find a progressive strengthening of Thought, its enemy and destroyer; and at the time of the Pelopounesian War science was already developed. With the Sophists began the process of reflection on the existing state of things, and of ratiocination. That very diligence and activity which we observed among the Greeks in their practical life, and in the achievement of works of art, shewed itself also in the turns and windings which these ideas took; so that, as material things are changed, worked up and used for other than their original purposes, similarly the essential being of Spirit — what is thought and known — is variously handled; it is made an object about which the mind can employ itself, and this occupation becomes an interest in and for itself. The movement of Thought — that which goes on within its sphere [without reference to an extrinsic object] — a process which had formerly no interest — acquires attractiveness on its own account.

plain: No further citations are required, since readers can easily locate these sources in any standard encyclopedia. In the historical development of Greek philosophy, scholars traditionally arranged thinkers based on apparent external links, specifically the master-disciple relationship. This perspective implies that a particular philosopher might have inherited ideas partly from Thales and partly from Pythagoras. Yet, this approach is fundamentally flawed because it relies on superficial connections rather than intrinsic ones. The collective of thinkers associated with the system stemming from Thales progresses along a trajectory that remains distinct, both temporally and intellectually, from the other faction. In reality, no such isolated sequence ever truly exists. Even if individuals had formed a continuous chain of instruction, which historically did not happen, the mind operates according to a completely different logic. These sequential groups are deeply intertwined in their spiritual essence, just as they are in their specific content. We encounter Thales initially among the Ionic people, a group that included the Athenians or from which the western Asian Ionian population as a whole originated. This Ionic race appears earlier in the Peloponnese, though it seems to have been displaced from there. It remains unclear which specific nations belonged to this group, since, as Herodotus notes in Book I, section 143, the remaining Ionian peoples, and even the Athenian citizens, eventually abandoned the designation.
original: I need give no more references, for they may be found without trouble in any compendium. In the progress of Greek philosophy men were formerly accustomed to follow the order that showed, according to ordinary ideas, an external connection, and which is found in one philosopher having had another as his teacher—this connection is one which might show him to be partly derived from Thales and partly from Pythagoras. But such a connection is in part defective in itself, and in part it is merely external. The one set of philosophic sects, or of philosophers classed together, which is considered as belonging to a system—that which proceeds from Thales—pursues its course in time and mind far separate from the other. But, in truth, no such series ever does exist in this isolation, nor would it do so even though the individuals were consecutive and had been externally connected as teacher and taught, which never is the case; mind follows quite another order. These successive series are interwoven in spirit just as much as in their particular content. We come across Thales first amongst the Ionic people, to whom the Athenians belonged, or from whom the Ionians of Asia Minor, as a whole, derived their origin. The Ionic race appears earlier in Peloponnesus, but seems to have been removed from thence. It is, however, not known what nations belonged to it, for, according to Herodotus (I. 143), the other Ionians, and even the Athenians, laid aside the name.

plain: This is the famous Socratic irony. In his specific situation, it functions as a distinct way of interacting with others, making it merely a subjective shape of dialectic, since genuine dialectic engages with the underlying reasons for things. His goal was to ensure that when others presented their principles, he would derive the direct opposite of what they claimed from each specific proposition, or alternatively, let the opposite emerge from their own inner awareness without directly opposing their explicit statements. Occasionally, he also extracted the opposite from a concrete instance. However, because this opposite was a principle the men held just as strongly as the original one, he proceeded to demonstrate that they were contradicting themselves. In this way, Socrates taught his companions to recognize that they knew nothing. Furthermore, he himself claimed to know nothing, and consequently, he taught nothing. It can genuinely be stated that Socrates knew nothing, as he never achieved the systematic structure of a philosophy. He was aware of this fact, and establishing a science was never his objective. From one perspective, this irony appears to be something false. Yet, when we discuss subjects that hold universal interest and speak about them to various individuals, it is invariably the case that one person fails to grasp another’s conception of the subject.
original: This is the celebrated Socratic irony, which in his case is a particular mode of carrying on intercourse between one person and another, and is thus only a subjective form of dialectic, for real dialectic deals with the reasons for things. What he wished to effect was, that when other people brought forward their principles, he, from each definite proposition, should deduce as its consequence the direct opposite of what the proposition stated, or else allow the opposite to be deduced from their own inner consciousness without maintaining it directly against their statements. Sometimes he also derived the opposite from a concrete case. But as this opposite was a principle held by men as firmly as the other, he then went on to show that they contradicted themselves. Thus Socrates taught those with whom he associated to know that they knew nothing; indeed, what is more, he himself said that he knew nothing, and therefore taught nothing. It may actually be said that Socrates knew nothing, for he did not reach the systematic construction of a philosophy. He was conscious of this, and it was also not at all his aim to establish a science. On the one view, this irony seems to be something untrue. But when we deal with objects which have a universal interest, and speak about them to one and to another, it is always the case that one does not understand another’s conception of the object.

ref: Virtue and the Course of the World
plain: Out of this conflict, the outcome is that consciousness sheds the notion of an intrinsic good that lacks actual existence, treating it as a mere covering. Through its struggle, consciousness has learned that the world’s development is not as flawed as it appeared, because the reality of the world’s development belongs to the universal. Once this is recognized, it becomes clear that sacrificing individuality cannot produce the good, since the means for such action have vanished. Individuality is exactly the explicit realization of what is implicitly and inherently real, namely the universal. Consequently, the distortion is no longer viewed as a corruption of goodness, but rather as the transformation of the good, as a bare purpose, into actual reality. The dynamic process of individuality is the realization of the universal.
original: The result, then, arising from this opposition, consists in the fact that consciousness lets the idea of an inherent good, which yet has no actual reahty, slip from it like a mere cloak. Consciousness has learned in the course of its struggle that the world's process is not so bad as it looked; for the reality of the world's process is that of the universal. With the discovery of this it is seen that there is no way of producing the good through the sacrifice of individuality, the means for doing so have gone; for individuality is precisely the explicit actualisation of what is implicitly and inherently real (i.e. the universal); and the perversion ceases to be looked at as a perversion of goodness, for it is just the transmuting of the good, qua bare purpose, into actual reality. The moving process of individuality is the realising of the universal.

plain: Monogamy, rather than marriage itself, stands as a fundamental pillar for the moral life of any society. Consequently, the establishment of marriage is often depicted as a key element in the divine or heroic creation of the state. Because marriage stems from the voluntary surrender by both partners of the unique personality that belongs exclusively to them, it cannot happen within the sphere of natural kinship, which is characterized by deep closeness and unrestricted familiarity. Inside such a group, individuals do not possess a distinct, exclusive identity. Therefore, marriage should occur between unrelated families and between people who have separate origins. For this reason, unions between blood relatives contradict the very idea of marriage. It is a moral action performed in freedom, not governed by direct biological conditions or their drives. Unions within these close limits also conflict with genuine natural sentiment. Theories that base marriage on natural sexual urges rather than a natural right, that treat it as an arbitrary agreement, that justify monogamy by citing the ratio of men to women, or that rely on vague emotions to ban unions between relatives, all stem from the prevailing notion of a state of nature. They also arise from the belief that such a state holds rights. However, these views lack any understanding of rationality and freedom.
original: Marriage, or monogamy, rather, is one of the principles on which the ethical life of a community depends most absolutely. Hence the institution of marriage is represented as one of the features of the divine or heroic founding of the state. Since marriage proceeds out of the free resignation by both sexes of that personality which is infinitely peculiar to themselves, it must not occur within the bounds of natural identity, which involves great intimacy and unlimited familiarity. Within such a circle individuals have no exclusive personality. Marriage must rather take place in families that are unconnected, and between persons who are distinct in their origin. Between persons related by blood, therefore, marriage is contrary to the conception of it. It is an ethical act done in freedom, and not controlled by direct natural conditions and their impulses. Marriage within these limits is likewise contrary to true natural feeling. To regard marriage as grounded not on a right of nature but on natural sexual impulse, to view it as a capricious contract, to give such an external reason for monogamy as the number of men in relation to the number of women, and to give only vague feelings as cause sufficient to prohibit marriage between blood connections, all such theories are due to the current idea of a state of nature, and to the opinion that such a state possesses rights. They are, however, devoid of the conception of rationality and freedom.

plain: In habitual existence, a person’s way of being is "natural," which makes it unfree. Yet it remains free to the extent that habit reduces the purely natural aspect of feeling to a simple state of being. The individual is no longer pulled or pushed involuntarily by these feelings, nor are they concerned, engaged, or reliant upon them. The lack of freedom in habit is partly just a matter of form, since habit merely connects to the soul’s state. It is also partly relative, because it truly appears only with bad habits, or when a habit clashes with another aim. In contrast, the habit of rightness and goodness embodies liberty. The key aspect of Habit is that it frees people from their feelings, even while they are experiencing them. These variations can be outlined as follows: (α) The immediate feeling is denied and viewed as irrelevant. Someone who becomes accustomed to external sensations (cold, heat, limb fatigue, etc., pleasant tastes, etc.), and who toughens their heart against bad luck, gains a strength. This strength means that although the cold, etc.—or the bad luck—is sensed, the emotional impact is reduced to a mere external and immediate fact. The broader mental life maintains its own abstract independence within this, and the sense of self, awareness, reflection, and any other goals or actions are no longer disturbed by it.
original: In habit the human being’s mode of existence is “natural,” and for that reason not free; but still free, so far as the merely natural phase of feeling is by habit reduced to a mere being of his, and he is no longer involuntarily attracted or repelled by it, and so no longer interested, occupied, or dependent in regard to it. The want of freedom in habit is partly merely formal, as habit merely attaches to the being of the soul; partly only relative, so far as it strictly speaking arises only in the case of bad habits, or so far as a habit is opposed by another purpose: whereas the habit of right and goodness is an embodiment of liberty. The main point about Habit is that by its means man gets emancipated from the feelings, even in being affected by them. The different forms of this may be described as follows: (α) The immediate feeling is negated and treated as indifferent. One who gets inured against external sensations (frost, heat, weariness of the limbs, &c., sweet tastes, &c.), and who hardens the heart against misfortune, acquires a strength which consists in this, that although the frost, &c.—or the misfortune—is felt, the affection is deposed to a mere externality and immediacy; the universal psychical life keeps its own abstract independence in it, and the self-feeling as such, consciousness, reflection, and any other purposes and activity, are no longer bothered with it.

plain: A state where a nation exists in this way is one of anarchy, moral decay, and savagery. In such a state, the nation acts merely as a formless, chaotic, and unguided power, resembling the violent, natural sea. However, unlike the sea, the nation is a spiritual entity, and this condition would lead to its own destruction. Despite this, people frequently describe this state as true freedom. If we are to give any meaning to the topic of private individuals taking part in public business, we must assume a nation that is already organized and possesses a governing authority, rather than a savage crowd. The value of such involvement does not lie in the idea that private citizens are smarter than government officials, as the opposite might be true, nor does it rest on their greater desire for the common good. Instead, members of civil society, in their capacity as such, typically see their primary obligation in their personal interests and, particularly within feudal systems, in the interests of their exclusive groups. Consider England, which has been viewed as possessing the most free constitution of all because private individuals hold a dominant role in public matters.
original: Such a condition of a nation is a condition of lawlessness, demoralisation, brutishness: in it the nation would only be a shapeless, wild, blind force, like that of the stormy, elemental sea, which however is not self-destructive, as the nation—a spiritual element—would be. Yet such a condition may be often heard described as that of true freedom. If there is to be any sense in embarking upon the question of the participation of private persons in public affairs, it is not a brutish mass, but an already organised nation—one in which a governmental power exists—which should be presupposed. The desirability of such participation however is not to be put in the superiority of particular intelligence, which private persons are supposed to have over state officials—the contrary may be the case—nor in the superiority of their good will for the general best. The members of civil society as such are rather people who find their nearest duty in their private interest and (as especially in the feudal society) in the interest of their privileged corporation. Take the case of England which, because private persons have a predominant share in public affairs, has been regarded as having the freest of all constitutions.

ref: Introduction: the Geographical Basis of History
plain: Farming, the main way people here survive, benefits from predictable seasons that demand specific farming tasks. This leads to land ownership and the resulting legal ties. These ties form the State’s base, which can only exist when such connections are present. (3.) Coastal areas. Rivers split regions apart, but the ocean does so even more strongly, and we usually see water as a divider. Recently, people have argued that states must be split by natural barriers. However, a core idea suggests water actually unites things, since countries are essentially areas covered by waterways. For example, Silesia is the Oder’s valley; Bohemia and Saxony are the Elbe’s valley; and Egypt is the Nile’s valley. The ocean works the same way, as noted before. Only mountains truly divide. The Pyrenees, for instance, clearly separate Spain from France. Since their discovery, Europeans have stayed connected to America and the East Indies. They have barely entered Africa’s and Asia’s interiors because traveling over land is far harder than traveling over water. The Mediterranean became a center of national life only because it is a sea.
original: For agriculture, which prevails here as the primary principle of subsistence for individuals, is assisted by the regularity of seasons, which require corresponding agricultural operations; property in land commences, and the consequent legal relations;— that is to say, the basis and foundation of the State, which becomes possible only in connection with such relations. (3.) The coast land. A River divides districts of country from each other, but still more does the sea; and we are accustomed to regard water as the separating element. Especially in recent times has it been insisted upon that States must necessarily have been separated by natural features. Yet on the contrary, it may be asserted as a fundamental principle that nothing unites so much as water, for countries are nothing else than districts occupied by streams. Silesia, for instance, is the valley of the Oder; Bohemia and Saxony are the valley of the Elbe; Egypt is the valley of the Nile. With the sea this is not less the case, as has been already pointed out. Only Mountains separate. Thus the Pyrenees decidedly separate Spain from France. The Europeans have been in constant connection with America and the East Indies ever since they were discovered; but they have scarcely penetrated into the interior of Africa and Asia, because intercourse by land is much more difficult than by water. Only through the fact of being a sea, has the Mediterranean become a focus of national life.

plain: All around us, a chaotic mix of events pulls us into their sphere of influence, and as soon as one set of circumstances disappears, another takes its place right away. The broad concept that first emerges from this constant shifting of individuals and nations, which exist for a while and then cease to be, is the idea of change in general. Looking at the remains of an old empire immediately directs our attention to this notion of change from a negative perspective. Which traveler visiting the ruins of Carthage, Palmyra, Persepolis, or Rome has not been prompted to think about the temporary nature of states and people, and to feel sorrow for a strong and abundant existence that is now gone? This is not a sadness focused on personal losses or the unpredictability of one’s own projects, but rather an impartial grief over the decline of a magnificent and highly developed national culture.
original: On every hand there is the motliest throng of events drawing us within the circle of its interest, and when one combination vanishes another immediately appears in its place. The general thought — the category which first presents itself in this restless mutation of individuals and peoples, existing for a time and then vanishing — is that of change at large. The sight of the ruins of some ancient sovereignty directly leads us to contemplate this thought of change in its negative aspect. What traveller among the ruins of Carthage, of Palmyra, Persepolis, or Rome, has not been stimulated to reflections on the transiency of kingdoms and men, and to sadness at the thought of a vigorous and rich life now departed— a sadness which does not expend itself on personal losses and the uncertainty of one's own undertakings, but is a disinterested sorrow at the decay of a splendid and highly cultured national life!

ref: The Philosophy of the Stoics, Ethics
plain: Since Stoic ethics claims that the mind must align with itself, we must not treat this as a mere formality. Consequently, we should not exclude anything that lies outside this self-contained unit. The freedom the Stoics grant to humans is not unrelated to things outside the self. Therefore, humans are genuinely dependent, and happiness truly belongs to this category of dependence. My independence is only one aspect, and the specific aspect of my existence does not yet match it. The ancient question, which resurfaced at this point, concerns the alignment between virtue and happiness. We use the term morality instead of virtue because the standard for guiding my actions is not my will, as it has become customary, but rather something else. Morality actually involves my personal belief that my actions align with rational will decisions and universal duties. This question is essential. It was a problem that engaged people even during Kant’s era. To solve it, we must start by defining what happiness means. Later, more is said about where satisfaction should be sought. However, we must immediately detach ourselves from external factors and chance events. Generally, happiness simply means the sensation of being in harmony with oneself.
original: Now because the principle of the Stoic morality professes to be the harmony of mind with itself, what should be done is not to let this remain formal, and therefore not to let what is not contained in this self-contained be any longer shut out of it. That freedom which the Stoics ascribe to man is not without relation to what is other than himself; thus he is really dependent, and under this category happiness really falls. My independence is only one side, to which the other side, the particular side of my existence, hence does not yet correspond. The old question, which at this time again came up, thus concerns the harmony between virtue and happiness. We speak of morality rather than virtue, because that according to which I ought to direct my actions is not, as in virtue, my will, as it has become custom. Morality really contains my subjective conviction that that which I do is in conformity with rational determinations of will, with universal duties. That question is a necessary one, a problem which even in Kant’s time occupied men, and in endeavouring to solve it we must begin by considering what is to be understood by happiness. Much more is afterwards said of that in which satisfaction is to be sought. However, from what is external and exposed to chance we must at once break free. Happiness in general means nothing more than the feeling of harmony with self.

plain: Our current use of this word carries much the same meaning. Individuals also refer to limited Essences, like humans. However, the word Essence itself signals that we have moved past limitation, making that label for humans somewhat inaccurate. People frequently add that a top Essence, or Being, exists, referring to God. Two points can be raised here. First, the words "there is" point only to the limited, similar to saying there are specific numbers of planets or plants with certain traits. In those instances, we discuss items that have others existing alongside or beyond them. Yet God, who is infinitely boundless, is not an entity with other essences existing outside or next to Him. Anything outside God, if cut off from Him, lacks true essence; when isolated, it turns into a mere appearance or illusion, lacking any independent foundation or reality. Second, describing God as the highest or supreme Essence is a weak way of speaking. The concept of quantity used in that phrase belongs properly within the realm of the limited. When we label one mountain the tallest on Earth, we picture other tall mountains standing next to it. The same logic applies when we call someone the wealthiest or most knowledgeable in their nation.
original: This usage of the term is not very different in its implication from our own. People also speak of finite Essences, such as man. But the very term Essence implies that we have made a step beyond finitude: and the title as applied to man is so far inexact. It is often added that there is a supreme Essence (Being): by which is meant God. On this two remarks may be made. In the first place the phrase 'there is' suggests a finite only: as when we say, there are so many planets, or, there are plants of such a constitution and plants of such an other. In these cases we are speaking of something which has other things beyond and beside it. But God, the absolutely infinite, is not something outside and beside whom there are other essences. All else outside f God, if separated from Him, possesses no essentiality: in its I isolation it becomes a mere show or seeming, without stay or essence of its own. But, secondly, it is a poor way of talking to call God the highest or supreme Essence. The category of quantity which the phrase employs has its proper place within the compass of the finite. When we call one mountain the highest on the earth, we have a vision of other high mountains beside it. So too when we call any one the richest or most learned in his country.

plain: As noted previously, the movement of necessity is structured to surpass the rigid external character it initially possesses, thereby exposing its internal nature. It becomes evident that the connected parts are not truly alien to one another; rather, they are components of a single unity. Each part, in its relationship with the others, feels at home and unites with itself. Through this transformation, necessity becomes freedom. This is not the freedom found in abstract negation, but rather a concrete and positive form of freedom. We can therefore see how erroneous it is to view freedom and necessity as mutually exclusive. Necessity, in its pure form, is certainly not freedom. However, freedom relies on necessity and incorporates it as a non-essential component within itself. A virtuous person recognizes that the general course of their behavior is fundamentally binding and necessary. This awareness does not diminish their freedom in any way. On the contrary, without this recognition, genuine and rational freedom cannot be separated from arbitrary selection. Such arbitrary freedom lacks reality and exists only as a possibility. A criminal, when facing punishment, might view it as a limitation on their liberty. In truth, the punishment is not an external force imposed upon them, but the expression of their own action. If they acknowledge this, they behave as a free individual. Ultimately, a person achieves the greatest independence when they understand that they are determined by the absolute idea in every respect.
original: But, as we have seen already, the process of necessity is so directed that it overcomes the rigid externality which it first had and reveals its inward nature. It then appears that the members, linked to one another, are not really foreign to each other, but only elements of one whole, each of them, in its connexion with the other, being, as it were, at home, and combining with itself. In this way necessity is transfigured into freedom,--not the freedom that consists in abstract negation, but freedom concrete and positive. From which we may learn what a mistake it is to regard freedom and necessity as mutually exclusive. Necessity indeed quâ necessity is far from being freedom: yet freedom pre-supposes necessity, and contains it as an unsubstantial element in itself. A good man is aware that the tenor of his conduct is essentially obligatory and necessary. But this consciousness is so far from making any abatement from his freedom, that without it real and reasonable freedom could not be distinguished from arbitrary choice,--a freedom which has no reality and is merely potential. A criminal, when punished, may look upon his punishment as a restriction of his freedom. Really the punishment is not foreign constraint to which he is subjected, but the manifestation of his own act: and if he recognises this, he comports himself as a free man. In short, man is most independent when he knows himself to be determined by the absolute idea throughout.

plain: Aristotle identifies the third variant as follows: Zeno argues that a projectile in flight is actually at rest. His reasoning is that anything moving always occupies the identical instant and location, which are indistinguishable. It exists here, here, and here. One can describe the arrow as constant because it remains within the same spatial and temporal bounds. It fails to exceed its current position or occupy a different one, whether larger or smaller. This condition defines rest, not movement. Within the specific instant and location, the process of changing into something else is cancelled. A limit is set, but only for that fleeting moment. Because the specific instant and location contain no internal variation, continuity overrides the mere assumption of diversity. Every location is distinct, and therefore identical. Genuine, objective distinction does not emerge in these sensory connections, but rather in the realm of spirit.
original: (c) The third form, according to Aristotle, is as follows:—Zeno says: “The flying arrow rests, and for the reason that what is in motion is always in the self-same Now and the self-same Here, in the indistinguishable;” it is here and here and here. It can be said of the arrow that it is always the same, for it is always in the same space and the same time; it does not get beyond its space, does not take in another, that is, a greater or smaller space. That, however, is what we call rest and not motion. In the Here and Now, the becoming “other” is abrogated, limitation indeed being established, but only as moment; since in the Here and Now as such, there is no difference, continuity is here made to prevail against the mere belief in diversity. Each place is a different place, and thus the same; true, objective difference does not come forth in these sensuous relations, but in the spiritual.

plain: Theophrastus’s heirs eventually located the texts after an extensive search. They sold these documents to Apellicon of Teos. He attempted to repair the damage caused by insects and decay, yet he lacked the necessary expertise and skill to execute this task properly. Consequently, other scholars took over the manuscripts, filling in missing sections according to their own judgment and substituting damaged portions. This process resulted in significant alterations to the original works. However, the situation remained unresolved. Shortly after Apellicon died, the Roman general Sulla captured Athens. Among the plunder transported to Rome were Aristotle’s writings. The Romans, who were only beginning to encounter Greek science and art but had not yet valued Greek philosophy, failed to utilize this acquisition effectively. Later, a Greek man named Tyrannion received authorization to access and publish Aristotle’s manuscripts. He produced an edition of these texts, which also drew criticism for its lack of accuracy. In this instance, the manuscripts passed from booksellers to unskilled scribes, who introduced numerous further errors. This is the manner in which Aristotelian philosophy reached us. Aristotle certainly shared much with his contemporaries, specifically the writings housed in the Alexandrian library. Nevertheless, even those works appear to have had limited circulation. Indeed, many of them are severely corrupted, flawed, and, as seen in the case of the Poetics, unfinished.
original: Finally, the descendants of Theophrastus found them again after long search, and sold them to Apellicon of Teos, who restored what had been destroyed by worms and mould, but who did not possess the learning or the capacity so to do. Hence others went over them, filled up the blanks as they thought best, replaced what was damaged, and thus they were sufficiently altered. But still it was not enough. Just after Apellicon’s death, the Roman Sulla conquered Athens, and amongst the spoil carried off to Rome were the works of Aristotle. The Romans, who had just begun to become acquainted with Greek science and art, but who did not yet appreciate Greek philosophy, did not know how to profit from this spoil. A Greek, named Tyrannion, later on obtained permission to make use of and publish the manuscripts of Aristotle, and he prepared an edition of them, which, however, also bears the reproach of being inaccurate, for here they had the fate of being given by the dealers into the hands of ignorant copyists, who introduced a number of additional corruptions. This is the way in which the Aristotelian philosophy has come to us. Aristotle certainly made known much to his contemporaries, that is to say, the writings in the Alexandrian library, but even those works do not seem to have been widely known. In fact, many of them are most corrupt, imperfect, and, as, for example, the Poetics, incomplete.

plain: Claiming, as we have done, that the mind and its artistic beauty rank above natural beauty is, in broad terms, hardly decisive. The term "higher" is completely vague. It treats natural and artistic beauty as if they merely sit next to each other in the realm of imagination. It presents the gap between them as a simple quantity, and thus as something purely external. However, when the mind and its artistic beauty are called "higher" than nature, they possess a distinction that is not merely relative. Only the mind can grasp truth. It contains everything that exists. Consequently, anything beautiful is genuinely and truly beautiful only when it shares in this superior element and is produced by it. In this way, natural beauty appears as just a mirror of the beauty inherent in the mind. It is an imperfect and incomplete way of existing. Its truly substantial content resides within the mind itself. Furthermore, limiting our focus to fine art seems very natural. Although much has been said, both by us and, to a lesser extent, by the ancients, about the beauty of nature, no one has ever thought to highlight the perspective of natural objects' beauty. No one has tried to build a science, or a systematic explanation, of these natural beauties.
original: To say, as we have said, in general terms, that mind and its artistic beauty stand higher than natural beauty, is no doubt to determine almost nothing. For "higher" is an utterly indefinite expression, which designates the beauty of nature and that of art as if merely standing side by side in the space of the imagination, and states the difference between them as purely quantitative, and, therefore, purely external. But the mind and its artistic beauty, in being "higher" as compared with nature, have a distinction which is not simply relative. Mind, and mind only, is capable of truth, and comprehends in itself all that is, so that whatever is beautiful can only be really and truly beautiful as partaking in this higher element and as created thereby. In this sense the beauty of nature reveals itself as but a reflection of the beauty which belongs to the mind, as an imperfect, incomplete mode of being, as a mode whose really substantial element is contained in the mind itself. Moreover, we shall find the restriction to fine art very natural, for however much has been and is said--though less by the ancients than by ourselves--of the beauties of nature, yet no one has taken it into his head to emphasize the point of view of the beauty of natural objects, and to attempt to make a science, a systematic account of these beauties.

plain: The gap found in hypocrisy does not immediately close into alignment or identity simply because, as commonly stated, hypocrisy demonstrates its respect for duty and virtue. It does so by adopting their appearance and using this facade to conceal itself not only from others but also from its own awareness. This happens as if acknowledging and recognizing its opposite within itself automatically implied and included congruency and agreement. Nevertheless, this recognition in words is genuinely completed and reflected back into the self at that moment. In the very act of treating inherent and essential reality as something significant only to another consciousness, there is actually an implicit contempt for that inherent principle. This action also demonstrates the worthlessness of that reality for everyone. Anything that allows itself to be used as an external tool reveals itself to be an object lacking any proper weight or intrinsic value.
original: This return of the disparity, present in hypocrisy, into the state of congruency or identity is not at once brought to pass by the mere fact that, as people usually say, hypocrisy just proves, its reverence for duty and virtue -through assuming the appearance of them, and using this as a mask to hide itself from its own consciousness no less than from another — as if, in this acknowledgment and recognition in itself of its opposite, eo ipso congruency and agreement were implied and contained. Yet even then it is just as truly done with this recognition in words and is reflected into self; and in the very fact of its usiag the inherent and essential reality merely as something which has a significance for another consciousness, there is really implied its own contempt for that inherent principle, and the demonstration of the worthlessness of that reality for all. For what lets itself be used as an external instrument shows itself to be a thing, which has within it no proper weight and worth of its own.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The End of Art
plain: The absurdity here stems from the fact that the artwork is viewed as aiming for something else that consciousness treats as the fundamental standard and the ideal. Consequently, the artwork holds value only as a practical tool for achieving a goal that carries significant weight outside the realm of art. We must counter this by asserting that art’s calling is to disclose truth through sensory artistic form, to depict the resolved opposition just mentioned, and thus to find its purpose within that very depiction and disclosure. Other aims, such as teaching, moral cleansing, betterment, financial profit, or the pursuit of fame and honor, are irrelevant to the artwork in its own right and do not shape its creation. It is from this perspective, which emerges when we reflect on the issue, that we must grasp the concept of art in its internal necessity. Historically, it was also from this vantage point that the genuine appreciation and comprehension of art first arose. This opposition, which we have discussed, became apparent not only in broad reflective culture but also in philosophy itself. It was only when philosophy found a way to completely resolve this opposition that it understood its own nature and, to that same extent, the nature of both nature and art.
original: The perverseness of this lies in the point that the work of art would then be regarded as aspiring to something else which is set before consciousness as the essential and as what ought to be; so that then the work of art would only have value as a useful instrument in the realization of an end having substantive importance outside the sphere of art. Against this it is necessary to maintain that art has the vocation of revealing the truth in the form of sensuous artistic shape, of representing the reconciled antithesis just described, and, therefore, has its purpose in itself, in this representation and revelation. For other objects, such as instruction, purification, improvement, pecuniary gain, endeavour after fame and honour, have nothing to do with the work of art as such, and do not determine its conception. It is from this point of view, into which reflective consideration of the matter resolves itself, that we have to apprehend the idea of art in its inner necessity, as indeed it was from this point of view, historically speaking, that the true appreciation and understanding of art took its origin. For that antithesis, of which we spoke, made itself felt, not only within general reflective culture, but no less in philosophy as such, and it was not till philosophy discovered how to overcome this antithesis absolutely, that it grasped its own conception and, just in as far as it did so, the conception of nature and of art.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The End of Art
plain: People often defend deeply unethical depictions by arguing that we need to understand wickedness or transgression to behave ethically. In the opposite direction, some claim that artistic images of Mary Magdalene, the attractive woman who committed wrongs and later felt remorse, have lured many into wrongdoing. This happens because art makes the act of feeling sorry seem so appealing, and one must commit a wrong before one can feel sorry for it. However, the theory of ethical betterment, if applied consistently, typically goes even further. It would not settle for the chance to derive a lesson from a piece of art through analysis. Instead, it would present ethical teaching as the main goal of the artwork. In fact, it would allow only ethical topics, figures, deeds, and events to be depicted. Art has the freedom to select its subjects, unlike history or the sciences, which have their material predetermined for them.
original: Thus one may hear the most immoral representations defended by saying that we must know evil, or sin, in order to act morally; and, conversely, it has been said that the portrayal of Mary Magdalene, the beautiful sinner who afterwards repented, has seduced many into sin, because art makes it look so beautiful to repent, and you must sin before you can repent. But the doctrine of moral improvement, if consistently carried out, goes in general yet further. It would not be satisfied with the possibility of extracting a moral from a work of art by interpretation, but it would, on the contrary, display the moral instruction as the substantive purpose of the work of art, and, indeed, would actually admit to portrayal none but moral subjects, moral characters, actions, and incidents. For art has the choice among its subjects, in contradistinction to history or the sciences which have their matter fixed for them.

plain: Self-awareness rooted in nature, rather than in ethical living, only sketches the life of the spirit through symbols. It does not actually realize the spirit itself. Yet, this symbolic depiction finds its actualization in something outside itself. Consequently, this bond is not fulfilled within itself, but in the child. The child is an other, whose birth defines this bond and whose existence marks its end. This shift from one generation to the next is a constant feature of national life. The respectful affection between spouses is thus blended with natural ties and emotion, meaning their bond is not inherently self-sufficient. The same applies to the respectful affection between parents and children. Both bonds are defined by and contained within the temporary nature and the differences of the roles assigned to them. In contrast, the bond between siblings remains a pure, self-contained form. They share the same blood, which has reached a state of stable balance in them. Therefore, they lack the natural connection found between spouses and do not desire each other. They have neither granted nor received the independence of individual existence from one another. They remain free individuals in relation to each other.
original: Being natural self-knowledge, knowledge of self on the basis of nature, and not on that of ethical hfe, it merely represents and typifies in a figure the Hfe of spirit, and is not spirit itself actually reahsed. This figurative representation, however, gets its reahsation in an other than it is. This relationship, therefore, finds itself reahsed not in itself as such, but in the child — an other, in whose coming into being that relationship consists, and with which it passes away. And this change from one generation onwards to another is permanent in and as the life of a nation. The reverent devotion (Pietdt) of husband and wife towards one another is thus mixed up with a natural relation and with feeling, and their relationship is not inherently self-complete; similarly, too, the second relationship, the reverent devotion of parents and children to one another. Both these relationships are constituted by and hold within the transience and the dissimilarity of the two sides, which are assigned to them. An unmixed intransitive form of relationship, however, holds between brother and sister. They are the same blood, which, however, in them has entered into a condition of stable equihbrium. They therefore stand in no such natural relation as husband and wife, they do not desire one another; nor have they given to one another, nor received from one another, this iudependence of individual being; they are free individuahties with respect to each other.

plain: When any person reflects on their own mental activity, they will find, through direct awareness, that their ideas carry a universal quality, alongside other features of thinking that will be listed later. This observation presumes that the individual has previously trained their ability to focus and abstract, allowing them to accurately perceive the evidence within their own awareness and concepts. The earlier introduction already touched on the difference between Sense, Conception, and Thought. Since this distinction is crucial for grasping the nature and types of knowledge, it is useful to highlight it here. To explain Sense, the most straightforward approach is to point to its external origin: the sensory organs. However, merely naming the organ does little to clarify what is actually perceived through it. The true difference between sense and thought lies in the fact that the defining trait of the sensible is individuality. Because the individual, when reduced to its simplest form, is an atom, and because this atom is also part of a group, sensible existence appears as a collection of mutually exclusive units. To put it in more precise and abstract terms, these units exist next to each other and one after another. Conception, or picture-thinking, uses materials from this same sensory source. Yet, when these materials are conceived, they are explicitly marked as being within me and therefore belonging to me. Furthermore, they are characterized as universal, or simple, because they are referred only to the self.
original: In other words, every man, when he thinks and considers his thoughts, will discover by the experience of his consciousness that they possess the character of universality as well as the other aspects of thought to be afterwards enumerated. We assume of course that his powers of attention and abstraction have undergone a previous training, enabling him to observe correctly the evidence of his consciousness and his conceptions. This introductory exposition has already alluded to the distinction between Sense, Conception, and Thought. As the distinction is of capital importance for understanding the nature and kinds of knowledge, it will help to explain matters if we here call attention to it. For the explanation of Sense, the readiest method certainly is, to refer to its external source--the organs of sense. But to name the organ does not help much to explain what is apprehended by it. The real distinction between sense and thought lies in this--that the essential feature of the sensible is individuality, and as the individual (which, reduced to its simplest terms, is the atom) is also a member of a group, sensible existence presents a number of mutually exclusive units,--of units, to speak in more definite and abstract formulae, which exist side by side with, and after, one another. Conception or picture-thinking works with materials from the same sensuous source. But these materials when conceived are expressly characterised as in me and therefore mine: and secondly, as universal, or simple, because only referred to self.

plain: To the extent that these methods share a common trait, they can reasonably be seen as components of the arrogance that drives humans to rely solely on their own abilities to grasp reality. Adopting this stance entails a complete rupture, and when viewed from that perspective, it could be considered the root of all wrongdoing and the first major violation. Consequently, the only apparent path to reconciliation and peace seems to be giving up any assertion of the ability to think or understand. This departure from inherent oneness has not gone unnoticed, and societies throughout history have questioned the significance of this internal conflict within the mind. Such internal division does not exist in the natural world, where physical objects never perform harmful acts. The biblical narrative of humanity's fall has preserved an ancient depiction illustrating how this separation began and what results followed. The events in this story underpin a core belief in the faith, specifically the concept of inherited sinfulness and the resulting requirement for divine aid. It is appropriate to begin the study of logic by analyzing the tale that addresses the origins and implications of the very understanding that logic examines. While philosophy must not be intimidated by religion or accept its existence as a mere favor, it cannot ignore these widespread cultural ideas.
original: And so far as they have this in common, the methods which claim to apprehend the truth by thought may naturally be regarded as part and parcel of the pride which leads man to trust to his own powers for a knowledge of the truth. Such a position involves a thorough-going disruption, and, viewed in that light, might be regarded as the source of all evil and wickedness--the original transgression. Apparently therefore they only way of being reconciled and restored to peace is to surrender all claims to think or know. This lapse from natural unity has not escaped notice, and nations from the earliest times have asked the meaning of the wonderful division of the spirit against itself. No such inward disunion is found in nature: natural things do nothing wicked. The Mosaic legend of the Fall of Man has preserved an ancient picture representing the origin and consequences of this disunion. The incidents of the legend form the basis of an essential article of the creed, the doctrine of original sin in man and his consequent need of succour. It may be well at the commencement of logic to examine the story which treats of the origin and the bearings of the very knowledge which logic has to discuss. For, though philosophy must not allow herself to be overawed by religion, or accept the position of existence on sufferance, she cannot afford to neglect these popular conceptions.

plain: This final category contains eight distinct attributes. First, the ability to shrink to a tiny size, allowing the body to pass through any material. Second, the capacity to grow into an enormous form. Third, the ability to become so light that one can ride a sunbeam up to the sun. Fourth, unlimited strength in the limbs, enabling a person to touch the moon with their fingertips. Fifth, an unyielding will, which allows someone to sink into the earth as easily as they would into water. Sixth, control over all things, whether alive or inert. Seventh, the ability to alter the natural order. Eighth, the power to accomplish any desired task. Colebrooke notes that the belief in such supreme power being accessible to humans during their lifetime is not unique to the Sankhya school. Instead, it appears across all philosophical systems and religious concepts. In plays and folk stories, such abilities are sincerely attributed to many saints and Brahmins. Sensory proof does not contradict these claims, because for Indians, sensory perception is generally ignored. Everything takes the shape of mental images, and every dream is valued equally with reality and fact. Sankhya attributes this power to humans when they raise themselves through mental effort into inner subjectivity.
original: This last is eight-fold, and hence eight special qualities are given as being present; viz. the power to contract oneself into a quite small form, for which everything shall be penetrable; the power to expand into a gigantic body; the power to become light enough to be able to mount to the sun on a sunbeam; the possession of unlimited power of action in the organs, so that with the finger-tips the moon may be touched; irresistible will, so that, for instance, one may dive into the earth as easily as in the water; mastery over all living and lifeless existence; the power to change the course of nature; and the power to perform everything that is wished. “The feeling that such transcendent power,” Colebrooke goes on, “is within the reach of man in his life is not peculiar to the Sanc’hya sect, but is common to all systems and religious ideas, and such a power is in good faith ascribed to many holy men and Brahmins in dramas and popular narratives.” Sensuous evidence is of no account as opposed to this, for with the Indian, perception of the senses is, generally speaking, absent: everything adopts the form of imaginary images, every dream is esteemed just as much as truth and actuality. The Sanc’hya ascribes this power to man, in so far as he elevates himself through the working of his thought into inward subjectivity.

plain: Faith, academic theological study, and the intuitive wisdom of ordinary people have consistently upheld this view. This stance counters Spinoza by first claiming that free will is genuine and that badness actually happens. In contrast, Spinoza argues that only absolute, universal substance is truly real because it is not specific or limited. Therefore, particular or individual things, including my personal subjectivity and spiritual nature, do not possess absolute existence. They are merely restricted changes whose ideas rely on something else. Consequently, Spinoza views the soul or Spirit, when seen as a separate individual, as just a negation, similar to any other defined object. Since all distinctions and limits in objects and awareness collapse back into the single substance, one could say Spinoza’s system dumps everything into a pit of destruction. However, nothing rises from this pit. The specific items Spinoza mentions are merely assumed from standard thinking without proof. If he were to prove them, he would have to derive them from his Substance. But that Substance does not expand, so it lacks life, spirituality, or action. His philosophy features only a stiff, unyielding substance, not yet spirit. In this view, we do not feel comfortable with ourselves. God lacks spirit because He is not the Three in One.
original: This has been firmly maintained by religion, theology, and the sound common sense of the common consciousness, and this form of opposition to Spinoza appears first of all in the assertion that freedom is real, and that evil exists. But because for Spinoza, on the other hand, there exists only absolute universal substance as the non-particularized, the truly real—all that is particular and individual, my subjectivity and spirituality, has, on the other hand, as a limited modification whose Notion depends on another, no absolute existence. Thus the soul, the Spirit, in so far as it is an individual Being, is for Spinoza a mere negation, like everything in general that is determined. As all differences and determinations of things and of consciousness simply go back into the One substance, one may say that in the system of Spinoza all things are merely cast down into this abyss of annihilation. But from this abyss nothing comes out; and the particular of which Spinoza speaks is only assumed and presupposed from the ordinary conception, without being justified. Were it to be justified, Spinoza would have to deduce it from his Substance; but that does not open itself out, and therefore comes to no vitality, spirituality or activity. His philosophy has only a rigid and unyielding substance, and not yet spirit; in it we are not at home with ourselves. But the reason that God is not spirit is that He is not the Three in One.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The End of Art
plain: Accepting such a wide range of content immediately invites the objection that the various feelings and thoughts art seeks to trigger or strengthen overlap and conflict, effectively neutralizing each other through mutual interference. In this regard, because art stirs up directly opposing emotions, it merely amplifies the internal contradictions of our passions. It either leaves people reeling like frenzied worshippers or drives them into logical fallacy and doubt, much like formal debate does. This inherent variety in artistic material therefore forces us to reject a purely formal goal for art. Reason intrudes upon this chaotic diversity, demanding that a higher, more universal purpose emerge from these elements despite their internal conflicts, and requiring proof that this purpose is actually achieved. Similarly, we naturally assume that the state and human social existence serve the goal of developing and expressing all human abilities and individual strengths in every direction and with every inclination. However, against this broad perspective, a question immediately arises: what single unity must contain these diverse formations, and what one fundamental idea or ultimate end must they share?
original: But when we admit so great a variety of content we are at once met by the remark that the manifold feelings and ideas, which art aims at provoking or reinforcing, intersect and contradict, and by mutual interference cancel one another. Indeed, in this aspect, in so far as art inspires men to directly opposite emotions, it only magnifies the contradiction of our feelings and passions, and either sets them staggering like Bacchantes, or passes into sophistry and scepticism, in the same way as argumentation. This diversity of the material of art itself compels us, therefore, not to be content with so formal an aim for it, seeing that rationality forces its way into this wild diversity, and demands to see the emergence of a higher and more universal purpose from these elements in spite of their self-contradiction, and to be assured of its being attained. Just in the same way the State and the social life of men are, of course, credited with the purpose that in them all human capacities and all individual powers are to be developed and to find utterance in all directions and with all tendencies. But in opposition to so formal a view there at once arises the question in what unity these manifold formations must be comprehended, and what single end they must have for their fundamental idea and ultimate purpose.

plain: If that unity is inherently abstract and thus lacks substance, it naturally allows concrete things outside itself—whether they are many deities or secular, empirical individuals—to remain independent. Indeed, under a superficial understanding, pantheism could logically be termed monotheism. If God is identical to the world, and there is only one world, then that form of pantheism contains only one God. One might attribute an empty numerical unity to the world, but such abstract attribution holds no special interest. In fact, a mere numerical unity simply signifies that its content consists of an infinite multitude and variety of finite things. It is this illusion regarding empty unity that alone enables and prompts the mistaken notion of pantheism. Only the image of the world as a single entity, the all, hovering in an indefinite blue, could ever be seen as capable of merging with God. Only based on that premise could philosophy be thought to claim that God is the world. If the world were viewed as it actually is—as everything, as the endless collection of empirical existence—it would hardly seem possible to imagine a pantheism that declared such material to be God.
original: For that unity, if it be intrinsically abstract and therefore empty, tends of itself to let whatever is concrete, outside it—be it as a lot of Gods or as secular, empirical individuals—keep its independence. That pantheism indeed—on the shallow conception of it—might with a show of logic as well be called a monotheism: for if God, as it says, is identical with the world, then as there is only one world there would be in that pantheism only one God. Perhaps the empty numerical unity must be predicated of the world: but such abstract predication of it has no further special interest; on the contrary, a mere numerical unity just means that its content is an infinite multeity and variety of finitudes. But it is that delusion with the empty unity, which alone makes possible and induces the wrong idea of pantheism. It is only the picture—floating in the indefinite blue—of the world as one thing, the all, that could ever be considered capable of combining with God: only on that assumption could philosophy be supposed to teach that God is the world: for if the world were taken as it is, as everything, as the endless lot of empirical existence, then it would hardly have been even held possible to suppose a pantheism which asserted of such stuff that it is God.

ref: Separation of Philosophy from Other Allied…
plain: Greek religion shows the same pattern, as the deity worshipped transforms into mundane statues and marble. Painting reaches this external stage when the divine figure is reduced to simple canvas or wood. In the Lutheran view, the Eucharist relies solely on faith. It serves as a divine fulfillment rather than an object of worship, unlike the Host. Consequently, a holy image holds no more significance for us than a rock or ordinary object. Consciousness must initially adopt this second perspective. It needs to begin with an external understanding of the form. It must passively receive reports and store them in memory. However, staying in this position represents an unspiritual outlook. Remaining fixed in this second stance, trapped in a dead, distant historical gap, amounts to rejecting the Spirit. The sins of those who lie against the Holy Ghost cannot be pardoned.
original: It is the same thing in the Greek Religion where the god present in devotion changes into prosaic statues and marble; or in painting, where this externality is likewise arrived at, when the god becomes mere canvas or wood. The Supper is, according to the Lutheran conception, of Faith alone; it is a divine satisfaction, and is not adored as if it were the Host. Thus a sacred image is no more to us than is a stone or thing. The second point of view must indeed be that with which consciousness begins; it must start from the external comprehension of this form: it must passively accept report and take it up into memory. But if it remain where it is, that is the unspiritual point of view; to remain fixed in this second standpoint in this dead far-away historic distance, is to reject the Spirit. The sins of him who lies against the Holy Ghost cannot be forgiven.

plain: Yet, in this specific shape, the dynamic remains a requirement and a flow of comprehension. The dynamic itself is not what comprehension targets; rather, comprehension focuses on items within that flow, such as positive and negative electricity, distance, speed, attractive power, and countless other elements. These items constitute the substance of the dynamic’s stages. Precisely because of this, explanation brings such pleasure. If we may phrase it that way, awareness is in direct contact with itself and simply delights in itself. It may appear to be engaged with other matters, but in reality, it is constantly preoccupied only with itself. In the contrary rule, which reverses the initial rule or represents internal differentiation, infinity certainly becomes the target of comprehension. However, comprehension again fails to honor infinity in its pure form. Comprehension once more allocates what is essentially differentiation—namely, the self-repulsion of the identical and the self-attraction of dissimilar elements—to two realms or two substantial components. For comprehension, the dynamic observed in experience is merely an occurrence. The identical and the dissimilar are attributes, and their existence rests on a foundational base. What appears to comprehension as an object hidden by a sensory veil now presents itself to us in its fundamental shape as a pure concept.
original: This process or necessity is, however, in this form, still a necessity and a process of imderstanding, or the process as such is not the 'object of understanding; instead, understanding has as its objects in that process positive and negative electricity, distance, velocity, force of attraction, and a thousand other things — objects which make up the content of the moments of the process. It is just for that reason that there is so much satisfaction in explanation, because consciousness being there, if we may use such an expression, in direct conununion with itself, enjoys itself only. No doubt it there seems to be occupied with something else, but in point of fact it is busied all the while merely with itself. In the opposite law, as the inversion of the first law, or in internal distinction, infinitude doubtless becomes itself object of understanding. But once more understanding fails to do justice to infinity as such, since understanding assigns again to two worlds, or to two substantial elements, that which is distinction per se, — the self-repulsion of the selfsame, and the self-attraction of unhke factors. To understanding the process, as it is found in experience, is here an event that happens, and the selfsame and the unhke are predicates, whose reality is an underlying substratum. What is for understanding an object in a covering veil of sense, now comes before us in its essential form as a pure notion.

plain: When we discuss foundations, we must not base them on the concept of the state itself, which is inherent to it. Instead, we rely on something outside and foreign to the state, like the notion of the state’s or the people’s welfare. Using this approach, one can certainly derive the principle of hereditary succession through intermediate steps. However, different intermediate steps could lead to entirely different results. It is widely recognized what outcomes follow from focusing on the people’s welfare. Consequently, philosophy only examines sovereignty within the realm of thought. Any investigative method other than the speculative approach of the infinitely self-sustaining idea completely destroys the essence of sovereignty. Choosing a ruler by free election is easily seen as the most natural method. This view is closely related to the following superficial idea: Since the monarch’s duty is to address the people’s concerns and interests, the people must decide who they appoint to serve them, and the right to rule stems solely from such an appointment.
original: To speak of grounds is to propound as its basis not the idea of the state, which is internal to it, but something external in its nature and alien, such as the thought of the well-being of the state or of the people. By such a method inheritance can indeed be deduced through medii termini; but there might be other medii termini with quite other consequences. And it is only too well known what conse- quences may be drawn from the well-being of the people (solid du pewple). — Hence, philosophy ventures to contemplate majesty only in the medium of thought. Every other method of inquiry, except the speculative method of the infinite self-grounded idea, absolutely annuls the nature of majesty. Treely to elect the monarch is readily taken as the most natural way. It is closely allied to the following shallow thought: — " Because it is the concern and interest of the people which the monarch has to provide for, it must be left to the people to choose whom it will depute to provide for them, and only out of such a commission arises the right of governing."

plain: Selfhood, when it refers back to itself, is immediate. When the negative refers to itself, it becomes a self-existing entity, the One. Because this unity has no internal differences, it shuts out anything else. To exist for oneself, to be one, is finished Quality. In this state, it holds abstract Being and Being that has been changed, treating them as non-substantial parts. As plain Being, the One is a simple loop back to itself. As changed Being, it has specific character. However, this character is not limited. It is not a specific thing set apart from others. Instead, it is infinite because it takes in difference and cancels it out. The clearest example of selfhood is the "I." We recognize ourselves as existing things, first separated from other existing things, and connected to them in certain ways. Yet we also see this spread-out existence, with its connections, pulled back into a single point, taking the simple shape of selfhood. When we use the word "I," we show a self-reference that is both infinite and negative. One might argue that humans are set apart from the animal world, and thus from nature entirely, by knowing themselves as "I." This means natural objects never reach a free selfhood. Limited to existing here and now, they are always and only existing for something else. Furthermore, selfhood can be called ideality, just as existing here and now was called reality. It is claimed that alongside reality, there is also ideality.
original: (α) Being-for self, as reference to itself, is immediacy, and as reference of the negative to itself, is a self-subsistent, the One. This unit, being without distinction in itself, thus excludes the other from itself. To be for self--to be one--is completed Quality, and as such, contains abstract Being and Being modified as non-substantial elements. As simple Being, the One is simple self-reference; as Being modified it is determinate: but the determinateness is not in this case a finite determinateness--a somewhat in distinction from an other--but infinite, because it contains distinction absorbed and annulled in itself. The readiest instance of Being-for-self is found in the 'I.' We know ourselves as existents, distinguished in the first place from other existents, and with certain relations thereto. But we also come to know this expansion of existence (in these relations) reduced, as it were, to a point in the simple form of being-for-self. When we say 'I,' we express the reference-to-self which is infinite, and at the same time negative. Man, it may be said, is distinguished from the animal world, and in that way from nature altogether, by knowing himself as 'I': which amounts to saying that natural things never attain a free Being-for-self, but as limited to Being-there-and-then, are always and only Being for an other.--Again, Being-for-self may be described as ideality, just as Being-there-and-then was described as reality. It is said, that besides reality there is also an ideality.

plain: This view illustrates the problems inherent in these topics, issues that Berkeley tried to avoid through a novel approach. In this framework, God must resolve the inconsistency; He carries the burden and is left to solve the contradiction. Essentially, this idealism leaves the standard sensory view of the world, the distinction of reality, and the system of thought consisting of judgments lacking Notion exactly as they were. Clearly, the content remains unchanged; only the abstract form shifts to claim that everything is merely perception. This type of idealism addresses only the conflict between consciousness and its object, ignoring the expansion of concepts and the conflicts within empirical, varied content. If we inquire about the truth of these perceptions and concepts, just as we previously did about things, no answer emerges. It makes little difference whether we trust in things or in perceptions, provided self-consciousness is fully occupied by finalities. It accepts content in the usual manner, and that content is of the usual type. In its individual state, it fumbles through the concepts of purely empirical existence, understanding nothing else about the content. In other words, within this formal idealism, reason lacks any content of its own.
original: This conception gives an instance of the difficulties which appear in regard to these questions, and which Berkeley wished to escape from in a quite original way. The inconsistency in this system God has again to make good; He has to bear it all away; to Him the solution of the contradiction is left. In this idealism, in short, the common sensuous view of the universe and the separation of actuality, as also the system of thought, of judgments devoid of Notion, remain exactly as before; plainly nothing in the content is altered but the abstract form that all things are perceptions only. Such idealism deals with the opposition between consciousness and its object merely, and leaves the extension of the conceptions and the antagonisms of the empirical and manifold content quite untouched; and if we ask what then is the truth of these perceptions and conceptions, as we asked formerly of things, no answer is forthcoming. It is pretty much a matter of indifference whether we believe in things or in perceptions, if self-consciousness remains possessed entirely by finalities; it receives the content in the ordinary way, and that content is of the ordinary kind. In its individuality it stumbles about amid the conceptions of an entirely empirical existence, without knowing and understanding anything else about the content: that is to say in this formal idealism reason has no content of its own.

plain: Leucippus and Democritus aimed to push the theory further. They felt the need for a sharper distinction than the basic split between joining and parting. To achieve this, they attributed variety to the atoms, claiming this variety was endless. Aristotle, in Book I, Chapter 4 of his Metaphysics, notes that they tried to define this variety in three specific ways. He reports that they claimed atoms differ in shape, much like the letter A differs from N. They also differed in arrangement, similar to how the sequence AN differs from NA. Finally, they differed in orientation, such as whether a symbol stands upright or lies down, like Z versus N. Aristotle adds that all other variations must stem from these three. We observe that shape, arrangement, and orientation are merely external connections. These are indifferent determinations, meaning they are non-essential links that do not change the thing’s own nature or its internal definition. Their unity exists only in relation to something else.
