Viewed in isolation, this distinction is contradictory. Since atoms are completely simple, they are identical, so such variety cannot actually exist. Here, we see an attempt to reduce sensory experience to a small number of fixed traits. Aristotle, in Book I, Chapter 8 of On Generation and Corruption, comments on Leucippus in this context. He states that Leucippus wanted to align the concept of phenomena and sensory perception more closely with reality. By doing so, he treated motion, birth, and death as things that exist on their own. In this view, actuality is granted its proper status, whereas other thinkers speak only of illusion.
original: Since Leucippus and Democritus wished to go further, the necessity of a more definite distinction than this superficial one of union and separation was introduced, and they sought to bring this about by ascribing diversity to atoms, and, indeed, by making their diversity infinite. Aristotle (Met. I. 4) says: “This diversity they sought to determine in three ways. They say that atoms differ in figure, as A does from N; in order” (place) “as AN from NA; in position”—as to whether they stand upright or lie—“as Z from N. From these all other differences must come.” We see that figure, order and posture are again external relationships, indifferent determinations, i.e. unessential relations which do not affect the nature of the thing in itself nor its immanent determinateness, for their unity is only in another. Taken on its own account, this difference is indeed inconsistent, for as the entirely simple one, the atoms are perfectly alike, and thus any such diversity cannot come into question. We here have an endeavour to lead the sensuous back into few determinations. Aristotle (De gen. et corr. I. 8) says in this connection of Leucippus: “He wished to bring the conception of the phenomenal and sensuous perception nearer, and thereby represented movement, origination and decease, as existent in themselves.” In this we see no more than that actuality from him receives its rights, while others speak only of deception.

plain: It exists as the essential character or its mirror image within the self. Yet, the way these parts displace one another shows up here as their placement in awareness, not in themselves, but only for a different awareness. This awareness highlights one part of the content, placing it in the light and offering it as a target for others. Simultaneously, awareness reflects back from that part onto itself, so the opposing element is also present inside it, held as its own property. Furthermore, no single part can be simply pushed out while another is simply kept in; instead, awareness shifts back and forth between them, because it must make both parts vital for itself and for others. The entire system is the active process of blending individual identity with the universal. However, since this awareness views this whole system as just the basic underlying reality and therefore the abstraction of "the fact itself," the parts of this system seem separate from the "fact" and from each other. As a unified whole, it is fully displayed only through the process of alternately revealing its components and holding them inside itself.
original: is present as the inherent nature or its reflection into self; the ousting of the moments by each other there finds expression, however, in their being estabhshed in consciousness, not per se, but only for another consciousness. One of the moments of the content is exposed by it to the light, and presented as an object for others. Consciousness, however, is at the same time reflected therefrom back upon itself, and the opposite is thus equally present within it, is retained for itself as its own. There is, too, not one of them which could be merely and solely put outside, and another merely retained within; rather, consciousness operates alternately with them, for it has to make one as well as another essential for itself and for others. The whole is the moving process of permeating individuality with the universal. In that this consciousness finds this whole, however, to be merely the simple ultimate nature (Wesen) and thus the abstraction of " fact itself," the moments of this whole appear as distinct outside the " fact " and outside one another. As a single whole it is only exhaustively exhibited by the process of alternately exposing its elements to view and keeping them within itself.

plain: Against this inward shaping stands the factor of being, the all-encompassing awareness. For this latter, the essential reality is rather the universal and the obligatory. Individuality, which exists for its own sake and opposes the universal, holds only the worth of a passed phase. The awareness that stands with the fact of obligation regards the initial awareness as wicked, because its inner subjective life lacks alignment or oneness with the universal. Since the initial awareness simultaneously claims its action to be one with itself, to be obligation and sincerity, that all-encompassing awareness regards it as deceit. The path of this conflict begins with the formal restoration of the oneness between what the wicked awareness essentially is and what it claims to be. It must be shown that it is wicked, and its objective presence must be brought into alignment with its true nature; the deceit must be exposed.
original: Over against this internal determination there thus stands the element of existence, the universal consciousness; and for this latter it is rather universality, duty, which is the essential fact, while individuality, which exists for itself and is opposed to the imiversal, has merely the value of a superseded moment. The first consciousness is held to be Evil by the consciousness which thus stands by the fact of duty, because of the lack of congruity or identity of its internal subjective Ufe with the universal; and since at the same time the first consciousness declares its act to be identity with itself, to be duty and conscientiousness, it is held by that universal consciousness to be Uyfocrisy. The course taken by this opposition is, in the first instance, the formal reinstatement of the identity between what the evil consciousness is in its own nature and what it declares itself to be. It has to be made manifest that it is evil, and its objective existence thus made congruent with its real nature; the hypocrisy must be unmasked.

plain: Once we stop treating divine existence as a starting assumption and instead derive it through reasoning, self-awareness begins to turn inward. This shift introduces the inquiry into whether God exists, whereas the previously central question was what God is. Consequently, the ontological argument, which serves as the first strictly metaphysical demonstration of divine existence, now signifies that God, conceived as the idea of existence that encompasses all reality, also possesses actual existence within himself. This proof derives from the concept of God as the universal essence underlying all essences. Anselm outlines the logic of this argument in the second chapter of his *Proslogium*. He argues that there is a distinct difference between having a concept in the mind and recognizing that it exists in reality. Even a foolish person can be convinced that there is something in the mind beyond which nothing greater can be conceived. When such a person hears this description, they understand it, and anything understood resides in the mind. However, the thing beyond which nothing greater can be conceived cannot exist solely in the mind. If we assume it exists only in thought, we can proceed to assume it exists in reality, which represents a greater state than mere thought.
original: Thus if the existence of God is once abandoned as the first hypothesis, and established as a result of thought, self-consciousness is on the way to turn back within itself. Then we have the question coming in, Does God exist? while on the other side the question of most importance was, What is God? The ontological proof, which is the first properly metaphysical proof of the existence of God, consequently came to mean that God as the Idea of existence which unites all reality in itself, also has the reality of existence within Himself; this proof thus follows from the Notion of God, that He is the universal essence of all essence. The drift of this reasoning is, according to Anselm (Proslogium, c. 2), as follows: “It is one thing to say that a thing is in the understanding, and quite another to perceive that it exists. Even an ignorant person (insipiens) will thus be quite convinced that in thought there is something beyond which nothing greater can be thought; for when he hears this he understands it, and everything that is understood is in the understanding. But that beyond which nothing greater can be thought cannot certainly be in the understanding alone. For if it is accepted as in thought alone, we may go on farther to accept it as existent; that, however, is something greater” than what is merely thought.

plain: Deception ends up in the care of worried, anxious old age, whose concerns are limited to the specific details of daily life. The pure ideas of the Beautiful and the Good now present a comic scene. By being freed from opinion, which holds both their specific content and their absolute definition, and by losing the firm grasp that consciousness had on them, these ideas become empty. Consequently, they become the plaything of the private views and whims of any random individual. Here, Fate, which previously lacked awareness and consisted only of stillness and forgetting, is joined with self-consciousness. The individual self acts as the negative power through which the gods, along with their aspects—nature as an existing fact and the thoughts defining their specific traits—vanish and cease to be. Yet, the individual self is not just the emptiness of that vanishing. It maintains itself within that very nothingness, clings to itself, and stands as the only true reality. The religion of art reaches its completion and fulfillment in this state, having come full circle.
original: of deception into the hands of solicitous and apprehensive old age, restricted in its interests to the individual details of hfe. The pure thoughts of the Beautiful and the Good thus display a comic spectacle: — through their being set free from opinion, which contains both their determinateness in the sense of content and also their absolute determinateness, the firm hold of consciousness upon them, they become empty, and, on that very accoimt, the sport of the private opinion and caprice of any chance individuahty. Here, then, the Fate, formerly without consciousness, consisting in mere rest and forgetfulness, and separated from self-consciousness, is united with self-consciousness. The individual self is the negative force through which and in which the gods, as also their moments, (nature as existent fact and the thoughts of their determinate characters), pass away and disappear. At the same time, the individual self •• is not the mere vacuity of disappearance, but preserves itself in this very nothingness, holds to itself and is the sole and only reality. The rehgion of art is fulfilled and consummated in it, and is come full circle.

plain: Every sphere functions as a triad, meaning each abstract moment within this triad is also understood as a complete whole. Truth belongs only to that which reveals itself while maintaining its unity. The Alexandrian thinkers depict the concrete whole in its own right and recognize the essence of spirit. Yet, they fail to emerge from the profound depths of infinite subjectivity and its absolute void, nor do they grasp the absolute, or, if preferred, the abstract liberty of the "I" as the infinite worth of the subject. Therefore, the Neo-Platonic perspective is not a philosophical anomaly, but rather a progression of the human intellect, the world, and the world-spirit. The disclosure of God did not arrive from an external, foreign origin. What appears to us here as dry and abstract is actually concrete. Critics claim that what we examine in our studies, where philosophers debate and arbitrarily decide matters one way or another, consists merely of verbal abstractions. On the contrary, these are the actions of the world-spirit, and thus of destiny. In this work, philosophers stand closer to God than those raised on mere spiritual fragments; they read or write the commands exactly as they receive them in their original form, and they must keep writing.
original: But each sphere is a trinity in itself, so that each of the abstract moments of this triad is itself likewise grasped as a totality. Only that which manifests itself, and therein retains itself as the one, is held to be true. The Alexandrians thus represent the concrete totality in itself, and they have recognized the nature of spirit; they have, however, neither gone forth from the depths of infinite subjectivity and its absolute chasm, nor have they grasped the absolute, or, if we will, abstract freedom of the “I” as the infinite value of the subject. The Neo-Platonic standpoint is thus not a philosophic freak, but a forward advance on the part of the human mind, the world and the world-spirit. The revelation of God has not come to it as from an alien source. What we here consider so dry and abstract is concrete. “Such rubbish,” it is said, “as we consider when in our study we see philosophers dispute and argue, and settle things this way and that at will, are verbal abstractions only.” No, no; they are the deeds of the world-spirit, gentlemen, and therefore of fate. The philosophers are in so doing nearer to God than those nurtured upon spiritual crumbs; they read or write the orders as they receive them in the original; they are obliged to continue writing on.

ref: Artistic Beauty, The End of Art
plain: Philosophy offers a deep understanding of the core conflict by revealing that truth consists solely in resolving that conflict. This resolution does not deny the existence of the conflict or its opposing sides; rather, it acknowledges them as existing within a state of reconciliation. (d) Just as moral progress implies a superior perspective, we must establish that same superior perspective for art. Doing so immediately rejects the mistaken view, previously noted, that art exists merely to serve moral goals. It is wrong to claim that art contributes to the world’s moral good through teaching and ethical betterment, thereby locating its true purpose outside itself and in something external. Consequently, if we continue to discuss goals or purposes, we must first discard the flawed notion that asking "What is the aim?" secretly retains the secondary meaning of "What is the utility?".
original: All that philosophy does is to furnish a reflective insight into the essence of the antithesis in as far as it shows that what constitutes truth is merely the resolution of this antithesis, and that not in the sense that the conflict and its aspects in any way are not, but in the sense that they are, in reconciliation. (d) Now, as an ultimate aim implied a higher standpoint in the case of moral improvement, we shall have to vindicate this higher standpoint for art no less than for morals. Thereby we at once lay aside the false position, which has already been remarked upon, that art has to serve as a means for moral ends, and to conduce to the moral end of the world, as such, by instruction and moral improvement, and thereby has its substantive aim, not in itself, but in something else. If, therefore, we now continue to speak of an aim or purpose, we must, in the first instance, get rid of the perverse idea, which, in asking "What is the aim?" retains the accessory meaning of the question, "What is the use?".

plain: We find here, right away, force in its independent state, force held back within itself, and its outward display. We also see force acting as the starter and force acting as the one started. These aspects are not split apart or treated as two separate ends that merely oppose one another. Instead, their real character is simply to exist through the other. At first, they are nothing more than what they become through that mutual relationship, because that is exactly what they are. Consequently, they do not possess any independent substance that could hold them up or keep them going. The concept of force actually sustains itself as the core within its own reality. When force is real, it exists entirely and exclusively in its outward display. At the same time, this display is nothing but a process of negating itself. If we picture this real force as separated from its display and existing on its own, we are describing force turned back inward. However, this inward turn is, in reality, just one part of the force’s outward display, as shown earlier. Therefore, the true nature of force remains only the thought or idea of force. The stages in its realization, its independent substance, and its process, all merge without pause into a single, unbroken unity. This unity is not force pulled back into itself, since that is just one of the stages. Rather, it is the concept of force in its pure form.
original: We have there immediately both force as it is independently, force repressed within itself, and also its expression, force inciting and force being incited. These moments are thus not divided and set up as two extremes, offering each other only an opposite pole: rather their true nature is simply and solely to be each through the other, and to be in the first instance no more than just what each is thus through the other, since it is just that. They have thus, in point of fact, no substances of their own which could support and maintain them. The notion of force rather maintains itself as the essence in its very actuality: force when actual exists wholly and only in its expression; and this, at the same time, is nothing else than a process of cancelling itself. This actual force, when represented as detached from its expression and existing by itself, is force driven back into itself; but this feature is itself, in point of fact, as appears from the foregoing, merely a moment in the expression of force. The true nature of force thus remains merely the thought or idea of force; the moments in its realisation, its substantial independence and its process, rush, without let or hindrance, together into one single undivided unity, a unity which is not force withdrawn into itself (for this is merely one of those moments), but is its notion qua notion.

plain: Light, understood in both physical and spiritual terms, implies a rise above the purely natural. Humans relate to Light, or the Abstract Good, as an objective reality that they recognize, respect, and call into action through their will. If we review the stages we have covered to reach this point, we see that China presents a complete moral whole, yet it lacks subjectivity. This whole is split into parts, but those parts lack independence. We observed only an external structure for this political unity. In contrast, India highlights distinctions, but the principle of separation lacks spirit. We detected emerging subjectivity, yet it is constrained by the condition that this separation cannot be overcome. Spirit remains trapped within natural limits, creating a self-contradiction. Above the purity of castes stands the purity of Light seen in Persia. This Abstract Good allows everyone equal access and offers equal sanctification to all. Consequently, unity now becomes a principle rather than an external tie of lifeless order. Because each person shares in this principle, they possess personal dignity. First, regarding geographical location, we observe China and India displaying what seems like a dim, half-aware brooding
original: Light, in a physical and spiritua sense, imports, therefore, elevation — freedom from the merely natural. Man sustains a relation to Lightto the Abstract Good — as to something objective, which is acknowledged, reverenced, and evoked to activity by his Will. If we look back once more, — and we cannot do so too frequently,— on the phases which we have traversed in arriving at this point, we perceive in China the totality of a moral Whole, but excluding subjectivity; — this totality divided into members, but without independence in its various portions. We found only an external arrangement of this political Unity. In India, on the contrary, distinctions made themselves prominent; but the principle of separation was unspiritual. We found incipient subjectivity, but hampered with the condition, that the separation in question is insurmountable; and that Spirit remains involved in the limitations of Nature, and is therefore a self-contradiction. Above this purity of Castes is that purity of Light which we observe in Persia; that Abstract Good, to which all are equally able to approach, and in which all equally may be hallowed. The Unity recognized therefore, now first becomes a principle, not an external bond of soulless order. The fact that every one has a share in that principle, secures to him personal dignity. plain: Treating conscious individuality as a specific phenomenon and handling it with such rigidity creates a logical contradiction, since the core essence of individuality resides within the universal aspect of mind. However, the act of grasping this concept simultaneously transforms it into a universal form. Therefore, to understand it is to discover its governing law, which appears to serve a rational aim and fulfill a required role. The components that make up this law consist, on one side, of individuality itself, and on the other, of its universal, non-living nature, such as existing conditions, circumstances, habits, customs, and religion. A specific individual must be interpreted and understood through these factors. These elements possess both particular, definite characteristics and universal qualities. They are also immediately available, providing data for observation, while simultaneously manifesting themselves through the form of individuality.
original: To take conscious individuahty, on the other hand, as a particular phenomenal entity, and treat it in so wooden a fashion, is self-contradictory, because the essential nature of individuality Ues in the universal element of mind. Since, however, the process of apprehending it causes it at the same time to pass into the form of universahty, to apprehend it is to find its law, and seems in this way to have a rational purpose in view, and a necessary function to fulfil. The moments constituting the content of the law are on the one hand individuality itself, on the other its universal inorganic nature, viz. the given circumstances, situation, habits, customs, rehgion, and so forth; from these the determinate individuahty is to be understood and comprehended. They contain something specific, determinate, as well as universal, and are at the same time something lying at hand, which furnishes material for observation and on the other side expresses itself in the form of individuahty.

plain: Mental development moves from the unique character of a thing, through a state where that character is ignored, to the realm of amount. In math, circles, ellipses, and parabolas are distinct types, yet the difference between them is only a matter of degree, specifically a numerical change in their coefficients. Within the category of property, the numerical aspect that emerges from the qualitative is called value. The qualitative side dictates the amount, so it remains present even as it is overcome. When we look at the idea of value, the object is seen merely as a marker, valued not for its own nature but for its worth. A bank note, for instance, is not just a piece of paper; it serves as a symbol for a broader concept, which is its stated monetary amount. The particular worth of an item shifts based on need, but to express general worth, we rely on currency.
original: Thought in its progress starts from the special quality of an object, passes through indifference with regard to the quality, and finally reaches quantity. So in mathematics the circle, ellipse and parabola are specifically different, and yet the distinction of one curve from another is merely quantitative, being reduced to a mere quantitative difference in the largeness of their coefficients. In property the quantitative aspect, which issues from the qualitative, is value. The qualitative determines the quantum, however, and is therefore quite as much retained as superseded. When we consider the conception of value, the object is regarded only as a sign, counting not for what it is but for what it is worth. A letter of credit, e.g., is not a kind of paper, but a sign of another universal, namely, its face value. The specific value of an object varies according to the want, but in order to express abstract worth, we use money.

plain: A self-assured spirit, taking the shape of a "beautiful soul," lacks the ability to let go of its isolated, non-communicative self-knowledge. Because it refuses to release this grip, it fails to merge with the consciousness it rejects. Consequently, it cannot perceive the unity of its own self within another life, nor can it achieve objective existence. Therefore, any equality that emerges is purely negative, representing a state stripped of spiritual quality. The "beautiful soul" thus lacks concrete reality. It persists within the tension between its pure self and the pressure this self feels to externalize itself and become actual. It dwells in the immediate, fixed opposition of this tension. This immediacy serves as the sole middle term, mediating and reconciling an opposition that has reached pure abstraction, which is equivalent to pure being or empty nothingness. Since the "beautiful soul" remains aware of this contradiction in its unreconciled immediacy, it becomes unstable, disordered, and descends into madness. It fades away in longing and is consumed by pining starvation. In doing so, it factually abandons its rigid claim to separate, independent existence. However, this abandonment only produces the soulless, spiritless unity of abstract being.
original: Now, so far as the spirit which is certain of itself, in the form of a " beautiful soul," does not possess the faculty of relinquishing the self-absorbed uncommunicative knowledge of itself, it cannot attain to any identity with the consciousness that is repulsed, and so cannot succeed in seeing the unity of its self in another hfe, cannot reach objective existence. The equahty comes about, therefore, merely in a negative way, as a state of being devoid of spiritual character. The "beautiful soul," then, has no concrete reahty; it subsists in the contradiction between its pure self and the necessity felt by this self to externalise itself and turn into something actual; it exists in the immediacy of this rooted and fixed opposition, an immediacy which alone is the middle term mediating and reconciling an opposition which has arisen to its pure abstraction, and is pure being or empty nothingness. Thus the " beautiful soul," being conscious of this contradiction in its unreconciled immediacy, is unhinged, disordered, and runs to madness, passes away in yearning, and is consimied in pining inanition. Thereby it gives up, as a fact, its stubborn insistence on its own isolated self-existence, but only to bring forth the soulless, spiritless unity of abstract being.

plain: It is necessary to concede that a deep, philosophical artistic intuition preceded formal philosophy. This intuition demanded and articulated the principle of totality and reconciliation. It stood against the abstract, unending character of reflective thinking. It also opposed duty pursued merely for itself and intelligence lacking plastic form. Such abstract views treat nature, reality, sensation, and feeling as mere boundaries and as fundamentally antagonistic elements. Schiller deserves significant credit for overcoming the subjectivity and abstract quality of Kantian thought. He attempted to surpass these boundaries. He did this by intellectually apprehending the principles of unity and reconciliation as true. He then embodied these principles within art. In his aesthetic writings, Schiller did not simply focus on art and its specific interests. He also examined its connection to proper philosophy. He contrasted his concern for artistic beauty with philosophical principles. Only by beginning with these principles and utilizing their assistance did he uncover the deeper nature and concept of the beautiful. Consequently, we observe a characteristic in a specific phase of his output. He engaged extensively with thought. He perhaps did so to a degree that hindered the unadorned beauty of his artistic creations.
original: And so it must be admitted that the artistic sense of a profound, and, at the same time, philosophic mind was beforehand with philosophy as such, in demanding and enunciating the principle of totality and reconciliation as against that abstract endlessness of reflective thought, that duty for duty's sake, that intelligence devoid of plastic shape, which apprehend nature and reality, sensation and feeling as a mere limit, and as an absolutely hostile element. For Schiller must be credited with the great merit of having broken through the Kantian subjectivity and abstractness of thought, and having dared the attempt to transcend these limits by intellectually grasping the principles of unity and reconciliation as the truth, and realizing them in art. Schiller, in his æsthetic discussions, did not simply adhere to art and its interest without concerning himself about its relation to philosophy proper, but compared his interest in artistic beauty with the principles of philosophy; and it was only by starting from the latter, and by their help that he penetrated the profounder nature and notion of the beautiful. Thus we feel it to be a feature in one period of his works that he has busied himself with thought--more perhaps than was conducive to their unsophisticated beauty as works of art.

plain: This core conflict inherent in labor reveals the truth about individuality, which mistakenly believes itself to be fundamentally real. Consequently, every aspect of individuality reappears as contradictory. Labor constitutes the substance of the whole individuality expressed through action. Action serves as the negative unity that encompasses all elements. However, once labor gains existence, it releases these elements. As existing things, they remain indifferent to one another. The concept and its reality split into purpose and original essential nature. It is accidental whether the purpose possesses true being or whether the implicit inherent nature becomes a purpose. Likewise, the concept and reality divide into the transition to actuality and the purpose. It is accidental that the means expressing the purpose are actually selected. Finally, whether these internal moments possess intrinsic unity or not, the individual’s action remains accidental regarding actuality in general. Chance favors poorly defined purposes and poorly chosen means just as much as it opposes them.
original: In this fundamental contradiction characteristic of work — which contains the truth of this individuahty that takes itself to be inherently real — all the aspects of individuality thus appear again as contradictory. In other words, work, being the content of the entire individuality put forth by action, which is the negative unity and holds in its grasp all the elements, now sets them free, when it is given existence. As subsisting, they stand indifferently over against each other. The notion and its reality are thus separated into purpose and the original essential nature (Wesenheit). It is an accident that the purpose should have a true being, or that the implicit inherent nature should be made a purpose. Similarly, again, notion and reality fall apart as transition to actuality and as purpose; in other words, it is an accident that the means expressing the purpose should actually be chosen. While, finally, should these inner moments taken together have some intrinsic unity or not, the action of the individual is once more an accident so far as actuahty in general is concerned: fortune decides in favour of a badly determined purpose, and badly selected means, just as much as against them.

plain: We could broaden the concept of "aberration" past the subject's mere mental imagery and the actual state they contradict, labeling this perspective on property a personality aberration. If these connections held nothing beyond the understanding's formal distinctions, we would face an owner against a hollow master, rather than two masters. However, because of levies or duties, two owners exist in relation to one another, even without sharing a common holding. This dynamic marks the shift from ownership to utilization. This shift is already active when ownership, previously seen as more prestigious, takes a back seat, while the utility or yield of direct dominion is viewed as the core and logical element. This universal trait, which stems from the specific item but ignores its unique features, is value. Value represents the object's genuine essence or substance, and by having value, the item becomes a target for awareness. As the full holder of the item, I possess both its value and its utility. The feudal tenant holds only the right to use, not the value. Here, quality transforms into quantity. Need is a concept shared by the widest range of items, allowing me to measure them against each other.
original: If we could extend the term " aberration " beyond the mere imagination of the subject, and the reality, with which he is directly at variance, we might call such a view of property an aberration of personality. If these relations contained no more that the formal distinction of the understanding, there would be opposed to each other not two masters (domini), but an owner and an empty master. But by virtue of the charges or taxes it is two owners, who stand in relation to each other, though they are not related by a common possession. In this relation is to be found the transition from property to use, a transition already operating when ownership, which was formerly reckoned as the more honourable, is given a secondary place, while the utile or produce of a dominium directum is regarded as the essential and rational. This universal characteristic, which proceeds from the particular object and yet abstracts from its special qualities is the value. Value is the true essence or substance of the object, and the object by possessing value becomes an object for consciousness. As complete owner of the object, I am owner of its value as well as of its use. The feudal tenant is the owner of use only, not of the value. Quality here becomes quantity. Want is a term common to the greatest variety of things, and enables me to compare them.

plain: This marks a sharper break between the soul, understood as pure self-focus, and its prior state of natural, direct existence. It no longer shares an immediate identity with bodily nature; instead, the external body must first be brought into that role. Specific feelings can only take physical form in a very precise manner. The immediate part of the body serves as a specific possibility for a particular goal, representing a distinct aspect of its differentiated structure or a specific organ within its organic system. Shaping such a goal within the organic body reveals and expresses the “ideality” that is always latent in matter, particularly in that specific bodily part. This process allows the soul, characterized by its volitional and conceptual nature, to exist as substance within its corporeity. Consequently, an aptitude demonstrates that the body has become fully permeable and transformed into a tool. Thus, when a conception, such as a sequence of musical notes, resides in me, the body produces them accurately and effortlessly, without any resistance.
original: Thus comes out the more decided rupture between the soul as simple self-concentration, and its earlier naturalness and immediacy; it has lost its original and immediate identity with the bodily nature, and as external has first to be reduced to that position. Specific feelings can only get bodily shape in a perfectly specific way; and the immediate portion of body is a particular possibility for a specific aim (a particular aspect of its differentiated structure, a particular organ of its organic system). To mould such an aim in the organic body is to bring out and express the “ideality” which is implicit in matter always, and especially so in the specific bodily part, and thus to enable the soul, under its volitional and conceptual characters, to exist as substance in its corporeity. In this way an aptitude shows the corporeity rendered completely pervious, made into an instrument, so that when the conception (e.g. a series of musical notes) is in me, then without resistance and with ease the body gives them correct utterance.

plain: The Protestant Church strengthened and secured its political standing because one state that embraced Reformation principles rose to become an independent European power. This power was set to find a new vitality through Protestantism: specifically, Prussia, which emerged at the close of the seventeenth century. While its origins may not be entirely due to this, the consolidation of its strength was certainly owed to Frederick the Great. The Seven Years' War served as the conflict through which that consolidation was achieved. Frederick II proved the independent vigor of his state by standing against the combined forces of nearly all Europe, including its leading nations. He emerged as the champion of Protestantism, not just as an individual figure like Gustavus Adolphus, but as the sovereign of a state. Although the Seven Years' War was not inherently a religious conflict, it functioned as one in terms of its final outcomes and the mindset of both the soldiers and the rulers under whose flags they fought. The Pope consecrated the weapon of Field-Marshal Daun, and the primary goal of the Allied Powers was to crush Prussia, viewing it as the fortress of the Protestant Church. However, Frederick the Great not only established Prussia as a major European Protestant power, but he was also a philosophical king—a completely unique and singular phenomenon in modern history.
original: The Protestant Church increased and so perfected the stability of its political existence by the fact that one of the states which had adopted the principles of the Reformation raised itself to the position of an independent European power. This power was destined to start into a new life with Protestantism: Prussia, viz., which making its appearance at the end of the seventeenth century, was indebted, if not for origination, yet certainly for the consolidation of its strength, to Frederick the Great; and the Seven Tears' War was the struggle by which that consolidation was accomplished. Frederick II. demonstrated the independent vigour of his power by resisting that of almost all Europe — the union of its leading states. He appeared as the hero of Protestantism, and that not individually merely, like Gustavus Adolphus, but as the ruler of a state. The Seven Years' War was indeed in itself not a war of religion; but it was so in view of its ultimate issues, and in the disposition of the soldiers as well as of the potentates under whose banner they fought. The Pope consecrated the sword of Field-Marshal Daun, and the chief object which the Allied Powers proposed to themselves, was the crushing of Prussia as the bulwark of the Protestant Church. But Frederick the Great not only made Prussia one of the great powers of Europe as a Protestant power, but was also a philosophical King — an altogether peculiar and unique phenomenon in modern times.

plain: Consciousness recognizes that this feature belongs to it and accepts that ownership. Through this acceptance, consciousness obtains the genuine object in its pure form. Here, in the realm of perception, the aspect of consciousness is driven back onto itself, just as occurred with sensuous certainty. However, this return differs from the earlier instance. In that previous case, the truth of perception was contained within the aspect. Now, consciousness recognizes that the falsehood emerging there resides within it. By recognizing this, consciousness can negate and overcome that falsehood. It separates its grasp of the truth from the falsehood inherent in its perception. It amends that falsehood. To the extent that consciousness undertakes this amendment, the truth, specifically as the truth of perception, does indeed reside within its own consciousness.
original: Consciousness is aware that this aspect is at the same time its own, and takes it upon itself; and by so doing consciousness will thus get the true object bare and naked. In this way we have, now, in the case of perception, as happened in the case of sensuous certainty, the aspect of consciousness being forced back upon itself; but, in the first instance, not in the sense in which Perception.113 this took place in the former case — i.e. not as if the truth of perception fell within it. Rather consciousness is aware that the untruth, that comes out there, falls within it. By knowing this, however, consciousness is able to cancel and supersede this untruth. It distinguishes its apprehension of the truth from the untruth of its perception, corrects this untruth, and, so far as itself takes in hand to make this correction, the truth, qua truth of perception, certainly falls within its own consciousness.

plain: The household shields the deceased from degradation caused by unconscious biological drives and abstract elements. It substitutes its own deeds for these forces, joining the person with the earth, an elemental identity that remains. Thus, the household integrates the dead into a community that dominates and restrains specific material elements and lower creatures. These entities had attempted to exploit the dead and ruin him. This final obligation completes the divine law, or creates the positive ethical deed directed at the given individual. Other relationships with him that exceed mere love and become ethical fall under human law. They carry the negative significance of elevating the individual above the bounds of the natural group to which he attaches as a concrete being. Yet, although human law gains its substance and strength from the actual ethical substance that knows itself, namely the entire nation, divine law and right obtain theirs from the particular individual beyond the actual. Nevertheless, he is not impotent.
original: The family keeps away from the dead this dishonouring of him by the desires of unconscious organic agencies and by abstract elements, puts its own action in place of theirs, and weds the relative to the bosom of the earth, the elemental individuality that passes not away. Thereby the family makes the dead a member of a community f which prevails over and holds under control the powers of the particular material elements and the lower hving creatures, which sought to have their way with the dead and destroy him. This last duty thus accomplishes the complete divine law, or constitutes the positive ethical act towards the given individual. Every other relation towards him which does not remain at the level of love, but is ethical, belongs to human law, and has the negative significance of- lifting the individual above the confinement within the natural community to which he belongs as a concrete individual. But, now, though hmnan right has for its content and power the actual ethical substance consciously aware of itself, the entire nation, while divine right and law derive theirs from the particular individual who is beyond the actual, yet he is stni not without power.

plain: To clarify the gap between thinking and existence, he used the example of one hundred coins. For the concept itself, it makes no difference whether these coins actually exist or merely could exist, even though the impact on a person’s wallet is clearly distinct in the two scenarios. It is self-evident that just because we imagine or grasp something in our minds, it does not thereby become real. Mental images and conceptual understanding always remain separate from actual existence. However, it is arguably a linguistic error to apply the term "notion" to concrete items like a stack of coins. Once we correct that misuse, those who constantly oppose the philosophical Idea by highlighting the gap between existence and thought should acknowledge that philosophers were not completely unaware of this distinction. Is there a more common statement than this? Nevertheless, it is important to recall that when discussing God, we are dealing with a subject fundamentally different from a pile of coins, and unlike any specific concept, image, or whatever label one might attach to it.
original: To explain the difference between thought and being, he took the instance of a hundred sovereigns, which, for anything it matters to the notion, are the same hundred whether they are real or only possible, though the difference of the two cases is very perceptible in their effect on a man's purse. Nothing can be more obvious than that anything we only think or conceive is not on that account actual: that mental representation, and even notional comprehension, always falls short of being. Still it may not unfairly be styled a barbarism in language, when the name of notion is given to things like a hundred sovereigns. And, putting that mistake aside, those who perpetually urge against the philosophic Idea the difference between Being and Thought, might have admitted that philosophers were not wholly ignorant of the fact. Can there be any proposition more trite than this? But after all, it is well to remember, when we speak of God, that we have an object of another kind than any hundred sovereigns, and unlike any one particular notion, representation, or however else it may be styled.

ref: The Roman World, Rome to the Second Punic War
plain: The unique way the state was established serves as the fundamental root of Rome’s distinct character. This origin demands the harshest discipline and personal sacrifice for the greater goal of unity. A state that had to build itself from scratch and rests on power must rely on power to stay together. The result is not a voluntary, ethical bond, but a forced state of subordination. Roman *virtus* means courage; specifically, it is not just individual bravery, but a quality tied to the group of partners. This group is seen as the highest priority, even if it involves any kind of lawless aggression. Although the Romans created such a group, they did not face an internal fight with a conquered population, unlike the Spartans. Instead, a divide and conflict emerged between the Patricians and the Plebeians. This split was symbolically foreshadowed by the warring brothers Romulus and Remus. Remus was interred on the Aventine hill, a place dedicated to evil spirits, where the Plebeians held their secessions. The question arises: how did this division begin? As previously noted, Rome was built by bandit shepherds and a gathering of various outcasts. Later, people from towns that were seized and razed were also brought to the city.
original: It is this peculiarity in the founding of the State which must be regarded as'the essential basis of the idiosyncrasy of Home. For it directly involves the severest discipline, and self-sacrifice to the grand object of the union. A State which had first to form itself, and which is based on force, must be held together by force. It is not a moral, liberal connection, but a compulsory condition of subordination, that results from such an origin. The Roman virtus is valour; • not, however, the merely personal, but that which is essentially connected with a union of associates; which union is regarded as the supreme interest, and may be combined with lawless violence of all kinds. While the Romans formed a union of this kind, they were not, indeed, like the Lacedaemonians, engaged in an internal contest with a conquered and subjugated people; but there arose a distinction and a struggle between Patricians and Plebeians. This distinction, was mythically adumbrated in the hostile brothers, Romulus and Remus. Remus was buried on the Aventine mount; this is consecrated to the evil genii, and to it are directed the Secessions of the Plebs. The question comes, then, how this distinction originated?. It has been already said, that Rome was formed by robber-herdsmen, and the concourse of rabble of all sorts. At a later date, the inhabitants of captured and destroyed towns were also conveyed thither.

ref: Rome from the Second Punic War to the Emperors
plain: Caesar took control of Italy, Spain, and Greece one after another. He completely defeated his rival at Pharsalus in 48 B.C. He secured control of Asia and then went back to Rome as a winner. Through these actions, global Roman rule ended up in the hands of one person. We should not see this major shift as random. It was required by the conditions at the time. The democratic system in Rome could no longer function in reality, only in name. Cicero earned high regard for his skill in speaking. His knowledge gave him significant power. He consistently blamed the decay of the republic on specific people and their desires. Plato, whom Cicero claimed to follow, fully understood that the Athenian government, as he saw it, could not survive. Because of this, he outlined a model of a perfect government based on his ideas. Cicero, however, did not think it was impossible to keep the Roman Republic alive. He only asked for some short-term help during its difficult times. He failed to grasp the true nature of the state, and especially the Roman state. Cato also spoke about Caesar. He said that Caesar’s good qualities were to be hated because they had destroyed his country.
original: Caesar made himself master in succession, of Italy, Spain, and Greece, utterly routed his enemy at Pharsalus, forty-eight years.B.C., made himself sure of Asia, and so returned victor to Rome. In this way the world-wide sovereignty of Rome became the property of a single possessor. This important change must not be regarded as a thing of chance; it was necessary — postulated by the circumstances. The democratic constitution could no longer be really maintained in Home, but only kept up in appearance. Cicero, who had procured himself great respect through his high oratorical talent, and whose learning acquired him considerable influence, always attributes the corrupt state of the republic to individuals and their passions. Plato, whom Cicero professedly followed, had the full consciousness that the Athenian state, as it presented itself to him, could not maintain its existence, and therefore sketched the plan of a perfect constitution accordant with his views. Cicero, on the contrary, does not consider it impossible to preserve the Roman [Republic, and only desiderates some temporary assistance for it in its adversity. The nature of the State, and of the Roman State in particular, transcends his comprehension. Cato, too, says of Caesar: " His virtues be execrated, for they have ruined my country!

plain: It fails to grasp the connection between them, even when that connection has been clearly defined. For instance, it ignores the true nature of the linking verb in a statement. This verb asserts that the specific subject is, in reality, not unique but rather general. Furthermore, the understanding mistakenly treats its own mental activity as something external. It assumes that the self-same concept holds its own opposite or internal conflict, yet it views this as an outside reflection rather than an internal feature of the concept itself. In truth, this reflection is not a special trick of the understanding. The concept itself is the dialectical process that constantly separates and distinguishes the self-same from the varied, the subjective from the objective, and the limited from the unlimited, as well as spirit from matter. Only under these conditions does it become an endless creation, an endless life force, and an endless spirit. Although the concept shifts or transforms into the abstract understanding, it remains reason throughout. The concept is the dialectical force that causes this collection of understanding and variety to recognize its limited nature and the false independence of its creations. It then leads this variety back to a single unity. Because this two-way movement is not separated in time or in any other manner—otherwise it would merely repeat the abstract understanding—the concept is the eternal sight of itself in the other. It is the idea that has realized itself in its objective form, and the object that serves as the inner plan and essential subjectivity.
original: It no less mistakes the relation between them, ever when it has been expressly stated. Thus, for example it overlooks even the nature of the copula in the judgment, which affirms that the individual, or subject, is after all not individual, but universal. But, in the second place, the understanding believes its 'reflection,'--that the self-identical Idea contains its own negative, or contains contradiction,--to be an external reflection which does not lie within the Idea itself. But the reflection is really no peculiar cleverness of the understanding. The Idea itself is the dialectic which for ever divides and distinguishes the self-identical from the differentiated, the subjective from the objective, the finite from the infinite, soul from body. Only on these terms is it an eternal creation, eternal vitality, and eternal spirit. But while it thus passes or rather translates itself into the abstract understanding, it for ever remains reason. The Idea is the dialectic which again makes this mass of understanding and diversity understand its finite nature and the pseudo-independence in its productions, and which brings the diversity back to unity. Since this double movement is not separate or distinct in time, nor indeed in any other way--otherwise it would be only a repetition of the abstract understanding--the Idea is the eternal vision of itself in the other, --notion which in its objectivity has carried out itself,--object which is inward design, essential subjectivity.

plain: He largely moves through a sequence of the living and the dead, forcing them to face his objective, which is thinking thought, and he captures them within his comprehension. Every object is, in itself, a concept that is revealed through its specific traits, yet he also gathers these reflections together, and in doing so, he becomes speculative. Even if Plato generally worked in an empirical manner, picking up various ideas and examining each one in turn, this loose approach to procedure becomes even more evident with Aristotle. In Aristotle’s teaching, the concept of self-reflecting thought is thus understood as the ultimate truth; however, its actualization, the understanding of the natural and spiritual world, forms a lengthy list of specific concepts outside of that concept. These specific concepts are separate from one another, and they lack a unifying principle that runs through the particulars. Therefore, the highest concept in Aristotle’s work again exists merely as a specific item in its own right, without serving as the principle for his entire philosophy. Consequently, the next requirement in philosophy is that the full scope of what is known must appear as a single structure of the Concept. In this way, the diverse reality can be connected to that concept as the universal, and thereby defined.
original: He in great measure passes through a series of the living and the dead, makes them confront his objective, that is, conceiving thought, and grasps them in his understanding; each object is on its own account a conception which is laid open in its determinations, and yet he also brings these reflections together, and thereby is speculative. If even Plato on the whole proceeded in an empiric way, taking up this and that idea, each of which is in turn examined, with Aristotle this loose method of procedure appears still more clearly. In the Aristotelian teaching the Idea of the self-reflecting thought is thus grasped as the highest truth; but its realization, the knowledge of the natural and spiritual universe, constitutes outside of that Idea a long series of particular conceptions, which are external to one another, and in which a unifying principle, led through the particular, is wanting. The highest Idea with Aristotle consequently once more stands only as a particular in its own place and without being the principle of his whole philosophy. Hence the next necessity in Philosophy is that the whole extent of what is known must appear as one organization of the Notion; that in this way the manifold reality may be related to that Idea as the universal, and thereby determined.

plain: This principle possesses the boundless flexibility of the absolute shape, allowing it to overcome the corruption of that shape and its contents. It thereby achieves the spirit’s self-reconciliation. Consequently, in the Protestant conscience, the bases of religious and ethical awareness merge into a single entity. This unified entity is the free spirit recognizing its own rationality and truth. Within the Protestant state, the constitution, legal codes, and their specific implementations reflect the principle and growth of moral existence. This moral existence flows solely from religious truth. That truth must be restored to its foundational source to become genuinely real. Therefore, the state’s moral life and its religious spirit serve as mutual sources of strength. The concept of mind finds its actuality within the mind itself. For this reality to exist as awareness of the absolute Idea, the inherently free intellect must be freed in its actual state to align with its concept. This alignment is necessary if that state is to be a fitting vessel for it. Subjective and objective spirit should be viewed as the path where this aspect of reality matures.
original: Still the principle has in it the infinite “elasticity” of the “absolute” form, so as to overcome this depraving of the form-determination (and of the content by these means), and to bring about the reconciliation of the spirit in itself. Thus ultimately, in the Protestant conscience the principles of the religious and of the ethical conscience come to be one and the same: the free spirit learning to see itself in its reasonableness and truth. In the Protestant state, the constitution and the code, as well as their several applications, embody the principle and the development of the moral life, which proceeds and can only proceed from the truth of religion, when reinstated in its original principle and in that way as such first become actual. The moral life of the state and the religious spirituality of the state are thus reciprocal guarantees of strength. The notion of mind has its reality in the mind. If this reality in identity with that notion is to exist as the consciousness of the absolute Idea, then the necessary aspect is that the implicitly free intelligence be in its actuality liberated to its notion, if that actuality is to be a vehicle worthy of it. The subjective and the objective spirit are to be looked on as the road on which this aspect of reality or existence rises to maturity.
